entities.variants: Puerperal (lactational) mastitis; non-puerperal mastitis; mastitis neonatorum; peripheral vs subareolar abscess
entities.remarks: Usually Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA increasingly) or Streptococcus via nipple fissures in early lactation; neutrophilic infiltrate, necrosis, abscess formation.
entities.histo: Acute mastitis and breast abscess usually follow nipple fissures in early lactation, with Staphylococcus aureus (increasingly MRSA) or streptococci the usual organisms. Grossly the tissue is indurated and erythematous, and an abscess forms a cavity containing pus with a shaggy necrotic wall. Microscopically there is a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in ducts, lobules and stroma, with liquefactive necrosis, fibrin, oedema and congested vessels, later rimmed by granulation tissue and histiocytes. Puerperal mastitis is lobular and lactational, with secretory change in the background. Non-puerperal and subareolar abscesses centre on large ducts and often show squamous metaplasia and keratin. Mastitis neonatorum occurs in infant breast buds under maternal hormonal influence. Peripheral abscesses are usually puerperal or associated with diabetes and immunosuppression. Differentials include inflammatory carcinoma (dermal lymphatic tumour emboli rather than neutrophils), granulomatous mastitis, cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis and infected cysts or galactocele, so persistent lesions merit biopsy and culture.
entities.cyto: FNA of acute mastitis or abscess yields thick purulent material with highly cellular smears dominated by neutrophils, many degenerate, admixed with histiocytes, fibrin and necrotic debris. Ductal epithelial cells, when present, are few and may show reactive nuclear enlargement, prominent nucleoli and occasional squamous metaplasia, which can mimic atypia. Bacteria may be visible on Gram stain, and material should be sent for culture. Pitfalls include necrotic or inflammatory carcinoma and abscessed cyst; persistent masses after drainage need re-aspiration or core biopsy. Usually categorised as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), or Category 3 if reactive atypia is marked.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry has essentially no diagnostic role in acute mastitis or breast abscess, which is a clinical and microbiological diagnosis supported by sheets of neutrophils, necrotic debris and granulation tissue. Gram stain and culture of pus are the relevant ancillary tests, and culture with sensitivity matters because MRSA is increasingly common. IHC becomes relevant only when a non-resolving 'abscess' raises concern for inflammatory or necrotic carcinoma: pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) highlights infiltrating carcinoma cells hidden within the inflammation, while CD68 or CD163 confirms that atypical-looking mononuclear cells are histiocytes. In older or non-lactating women with persistent inflammation, biopsy and keratin stains help exclude an underlying carcinoma.

entities.entity: Subareolar abscess / recurrent subareolar abscess (Zuska disease)
entities.variants: Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD); mammary duct (periareolar) fistula
entities.remarks: Keratinising squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts → keratin plugging, rupture, keratin granulomas, sinus tract opening at areolar margin; strongly associated with smoking.
entities.histo: Subareolar abscess (Zuska disease) results from squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD). It is strongly associated with smoking and tends to recur. Keratinising squamous epithelium replaces the normal two-layered lining of one or more lactiferous ducts deep to the nipple and forms keratin plugs that distend the duct. Rupture releases keratin into the periductal stroma, provoking an acute and chronic inflammatory reaction with abscess formation, foreign-body giant cells around keratin flakes (keratin granulomas) and granulation tissue. Recurrent episodes produce a fibrotic sinus tract or mammary duct fistula opening at the areolar margin, sometimes lined partly by squamous epithelium. Excision should include the involved duct up to the nipple to prevent recurrence. The differential includes periductal mastitis and duct ectasia (no squamous metaplasia), an epidermal inclusion cyst, and squamous cell carcinoma, from which it is separated by bland cytology and the absence of invasive nests.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of subareolar abscess (Zuska disease) characteristically show anucleate and nucleated keratinous squames, keratin debris and cholesterol crystals with neutrophils, foamy macrophages and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells reacting to keratin. Metaplastic squamous cells with reactive changes and parakeratosis may be seen, along with granulation tissue fragments. The main pitfall is over-calling reactive squamous atypia as squamous cell carcinoma or an epidermoid cyst with rupture; the clinical setting of a recurrent periareolar sinus in a smoker is helpful. Usually reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign).
entities.ihc: IHC plays only a supportive role in subareolar abscess (SMOLD). The diagnosis rests on keratinising squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, keratin plugging, duct rupture, and a foreign-body giant cell reaction to keratin with sinus formation. When needed, p63 and CK5/6 (or high-molecular-weight keratin 34βE12) confirm that the metaplastic epithelium is squamous and benign. Its bland maturation and lack of infiltration separate it from squamous cell carcinoma or metaplastic carcinoma, so keratin stains are not needed to look for invasion. CD68 highlights histiocytes and giant cells. Gram stain and culture address the mixed, often anaerobic, secondary infection. Molecular testing has no role.

entities.variants: Plasma cell mastitis (plasma-cell-rich variant)
entities.remarks: Periductal chronic inflammation ± duct rupture; overlaps with duct ectasia; smoking association; may mimic carcinoma clinically (nipple retraction, mass).
entities.histo: Periductal mastitis affects younger women, often smokers, and centres on subareolar ducts. It may present with a mass, pain, nipple retraction or discharge that clinically mimics carcinoma. Microscopically, ducts of normal or mildly increased calibre are surrounded by chronic inflammation composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells, sometimes with neutrophils. Duct rupture leads to periductal foamy histiocytes and giant cells, and later concentric periductal fibrosis. In the plasma-cell-rich variant (plasma cell mastitis), sheets of plasma cells dominate and can mimic lymphoma or plasmacytoma, but they are polytypic. The condition overlaps with mammary duct ectasia, which shows more marked dilatation and inspissated secretions in older women. Differentials include IgG4-related mastitis (storiform fibrosis, phlebitis, high IgG4 counts), subareolar abscess with squamous metaplasia, granulomatous lobular mastitis, which is lobulocentric rather than ductocentric, and carcinoma, which is excluded by the absence of infiltrating atypical epithelium.
entities.cyto: Periductal mastitis aspirates show a mixed inflammatory background of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and abundant foamy histiocytes, sometimes with multinucleated giant cells, amorphous proteinaceous secretion and occasional cholesterol crystals. Ductal epithelial cells are scanty, cohesive and bland, sometimes with apocrine or squamous metaplasia. Nipple discharge cytology shows foamy macrophages and inflammatory cells. Differentials include duct ectasia (overlapping spectrum), fat necrosis, granulomatous mastitis and, rarely, necrotic carcinoma; reactive epithelial atypia should not be over-interpreted. Usually Yokohama Category 2 (Benign).
entities.ihc: Periductal mastitis and its plasma-cell-rich variant are diagnosed on morphology: periductal chronic inflammation, foamy histiocytes, duct ectasia and periductal fibrosis. IHC has a limited role. CD68 or CD163 confirms foamy histiocytes and helps separate them from histiocytoid or lobular carcinoma cells, which are keratin-positive and E-cadherin-negative in the lobular case. Where plasma cells dominate, CD138 with kappa and lambda in situ hybridisation shows polyclonality and excludes a plasmacytoma or lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation. IgG and IgG4 counts with the IgG4:IgG ratio help exclude IgG4-related mastitis when fibrosis is storiform. Myoepithelial markers such as p63 show the intact outline of ectatic ducts when stromal distortion mimics invasion.

entities.remarks: Distinctive suppurative lipogranulomas with central clear (cystic) vacuoles rimmed by neutrophils; Gram-positive bacilli (Corynebacterium spp., esp. C. kroppenstedtii) within vacuoles.
entities.histo: Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis is a distinctive pattern of granulomatous lobular mastitis in young, often parous women and is linked to Corynebacterium species, especially C. kroppenstedtii. Grossly there are firm areas with small abscesses. Microscopically the lesion is lobulocentric, and its hallmark is suppurative lipogranulomas: round, clear, empty-looking (cystic) vacuoles produced by dissolved lipid. Each vacuole is rimmed by a cuff of neutrophils and in turn by epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes and plasma cells. Sparse Gram-positive bacilli are found inside the vacuoles on a careful Gram stain, and culture or 16S PCR helps confirm the organism. Fat necrosis-like changes and fibrosis accompany the lesion. Differentials include idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis without vacuoles, tuberculous mastitis with caseation and acid-fast bacilli, fungal infection, fat necrosis and sarcoidosis. Prolonged lipophilic antibiotics are often needed.
entities.cyto: Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis shows cellular smears with epithelioid histiocyte clusters, multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes and numerous neutrophils, often around clear empty vacuoles representing lipid spaces. Gram-positive bacilli (Corynebacterium species) may occasionally be seen within these vacuoles on Gram stain, and culture is recommended though often negative. Necrosis is typically absent, helping separate it from tuberculosis. Differentials include idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, tuberculosis, fungal infection and abscess. Ductal cells may be reactive. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) with a descriptive comment suggesting the diagnosis and microbiological correlation.
entities.ihc: Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis has no specific immunohistochemical profile. The diagnosis rests on lipogranulomas with central clear vacuoles rimmed by neutrophils and epithelioid histiocytes. The key ancillary test is a Gram stain, which shows gram-positive bacilli (Corynebacterium species, especially C. kroppenstedtii) inside the clear vacuoles. Culture is often negative unless lipophilic media are used, and 16S rRNA PCR can identify the organism. CD68 and CD163 highlight the histiocytes but don't distinguish this from other granulomatous mastitides. Ziehl–Neelsen and GMS stains should be done to exclude mycobacteria and fungi. Pan-keratin is useful only if a carcinoma is a clinical concern.

entities.remarks: Lobulocentric non-necrotising granulomas with neutrophils/microabscesses; young parous women; diagnosis of exclusion (rule out TB, fungi, Corynebacterium, sarcoid).
entities.histo: Idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis typically affects young parous women within a few years of pregnancy and presents as a firm, sometimes painful mass, often with abscesses, sinus formation and skin changes that mimic carcinoma. Microscopically, non-necrotising granulomas are centred on lobules, with epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans and foreign-body giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells and frequent neutrophils forming microabscesses. Neighbouring granulomas coalesce and efface the lobular architecture, and lobular acini persist within the inflammation. Caseation is absent, although small foci of suppurative necrosis occur. The diagnosis is one of exclusion. Ziehl-Neelsen, Gram, GMS and PAS stains, together with culture and molecular tests such as GeneXpert, are needed to exclude tuberculosis, fungi and Corynebacterium. Vacuolated lipogranulomas point towards cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis. Sarcoidosis has naked granulomas and systemic disease, duct ectasia is ductocentric, and fat necrosis lacks lobulocentric granulomas.
entities.cyto: Idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis yields moderately to highly cellular smears with cohesive clusters of epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans and foreign-body giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells and often many neutrophils, sometimes forming microabscesses. Caseous necrosis is usually absent. Reactive ductal epithelial cells with mild atypia may be present and can be worrying. Ziehl-Neelsen, PAS/GMS and Gram stains plus culture are needed to exclude tuberculosis, fungi and Corynebacterium. Clinically and radiologically it may mimic carcinoma, so the absence of malignant cells must be correlated with imaging. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), granulomatous mastitis, with a comment on excluding infection.
entities.ihc: Idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis is a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific IHC. CD68 or CD163 highlights the lobulocentric non-necrotising granulomas, and keratin (AE1/AE3) can show the surviving lobular epithelium and confirm the lobulocentric pattern. The essential workup is histochemical and microbiological: Ziehl–Neelsen or auramine and PCR (GeneXpert) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, GMS and PAS for fungi, and a Gram stain to look for Corynebacterium, which would point to cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis. Serum ACE and clinical correlation address sarcoidosis. IgG4 immunostaining excludes IgG4-related disease when plasma cells and fibrosis are prominent. Lack of response or a mass should prompt correlation with imaging to exclude carcinoma.

entities.variants: Nodular, disseminated, sclerosing; primary vs secondary (spread from chest wall/axillary nodes)
entities.remarks: Caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells; AFB/ZN, CBNAAT/GeneXpert, culture; important differential in India; may mimic carcinoma.
entities.histo: Tuberculous mastitis is uncommon in the West but an important differential in India. It presents as a nodular, disseminated or sclerosing lesion, often with sinuses, axillary lymphadenopathy or an abscess that mimics carcinoma. It may be primary, or secondary to spread from the chest wall, ribs or axillary nodes. Grossly there are caseous, cheesy yellow areas or abscess cavities. Microscopically, epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and a lymphocytic cuff are present, many with central caseous necrosis, and they involve ducts, lobules and stroma rather than being strictly lobulocentric. The sclerosing form shows dense fibrosis with few granulomas, typically in elderly women. Acid-fast bacilli are scanty on Ziehl-Neelsen stain, so CBNAAT/GeneXpert, culture and correlation with chest imaging are often required. Differentials include idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis (lobulocentric, non-caseating, neutrophil-rich), fungal infection, sarcoidosis, fat necrosis and carcinoma with granulomatous reaction.
entities.cyto: Tuberculous mastitis aspirates show epithelioid cell granulomas, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes and, characteristically, granular eosinophilic caseous necrosis; in some cases necrosis with degenerated neutrophils predominates without well-formed granulomas. Ziehl-Neelsen staining may demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, though often scanty, and material should be sent for GeneXpert/culture where available. Differentials include idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, fat necrosis, fungal infection, sarcoidosis and carcinoma with granulomatous reaction. In endemic settings such as India this is an important diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), granulomatous inflammation consistent with tuberculosis when necrosis or AFB are present.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry does little in tuberculous mastitis beyond confirming that the giant cells and epithelioid cells are histiocytic (CD68+, CD163+). The diagnosis rests on caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells, plus confirmation of the organism. A Ziehl–Neelsen or auramine-rhodamine stain may show acid-fast bacilli, but the yield in breast tissue is low. GeneXpert MTB/RIF or another PCR on tissue, and mycobacterial culture, are more sensitive and also test for rifampicin resistance. Anti-MPT64 immunohistochemistry is a useful adjunct where it's available. GMS and PAS stains exclude fungi. Pan-keratin and E-cadherin help only if coexisting carcinoma needs to be excluded, for example in nodal disease.

entities.variants: Often post-implant / post-procedure / nipple-piercing related
entities.remarks: Granulomatous inflammation; rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. fortuitum, M. abscessus, M. chelonae); culture/molecular confirmation.
entities.histo: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial mastitis is usually caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria such as M. fortuitum, M. abscessus and M. chelonae. It follows implant surgery, other procedures, injections or nipple piercing, and presents as delayed wound infection, a periprosthetic abscess or draining sinuses. Microscopically there is mixed suppurative and granulomatous inflammation: microabscesses with neutrophils surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, often within lipid vacuoles or around implant capsules. Caseation is less typical than in tuberculosis. Acid-fast bacilli may be seen within clear vacuoles, but they are frequently sparse, and the Fite stain can be more sensitive than Ziehl-Neelsen. Confirmation requires culture or molecular identification, which guides prolonged multidrug therapy and often implant removal. Differentials include tuberculous mastitis, cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, fungal infection, silicone granuloma and foreign-body reaction.
entities.cyto: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial mastitis, often related to implants, piercing or surgery, shows suppurative granulomatous inflammation with neutrophils, epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells and necrotic debris. Caseation is less typical than in tuberculosis, and acid-fast bacilli are frequently sparse or not seen, so culture and molecular speciation are essential. Clear lipid vacuoles may be present, similar to cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis. Differentials include tuberculosis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, Corynebacterium infection and foreign-body reaction. The cytology is non-specific and is reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), granulomatous inflammation, with a recommendation for microbiological correlation.
entities.ihc: There's no specific IHC for non-tuberculous mycobacterial mastitis. CD68 shows the granulomatous and suppurative histiocytic reaction, and a Fite or modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain can reveal acid-fast bacilli, which are often sparse in fat vacuoles. Diagnosis depends on mycobacterial culture with species identification (M. fortuitum, M. abscessus, M. chelonae), or on PCR and sequencing, because this determines antibiotic choice and NTM tests negative on MTB-specific GeneXpert. Excluding fungi (GMS/PAS) and Corynebacterium (Gram stain) completes the infectious workup. In implant-associated cases, the capsule should be examined, and CD30 helps exclude BIA-ALCL if there's an effusion or atypical lymphoid cells.

entities.variants: Primary; secondary (from thoracic actinomycosis)
entities.remarks: Sulfur granules with filamentous Gram-positive bacteria, abscesses and sinus tracts.
entities.histo: Actinomycosis of the breast is rare. It may be primary, through nipple trauma or ducts, or secondary to thoracic actinomycosis, and presents as an indurated mass with abscesses and draining sinuses that can mimic carcinoma or tuberculosis. Grossly there are multiple interconnected abscesses with yellow sulphur granules in the pus. Microscopically, granules of tangled, radiating basophilic filaments with eosinophilic club-shaped tips (the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) lie within neutrophilic abscesses. They are surrounded by granulation tissue, foamy histiocytes, plasma cells and dense fibrosis. The filaments are Gram-positive, branched and beaded, GMS-positive and non-acid-fast on modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain. Differentials include nocardiosis (weakly acid-fast filaments), botryomycosis (granules made of cocci or bacilli), fungal mycetoma, tuberculous mastitis and granulomatous lobular mastitis. Recognising granules in the biopsy allows prolonged penicillin therapy and avoids unnecessary surgery.
entities.cyto: Aspiration of breast actinomycosis yields purulent material with abundant neutrophils, histiocytes and debris in which characteristic sulphur granules may be seen: dense basophilic colonies of filamentous, branching Gram-positive organisms with radiating club-like peripheral eosinophilic material. Granules may be few and are best seen grossly or on cell block. Epithelial cells are scanty and reactive. Differentials include Nocardia (weakly acid-fast), other bacterial abscess and botryomycosis. Clinically it may present with sinuses and mimic carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), suppurative inflammation with actinomycotic colonies, with a recommendation for culture.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role in breast actinomycosis. The diagnosis rests on suppurative inflammation with sulphur granules: basophilic colonies with radiating eosinophilic clubbing (the Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon). Special stains are what matter. A Gram stain shows branching, filamentous gram-positive bacilli, and these are negative with a modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain, which separates them from Nocardia (weakly acid-fast). GMS also highlights the filaments. Anaerobic culture confirms the organism but is often negative. CD68 highlights the surrounding histiocytes, and pan-keratin excludes carcinoma only when a fibrotic mass mimics malignancy. Secondary disease spreading from the thorax needs clinical and radiological correlation.

entities.variants: Syphilis (chancre of nipple, gumma); brucellosis; cat-scratch disease (Bartonella; intramammary node); leprosy
entities.remarks: Rare; mostly case reports; correlate with serology / special stains / molecular tests.
entities.histo: This group covers rare bacterial infections that are mostly documented in case reports. Syphilis can produce a nipple chancre with ulceration, a dense plasma-cell-rich infiltrate and endarteritis, or a tertiary gumma with necrosis and palisading histiocytes. Treponemes are shown by Treponema IHC or silver stains together with serology. Brucellosis gives non-caseating granulomas or abscesses in endemic regions and is confirmed by serology or culture. Cat-scratch disease involves intramammary lymph nodes with stellate necrotising granulomas containing neutrophils. Warthin-Starry staining or Bartonella PCR can show the bacilli. Leprosy of the breast skin follows the Ridley-Jopling spectrum, with neural granulomas and Fite-positive bacilli in multibacillary forms. All these overlap with tuberculous, fungal and idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, and with lymphoma in nodal disease. Diagnosis therefore relies on combining the pattern of inflammation with special stains, serology, culture and molecular tests rather than on morphology alone.
entities.cyto: Other rare bacterial mastitides, such as those due to Nocardia, Brucella, syphilis or cat-scratch-like organisms, generally produce non-specific acute or granulomatous inflammatory smears with neutrophils, histiocytes, giant cells and necrotic debris. Organisms are seldom visible on routine stains; special stains (Gram, modified acid-fast for Nocardia, silver stains) and culture or serology are required for specific identification. Epithelial cells are scanty and reactive. Cytology serves mainly to exclude malignancy and to triage material for microbiology. The differential includes tuberculosis, granulomatous mastitis and abscess. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) with a descriptive comment.
entities.ihc: For rare bacterial mastitides, IHC plays a small role, and the diagnosis depends on serology, culture and special stains. In syphilis, Treponema pallidum immunohistochemistry is more sensitive and specific than Warthin–Starry or Steiner silver stains for spirochaetes in a nipple chancre or gumma, and it should be done when a plasma-cell-rich infiltrate with endarteritis is seen. Brucellosis is diagnosed by culture and serology. For cat-scratch disease, Bartonella henselae can be shown by Warthin–Starry stain, Bartonella IHC or PCR. CD138 and kappa/lambda ISH exclude a plasma cell neoplasm, and keratin excludes carcinoma when a mass is present.

entities.variants: Blastomycosis; histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis; aspergillosis; coccidioidomycosis; candidal mastitis/nipple candidiasis (lactation)
entities.remarks: Granulomatous ± suppurative inflammation; GMS/PAS for organisms; often immunocompromised host (except lactational Candida).
entities.histo: Fungal mastitis is uncommon and mainly affects immunocompromised hosts or residents of endemic areas. Lactational candidiasis of the nipple and ducts is the exception, occurring in otherwise healthy nursing mothers with burning pain and nipple changes. The histology is granulomatous or mixed suppurative-granulomatous inflammation with necrosis, and the organisms are identified by morphology, highlighted with GMS and PAS. Blastomyces forms broad-based budding, thick-walled yeasts of 8 to 15 microns, whereas Histoplasma forms tiny yeasts within histiocytes. Cryptococcus shows yeasts of variable size with mucicarmine-positive capsules, and Coccidioides shows large spherules with endospores. Aspergillus has septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and is often angioinvasive, while Candida forms pseudohyphae and budding yeasts, mostly superficial in lactation. Culture, antigen tests and molecular methods confirm the species. Differentials include tuberculous and non-tuberculous mycobacterial mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, sarcoidosis and foreign-body reaction.
entities.cyto: Fungal mastitis is rare and usually seen in immunocompromised patients. Smears show suppurative or granulomatous inflammation with neutrophils, epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells and necrosis. Fungal elements may be identified on Pap or MGG and confirmed with PAS or GMS: budding yeasts (Candida, Cryptococcus with capsule, Histoplasma within histiocytes, Blastomyces) or septate or aseptate hyphae (Aspergillus, Mucorales). Careful search is needed as organisms may be sparse. Differentials include tuberculosis and idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, and contaminants must be excluded. Culture is recommended. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), with the organism described.
entities.ihc: Fungal mastitis is identified with histochemical stains rather than IHC. GMS and PAS (with diastase) show the organisms: broad-based budding yeasts in blastomycosis, small intracellular yeasts in histoplasmosis, and narrow-budding encapsulated yeasts in cryptococcosis, whose capsule is mucicarmine- and Alcian blue-positive and whose wall is Fontana–Masson-positive. Aspergillus shows septate hyphae branching at acute angles. CD68 highlights the granulomatous host response. Species-specific immunohistochemistry (for example for Aspergillus or Histoplasma) and PCR are available in some laboratories, and culture remains the reference. Immune status should be correlated, and keratin used to exclude carcinoma only if a mass lesion persists.

entities.variants: Wuchereria bancrofti; Brugia malayi; Dirofilaria (zoonotic)
entities.remarks: Endemic in India; painless mass with eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation around degenerating worms; microfilariae may be seen on FNAC; may calcify.
entities.histo: Filarial mastitis occurs in endemic regions such as India and is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi or, less often, zoonotic Dirofilaria. It typically presents as a painless, firm subcutaneous or parenchymal nodule that may be clinically or radiologically suspicious, and calcified dead worms can produce serpiginous calcifications on mammography. Microscopically, cross- or longitudinal sections of adult worms are found within dilated lymphatics or in the stroma. They show a cuticle, musculature and a uterus that may contain microfilariae. The worms are surrounded by eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells, Charcot-Leyden crystals, eosinophilic abscesses and later fibrosis or calcification. Fine-needle aspiration may show sheathed microfilariae in an eosinophilic background, and Dirofilaria shows a thick laminated cuticle with external longitudinal ridges. Differentials include other parasitic infections (cysticercosis, sparganosis), eosinophilic granulomatous mastitis, tuberculosis and fat necrosis.
entities.cyto: Filarial mastitis, seen in endemic regions including India, presents as a subcutaneous nodule. FNA shows microfilariae (Wuchereria bancrofti, sheathed with a tail free of nuclei) or fragments of adult worms, set in an inflammatory background rich in eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes and histiocytes, sometimes with granulomas and giant cells. Charcot-Leyden crystals may be present. Microfilariae are best seen on MGG or Pap at low power and may be few, so all slides should be screened. Differentials include other parasitic infestations and eosinophilic inflammation. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), with identification of the parasite.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role in filarial mastitis. The diagnosis rests on finding adult worms or microfilariae (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi or Dirofilaria) in dilated lymphatics or breast parenchyma, set within an eosinophil-rich granulomatous reaction that often includes calcified worm remnants and Splendore–Hoeppli material. Speciation uses morphology: cuticle, musculature, lateral cords and the internal structure of the worm. A night blood smear, serology for filarial antigen and the eosinophil count are the supporting tests. CD68 highlights the granulomas. In endemic areas such as India, recognising this on fine needle aspiration or biopsy avoids an unnecessary cancer workup, though imaging correlation is still advised for any mass.

entities.variants: Echinococcus granulosus
entities.remarks: Laminated acellular membrane, germinal layer and protoscolices/hooklets; rare primary site.
entities.histo: Hydatid cyst of the breast is a rare primary or secondary site of Echinococcus granulosus infection, usually in endemic sheep-rearing areas. It presents as a slowly growing, well-circumscribed, painless cystic mass that can mimic a fibroadenoma or a simple cyst, and imaging may show daughter cysts. Grossly a unilocular or multilocular cyst contains clear fluid, a white laminated membrane and daughter cysts. Microscopically, the diagnostic acellular, eosinophilic, PAS-positive laminated membrane lies inside the host-derived fibrous pericyst, which shows chronic inflammation, eosinophils and foreign-body giant cells. An inner nucleated germinal layer may give rise to brood capsules containing protoscolices with refractile hooklets, and the hooklets persist even in degenerated cysts. Spillage during aspiration risks anaphylaxis and seeding. Differentials include cysticercosis (scolex with a suctorial apparatus and convoluted bladder wall), galactocele, abscess, fat necrosis with an oil cyst and epidermal inclusion cyst. Serology and imaging help confirm the diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Hydatid cyst of the breast is rare; aspiration is generally discouraged because of the risk of anaphylaxis and spread, but may be done inadvertently. Fluid is clear to turbid and shows refractile hooklets, protoscolices with a double row of hooklets and suckers, and laminated acellular membrane fragments that stain on PAS, in a background of histiocytes, eosinophils and inflammatory cells. Calcareous corpuscles may be seen. The finding of hooklets alone is diagnostic. Differentials include other cysts and parasitic lesions; imaging and serology support the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), with a comment on the parasite.
entities.ihc: IHC isn't needed to diagnose a hydatid cyst of the breast. The diagnosis is morphological: a laminated, acellular, PAS-positive outer membrane, an inner germinal layer, and brood capsules with protoscolices bearing refractile hooklets, which are acid-fast and birefringent. Serology for Echinococcus antibodies and imaging (for daughter cysts or other organ involvement) are the relevant workup. CD68 can show the surrounding granulomatous host reaction. On aspiration, take care to avoid anaphylaxis and spillage. If only fragments of laminated membrane are seen, a PAS stain helps to recognise them. Keratin and other epithelial markers are generally unnecessary.

entities.variants: Cysticercosis (Taenia solium); sparganosis; trichinosis
entities.remarks: Cysticercus: cyst with scolex, surrounding granulomatous/eosinophilic reaction; endemic in India.
entities.histo: Other parasitic infestations of the breast include cysticercosis, sparganosis and trichinosis. Cysticercosis (Taenia solium larvae) is the most frequent in India. It produces a small, tender or painless cystic nodule in breast parenchyma or the pectoral muscle, sometimes with a scolex visible on ultrasound. Microscopically, a cyst wall with an undulating, folded tegument and an invaginated scolex bearing suckers and hooklets lies in a host fibrous capsule. This is surrounded by mixed eosinophil-rich, granulomatous and palisading histiocytic inflammation, and the lesion may calcify when it degenerates. Sparganosis (Spirometra plerocercoids) shows a solid, ribbon-like larva without a scolex in tunnels of eosinophilic necrosis. Trichinosis involves the pectoral muscle with coiled larvae in nurse cells rather than the parenchyma. Differentials include filariasis, hydatid disease, eosinophilic granulomatous mastitis, fat necrosis and tuberculous abscess, and serology and imaging provide useful supporting evidence.
entities.cyto: Other parasitic infestations, such as cysticercosis, dirofilariasis, sparganosis or Loa loa, are rare in breast. Aspirates typically show an eosinophil-rich mixed inflammatory infiltrate with histiocytes, granulomas, giant cells and necrotic material, sometimes with Charcot-Leyden crystals. Diagnosis depends on finding fragments of parasite, for example the bladder wall of Cysticercus with its tegument and nuclei, or worm fragments with cuticle and musculature. If the parasite is not seen, a descriptive report of eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation suggesting parasitic aetiology is given. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign).
entities.ihc: Other parasitic infestations of the breast are diagnosed by recognising the parasite morphologically, not by immunohistochemistry. In cysticercosis, the cyst wall and the invaginated scolex with suckers and hooklets are diagnostic. Sparganosis shows a solid plerocercoid larva without a scolex, with calcareous corpuscles. Trichinella encysts in muscle. The host response is eosinophil-rich and granulomatous, and CD68 highlights the histiocytes. Serology (for example cysticercus ELISA or immunoblot), imaging for disease elsewhere, and peripheral eosinophilia support the diagnosis. IHC for keratin or lymphoid markers is reserved for excluding carcinoma or lymphoma in difficult inflammatory masses.

entities.variants: Herpes simplex (lactational nipple HSV); herpes zoster; molluscum contagiosum
entities.remarks: Skin-type lesions; viral cytopathic changes.
entities.histo: Viral infections of the nipple-areola region produce skin-type lesions rather than parenchymal disease. Herpes simplex in lactating women (often transmitted from an infant with oral lesions) and herpes zoster in a dermatomal distribution cause intraepidermal vesicles with acantholysis and ballooning degeneration. The infected keratinocytes show multinucleation, nuclear moulding and chromatin margination with steel-grey nuclei, the classic three Ms, plus Cowdry A inclusions. Later lesions ulcerate, with necrosis, neutrophils and sometimes viral vasculitis. HSV-1/2 and VZV IHC or PCR distinguish the viruses. Molluscum contagiosum gives a cup-shaped, endophytic lobulated epidermal proliferation with large intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Henderson-Patterson inclusion (molluscum) bodies in the upper layers. Differentials include eczema, Paget disease (CK7-positive large atypical cells, no viral cytopathic change), impetigo, pemphigus, and nipple fissures with candidal infection. Recognition avoids unnecessary excision and allows antiviral therapy.
entities.cyto: Viral infections of the nipple-areola, such as herpes simplex, varicella-zoster or molluscum contagiosum, are diagnosed clinically and occasionally by scrape or Tzanck preparation rather than FNA. Herpetic scrapes show multinucleated squamous cells with nuclear moulding, margination of chromatin and ground-glass nuclei, sometimes with Cowdry A inclusions. Molluscum shows large intracytoplasmic eosinophilic to basophilic molluscum bodies within squamous cells. Background is inflamed with keratinous debris. Paget disease and eczema are the main clinical differentials. The Yokohama System is not designed for skin scrapes; findings are reported descriptively as benign or infective.
entities.ihc: Viral infections of the nipple-areola are mainly clinical and morphological diagnoses, but IHC is genuinely useful here. HSV-1/2 immunohistochemistry, and VZV immunohistochemistry for zoster, confirm the multinucleated keratinocytes with Cowdry A inclusions and margination, moulding and multinucleation. This separates herpetic infection from Paget disease and eczema. Molluscum contagiosum is recognised by its Henderson–Patterson bodies without IHC, and HPV-related warts can be supported by p16 or HPV ISH if needed. When intraepidermal atypical cells raise concern for Paget disease, CK7, GATA3 and HER2 stain Paget cells but not virally infected keratinocytes. PCR on swabs is the reference test.

entities.remarks: Non-necrotising well-formed granulomas; usually with systemic disease; exclude infection and granulomatous lobular mastitis.
entities.histo: Breast sarcoidosis is rare. It usually occurs in patients with known systemic sarcoidosis and occasionally presents first as a breast mass that clinically mimics carcinoma. Microscopically, tight, well-formed, non-necrotising epithelioid granulomas with sparse peripheral lymphocytes (naked granulomas) are distributed in both interlobular stroma and lobules. They may coalesce or show hyalinising fibrosis. Langhans and foreign-body giant cells may contain asteroid bodies, Schaumann bodies or calcium oxalate crystals, none of which is specific. Necrosis is absent or minimal. The diagnosis requires exclusion of infection with Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS and PAS stains, culture or GeneXpert, and correlation with chest imaging, serum ACE and calcium. Differentials include idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis (lobulocentric, neutrophilic microabscesses), tuberculous mastitis (caseation), fungal infection, foreign-body reaction, and sarcoid-like reactions adjacent to carcinoma or in draining lymph nodes, which should prompt a careful search for an underlying tumour.
entities.cyto: Breast sarcoidosis aspirates show cohesive aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes forming non-necrotising granulomas, with occasional multinucleated giant cells and a background of lymphocytes; necrosis and neutrophils are usually absent. Asteroid or Schaumann bodies are rarely seen. The cytological picture is non-specific, and sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring stains and culture for mycobacteria and fungi, plus clinical evidence of systemic disease. Differentials include tuberculosis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, foreign-body reaction and granulomatous reaction to carcinoma or lymphoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), non-necrotising granulomatous inflammation.
entities.ihc: IHC has no specific role in breast sarcoidosis, which is a diagnosis of exclusion. It shows tight non-necrotising epithelioid granulomas, sometimes with asteroid or Schaumann bodies. CD68 and CD163 highlight the granulomas. The key workup is to exclude infection, with Ziehl–Neelsen staining and mycobacterial PCR or GeneXpert, and GMS and PAS for fungi. Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, which is lobulocentric with neutrophils and microabscesses, should be considered too. A sarcoid-like reaction in the drainage area of a carcinoma, or after lymphoma, should be borne in mind, so correlate with any known malignancy and with serum ACE and chest imaging. Keratin is used only to exclude a coexisting carcinoma.

entities.variants: Silicone granuloma (siliconoma, from rupture/bleed or injection); paraffinoma; suture granuloma; reaction to other injected fillers (e.g. polyacrylamide gel)
entities.remarks: Vacuolated histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells around refractile/non-birefringent material; silicone may spread to axillary nodes (silicone lymphadenopathy).
entities.histo: A foreign-body granulomatous reaction in the breast follows silicone implant rupture or gel bleed, direct silicone or paraffin injection, retained sutures, or injected fillers such as polyacrylamide gel. Grossly there are firm, sometimes multiple nodules (siliconoma, paraffinoma) that can mimic carcinoma clinically and on imaging. Silicone produces sheets of histiocytes containing multiple clear, round, sharply punched-out vacuoles of varying size, with multinucleated giant cells, refractile, yellowish, non-birefringent or weakly birefringent material, and fibrosis. Paraffin gives Swiss-cheese-like vacuoles of variable size in sclerotic stroma, the pattern of sclerosing lipogranuloma. Sutures show birefringent filaments surrounded by giant cells, and polyacrylamide gel appears as pale basophilic, lace-like material with histiocytes. Silicone may migrate to axillary lymph nodes, producing silicone lymphadenopathy. Differentials include fat necrosis, liposarcoma (lipoblast-like vacuolated histiocytes), granular cell tumour, infection, and carcinoma or BIA-ALCL around implants.
entities.cyto: Foreign-body granulomatous reaction, for example to silicone, suture, paraffin or tattoo pigment, yields smears with foreign-body type multinucleated giant cells, foamy and vacuolated histiocytes, lymphocytes and fibroblasts. Silicone appears as clear, refractile, non-birefringent droplets or vacuoles within histiocytes and giant cells; suture and some other materials are birefringent under polarised light. Fat necrosis frequently coexists. The vacuolated histiocytes may resemble signet-ring or lipid-rich carcinoma cells, so attention to bland nuclei is important. Clinical history of implant or surgery is key. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign).
entities.ihc: Foreign-body granulomatous reaction in the breast is diagnosed morphologically. Silicone shows as clear, refractile, non-birefringent vacuoles in histiocytes and giant cells; paraffin or oil granulomas show variably sized lipid vacuoles; and suture material is polarisable. CD68 and CD163 confirm that the vacuolated cells are histiocytes. This matters most in separating siliconomas and lipogranulomas from signet-ring or histiocytoid carcinoma, which is pan-keratin-positive, and from liposarcoma, which shows MDM2 amplification. Polarisation and energy-dispersive X-ray analysis identify the material if needed. In an implant setting, CD30 IHC on any effusion or capsular lymphoid infiltrate excludes BIA-ALCL.

entities.variants: Diabetic (type 1 DM) and non-diabetic (autoimmune: Hashimoto, SLE) forms
entities.remarks: Dense keloid-like fibrosis, perilobular/periductal/perivascular B-lymphocytic infiltrate, epithelioid myofibroblasts; hard mass mimicking carcinoma.
entities.histo: Lymphocytic (diabetic) mastopathy occurs mainly in long-standing type 1 diabetes, and also in autoimmune conditions such as Hashimoto thyroiditis and SLE. It presents as a hard, irregular, mobile mass that may be bilateral and mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging, and core biopsies often yield little tissue. Grossly the cut surface is firm, white and rubbery. Microscopically there is dense keloid-like hyalinised stromal fibrosis with atrophic lobules and ducts. Perilobular, periductal and perivascular infiltrates of mature, predominantly B lymphocytes are present, sometimes with lymphocytic lobulitis and germinal centres. Characteristic epithelioid myofibroblasts are scattered in the collagen; they may look histiocyte-like or worrying, but they are keratin-negative, unlike lobular carcinoma cells. Differentials include lymphoma (MALT type), which shows sheets of monotypic B cells and lymphoepithelial lesions; IgG4-related mastitis; sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis of other causes; focal fibrous disease; and invasive lobular carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Lymphocytic (diabetic) mastopathy presents as a hard mass, and FNA is typically scanty or hypocellular because of dense keloid-like stroma. Smears show small mature lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, few fragments of fibrous stroma, sometimes with plump epithelioid fibroblasts, and very few bland ductal cells. Insufficient aspirates are common, and the lack of cells should not reassure the clinician when imaging is suspicious. Differentials include lymphoma (monomorphic lymphoid population, which needs flow cytometry), lobular carcinoma (dyscohesive cells in a hypocellular smear) and granular cell tumour. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 1 (Insufficient) as appropriate, with core biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: In lymphocytic (diabetic) mastopathy, IHC mainly serves to exclude lymphoma and carcinoma. The perilobular and perivascular lymphocytes are mostly polyclonal B cells (CD20+), with CD3+ T cells admixed, and they lack a monotypic light-chain pattern on kappa/lambda staining or flow cytometry. They don't form CD21-highlighted lymphoepithelial destruction or diffuse sheets of the kind seen in MALT lymphoma. The characteristic epithelioid myofibroblasts in the keloid-like stroma can look like infiltrating carcinoma or a granular cell tumour. They are keratin-negative and S100-negative, sometimes CD34-positive or desmin-positive. Pan-keratin therefore helps exclude invasive lobular carcinoma within the fibrosis.

entities.variants: Sclerosing mastitis; inflammatory pseudotumour-type
entities.remarks: Lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis; IgG4+ plasma cells >50/HPF and IgG4/IgG ratio >40%.
entities.histo: IgG4-related mastitis is part of systemic IgG4-related disease. It presents as a painless, firm, sometimes bilateral breast mass, often with lymphadenopathy, and other organs or a raised serum IgG4 may be involved. Microscopically a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with lymphoid follicles and germinal centres effaces lobules. This is accompanied by storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis (best seen on elastic stain), and eosinophils may be present. Lobules are atrophic or lost. IHC shows more than 50 IgG4-positive plasma cells per HPF (cut-offs vary with organ and series) and an IgG4/IgG ratio above 40%, while the plasma cells are polytypic for kappa and lambda. The sclerosing mastitis and inflammatory pseudotumour-type patterns overlap. Differentials include lymphocytic (diabetic) mastopathy, plasma cell or periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, MALT lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation (light chain restriction), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (ALK-positive in about half) and Rosai-Dorfman disease.
entities.cyto: IgG4-related mastitis has non-specific cytology: smears show numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells, sometimes with eosinophils, fragments of fibrous stroma with spindle cells, and scanty benign ductal epithelium. Storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, the key histological features, cannot be assessed on FNA, and IgG4/IgG ratios require tissue. Differentials include lymphoplasmacytic mastitis, marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation, plasmacytoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and Rosai-Dorfman disease. Cytology can raise the possibility and exclude carcinoma, but core biopsy with immunohistochemistry is required. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, or Category 3 if lymphoma cannot be excluded.
entities.ihc: IHC is central to diagnosing IgG4-related mastitis. Immunostains for IgG4 and total IgG should show raised IgG4-positive plasma cells, typically more than 50 per high-power field in the breast (many use a threshold above 10 per HPF), with an IgG4:IgG ratio above 40%. These counts must be read alongside the morphology (dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis) and serum IgG4, because raised IgG4 cells also occur in other inflammatory conditions and in MALT lymphoma. Kappa and lambda ISH show polyclonality, CD20 and CD3 exclude lymphoma, and ALK helps exclude inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour. Orcein or elastic stains highlight the phlebitis.

entities.variants: Lupus panniculitis (profundus) of breast
entities.remarks: Lobular panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis, lymphoid aggregates/germinal centres, lymphocytic vasculitis; SLE/discoid lupus.
entities.histo: Lupus mastitis is lupus panniculitis (lupus profundus) involving the breast fat in patients with SLE or discoid lupus. It may precede systemic disease and presents as firm, sometimes painful subcutaneous masses with overlying skin change, which can calcify and mimic carcinoma on mammography. Microscopically there is a lobular panniculitis with characteristic hyaline (eosinophilic, glassy) fat necrosis, a lymphocytic infiltrate with nodular lymphoid aggregates that often have germinal centres, and plasma cells. Lymphocytic vasculitis, mucin and later membranous lipid change and calcification may be present, and the overlying dermis can show interface change. Differentials include subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (rimming of adipocytes by atypical CD8-positive, beta-F1-positive T cells with a high Ki-67; reactive B-cell aggregates are not prominent), traumatic fat necrosis, lymphocytic mastopathy, morphoea profunda and erythema nodosum (septal). Correlation with clinical features and serology is essential.
entities.cyto: Lupus mastitis (lupus panniculitis of the breast) yields smears of fat necrosis with foamy histiocytes, lipophages, multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells and amorphous hyaline or necrotic material, sometimes with calcific debris. Epithelial cells are usually absent because the process is in the subcutaneous fat. The features are non-specific and indistinguishable from other causes of fat necrosis or panniculitis; the diagnosis rests on clinical history of lupus and histology showing lobular panniculitis with hyaline necrosis and lymphoid nodules. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), fat necrosis and chronic inflammation, with clinical correlation.
entities.ihc: IHC plays only a minor role in lupus mastitis (lupus panniculitis). The diagnosis rests on lobular panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis, lymphoid aggregates and follicles, plasma cells and calcification, together with clinical and serological lupus. The main differential is subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma. Here IHC is key: SPTCL shows atypical CD8+, βF1+, TIA-1/granzyme B+, CD56− T cells rimming adipocytes, with a high Ki-67 in the rimming cells and clonal TCR rearrangement. Lupus panniculitis has mixed CD4 and CD8 cells, CD20+ B-cell follicles, plasma cells and clusters of CD123+ plasmacytoid dendritic cells. Direct immunofluorescence can show basement membrane immunoreactants.

entities.variants: Giant cell arteritis; granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA); polyarteritis nodosa; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
entities.remarks: May present as a mass; localized or part of systemic vasculitis.
entities.histo: Breast vasculitis is rare and may be isolated (localised) or part of a systemic vasculitis. It typically presents as a tender mass, skin change or calcifications in older women, which raises concern for carcinoma. Giant cell arteritis involves medium-sized breast arteries with granulomatous panarteritis, multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, and it is often associated with polymyalgia or temporal arteritis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis shows geographic necrosis, necrotising vasculitis, scattered giant cells and neutrophilic microabscesses, with ANCA (PR3) support. Polyarteritis nodosa shows segmental fibrinoid necrosis of medium-sized arteries with mixed infiltrates and aneurysm formation. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis adds tissue eosinophilia and extravascular granulomas in a setting of asthma. An elastic stain helps to identify the vessel wall. Differentials include granulomatous lobular mastitis, infection, lupus mastitis, IgG4-related disease and Mondor disease, and serology together with assessment for systemic involvement is required.
entities.cyto: Breast vasculitis, such as giant cell arteritis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, is rarely diagnosed on cytology because the vessel wall changes need histology. Aspirates may show non-specific inflammation with neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, occasional giant cells, necrotic debris and fragments of fibrous stroma or fat necrosis. In granulomatosis with polyangiitis, smears may show necrotising granulomatous inflammation with basophilic necrosis. The cytology essentially excludes carcinoma and suggests an inflammatory process; biopsy and serology (ANCA) are required for diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) with a descriptive comment.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role in breast vasculitis. Its use is to confirm the vascular wall structure and characterise the infiltrate rather than to give a specific diagnosis. Elastic stains (EVG or orcein) show fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina in giant cell arteritis and help separate arteritis from phlebitis. CD68 highlights the giant cells and granulomas. In granulomatosis with polyangiitis, special stains for organisms (Ziehl–Neelsen, GMS) are needed to exclude infection, and ANCA serology (PR3, MPO) is the key adjunct. Lymphoid markers and kappa/lambda help exclude lymphoma in angiocentric infiltrates. Because breast vasculitis may be part of a systemic disease, clinical and serological correlation is essential.

entities.variants: Atopic, contact, irritant dermatitis; psoriasis
entities.remarks: Spongiotic dermatitis; key clinical differential of Paget disease (Paget cells absent; CK7 negative intraepidermal cells).
entities.histo: Eczema or dermatitis of the nipple-areola presents with itching, scaling, crusting and erythema, often bilateral. It is the main clinical differential of Paget disease. Atopic, allergic contact and irritant dermatitis show spongiotic dermatitis: intercellular oedema in the epidermis, with spongiotic vesicles in acute lesions, exocytosis of lymphocytes, parakeratotic scale crust and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, often with eosinophils in contact dermatitis. Chronic lesions show acanthosis, hyperkeratosis and dermal fibrosis (lichen simplex). Psoriasis shows regular psoriasiform hyperplasia with confluent parakeratosis, neutrophils in the stratum corneum and an absent granular layer. The essential task is to exclude Paget disease. No large atypical intraepidermal cells are present, and CK7 and HER2 staining is negative within the epidermis. Pitfalls are benign CK7-positive Toker cells, which are bland and HER2-negative, and clear keratinocytes. Bowen disease is also part of the differential.
entities.cyto: Eczema or dermatitis of the nipple-areola is a clinical diagnosis and is not sampled by FNA. Scrape or imprint cytology, if done, shows anucleate and nucleated squames, parakeratotic cells, inflammatory cells including lymphocytes and eosinophils, and keratinous debris, sometimes with bacteria or fungal elements from secondary infection. The key purpose of cytology is to exclude Paget disease, in which large atypical cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli are seen singly or in small groups among the squames. A negative scrape does not exclude Paget disease, and persistent lesions need punch biopsy. Reported descriptively; Yokohama categories apply loosely (Category 2).
entities.ihc: IHC is mainly used in nipple-areolar dermatitis to exclude Paget disease, which is the key clinical mimic. Spongiotic or psoriasiform dermatitis has no intraepidermal cells positive for CK7, GATA3 or HER2. In Paget disease, scattered large cells within the epidermis are CK7+, GATA3+, usually HER2+ (often 3+), CAM5.2+ and EMA+. Note that benign Toker cells in the nipple are also CK7+, but they're bland and HER2-negative. Pagetoid melanoma in situ (S100, SOX10, Melan-A+, CK7−) and Bowen disease (p63+, CK5/6+, CK7−, often diffusely p16+) are the other differentials. A PAS stain for fungi is useful in psoriasiform or eczematous patterns.

entities.variants: Synovial metaplasia of capsule; silicone-laden histiocytes; calcified capsule
entities.remarks: Fibrous capsule with synovial-like metaplasia, chronic inflammation; examine effusion/capsule for BIA-ALCL when seroma present.
entities.histo: Implant capsule inflammation and capsular contracture affect the fibrous capsule that forms around breast implants. Contracture produces a firm, painful, distorted breast and is graded clinically by the Baker scale. Grossly the capsule is thickened, sometimes calcified or containing silicone. Microscopically there is dense, layered collagenous fibrosis with variable chronic inflammation. The inner surface often shows synovial-like metaplasia, a palisaded layer of histiocyte-like cells with fibrin, resembling synovium. Silicone-laden vacuolated histiocytes and giant cells, refractile implant material and dystrophic calcification are common. Capsules removed for a delayed seroma, mass or effusion require careful sampling to exclude breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Atypical large cells along the luminal fibrin should prompt CD30 IHC, and effusion fluid should be sent for cytology and CD30 testing. Other differentials include infection (including mycobacteria), squamous cell carcinoma arising in capsules (very rare) and simple foreign-body reaction.
entities.cyto: Implant capsule inflammation and capsular contracture are usually assessed on surgical capsulectomy rather than cytology. Peri-implant fluid or capsule aspirates show foamy histiocytes, multinucleated foreign-body giant cells, lymphocytes, fibrin and refractile silicone droplets, sometimes with synovial-like metaplastic cells. The most important role of cytology of a late (more than a year) peri-implant seroma is to exclude breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma: large pleomorphic cells with horseshoe nuclei should prompt cell block with CD30 and ALK immunostaining and flow cytometry. Benign reactive effusions are reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or as benign fluid cytology.
entities.ihc: In implant capsule inflammation and contracture, IHC isn't needed for the benign changes: fibrous capsule, synovial-like metaplasia, silicone-laden CD68+ histiocytes and chronic inflammation. Its key role is excluding breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), especially if there's a late seroma, a mass or atypical large cells. CD30 should be done on effusion cell blocks and on the capsule. BIA-ALCL shows strong, uniform membrane and Golgi CD30 staining in large pleomorphic cells, with ALK negativity, variable loss of T-cell antigens (CD3, CD5), positive cytotoxic markers, and clonal TCR rearrangement. Scattered reactive CD30+ immunoblasts are common and must not be over-interpreted.

entities.variants: Amastia (absent breast + nipple); amazia (absent breast tissue, nipple present); athelia (absent nipple); hypoplasia; Poland syndrome association
entities.remarks: Congenital; Poland syndrome = unilateral pectoralis major absence with breast/limb anomalies.
entities.histo: Amastia, amazia and athelia are rare congenital developmental anomalies, and most are diagnosed clinically rather than histologically. Amastia is complete absence of breast tissue, nipple and areola. Amazia is absence of glandular tissue with the nipple preserved, and it may also follow surgery or radiotherapy in childhood. Athelia is absence of the nipple alone, and hypoplasia is underdevelopment of one or both breasts. Unilateral forms are frequently associated with Poland syndrome, which combines absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis major with chest wall, breast and ipsilateral upper limb anomalies such as syndactyly. Tissue, when examined, shows fibroadipose tissue lacking or with very scanty ducts and lobules. Any rudimentary ducts are normal two-layered structures without terminal duct lobular units. Differentials include acquired loss of breast tissue from trauma, burns, and iatrogenic injury to the breast bud in childhood (biopsy or radiotherapy). The pathologist's role is mainly to document absence of glandular tissue in reconstructive specimens.
entities.cyto: Amastia, amazia and athelia are congenital developmental anomalies diagnosed clinically and radiologically; there is no lesion to sample and cytology has no diagnostic role. If an aspirate were taken from the chest wall region in amazia (absence of glandular tissue with a nipple present), it would show only adipose tissue, fibrous stroma or skin elements without ductal epithelium. The condition may be associated with syndromes such as Poland syndrome or result from iatrogenic injury to the breast bud. Yokohama categorisation is not applicable; at most, a non-diagnostic or benign descriptive report would be given.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role in amastia, amazia or athelia. These are congenital developmental anomalies diagnosed clinically and radiologically, often as part of Poland syndrome (unilateral pectoral hypoplasia with hand anomalies), ectodermal dysplasias or other syndromic associations. Tissue is rarely sent to pathology, and when it is, the absence or hypoplasia of glandular elements is a morphological observation that doesn't need special stains. Genetic evaluation, for example for TBX3 in ulnar-mammary syndrome, may be relevant in syndromic cases, but routine immunohistochemistry isn't.

entities.variants: Polymastia (supernumerary breast); polythelia (supernumerary nipple); axillary accessory breast tissue; aberrant breast tissue (vulva, milk-line sites)
entities.remarks: Along embryonic milk line, commonest in axilla; subject to all diseases of normal breast incl. fibroadenoma and carcinoma.
entities.histo: Accessory (ectopic) breast tissue arises along the embryonic milk line from axilla to groin, and is commonest in the axilla. Polymastia refers to a supernumerary breast with glandular tissue, with or without a nipple. Polythelia refers to a supernumerary nipple alone, which shows dermal smooth muscle bundles, pigmented skin and lactiferous ducts. Aberrant breast tissue at unusual sites, such as the vulva, may lack connection to a nipple. Microscopically, normal ducts and lobules with luminal and myoepithelial layers sit in fibroadipose stroma, often within the axillary subcutis. They may show lactational change or swelling in pregnancy. Accessory tissue is subject to all diseases of the normal breast, including fibrocystic change, fibroadenoma, phyllodes tumour and carcinoma. Differentials in the axilla include lymph node metastasis (lymph node architecture), sweat gland (apocrine or eccrine) tumours and hidradenitis, while vulval mammary-like glands can give rise to hidradenoma papilliferum.
entities.cyto: Accessory (ectopic) breast tissue, commonly in the axilla, may be aspirated as an axillary lump. Smears show benign breast elements: cohesive monolayered sheets of ductal cells with myoepithelial cells, bare bipolar nuclei, adipose tissue and fibrous stroma, and during pregnancy lactational change with vacuolated cells. Any lesion of normal breast, including fibroadenoma, cyst or carcinoma, can arise here. The main differentials are axillary lymph node and sweat gland or other adnexal lesions; the absence of lymphoid cells and presence of breast-type epithelium help. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) with a comment consistent with accessory breast tissue.
entities.ihc: IHC is seldom needed for accessory (ectopic) breast tissue. Its main use is to confirm a mammary origin and to examine pathology arising in it. In the axilla or vulva, ectopic breast tissue can be confused with apocrine or eccrine glands or with metastatic carcinoma in a lymph node. Mammary epithelium is GATA3+, mammaglobin+, often ER/PR-positive, with an intact p63- or calponin-positive myoepithelial layer, which separates benign ectopic glands from nodal metastasis. The full range of breast disease, including fibroadenoma, phyllodes tumour and carcinoma, can arise in ectopic tissue, and these are worked up as in the orthotopic breast, including ER, PR and HER2 for carcinoma.

entities.entity: Congenital nipple inversion / tubular (tuberous) breast deformity
entities.remarks: Developmental; acquired nipple inversion should prompt exclusion of carcinoma/duct ectasia.
entities.histo: Congenital nipple inversion and tubular (tuberous) breast deformity are developmental anomalies that are usually managed by plastic surgeons, so histology is seldom diagnostic. Congenital inversion results from short lactiferous ducts and fibrous bands tethering the nipple. Excised tissue shows normal nipple skin with dermal smooth muscle, lactiferous ducts with two-cell lining and sometimes periductal fibrosis. Tubular breast shows a constricted base, herniation of glandular tissue into the areola, and dense fibrous bands within the periareolar fascia, with otherwise normal ducts and lobules. The key clinical point is that acquired, recent or unilateral nipple inversion is not developmental and should prompt investigation for underlying carcinoma, which retracts the nipple by desmoplasia. Other acquired causes include duct ectasia, periductal mastitis and subareolar abscess, all with periductal inflammation and fibrosis. Pathological examination therefore focuses on excluding these lesions, and on documenting the absence of carcinoma or Paget disease in excised nipple tissue.
entities.cyto: Congenital nipple inversion and tubular (tuberous) breast deformity are developmental anomalies diagnosed clinically; there is no mass to aspirate and cytology has no diagnostic role. If tissue were sampled, it would show normal breast components (bland ductal cells, myoepithelial cells, stroma and fat). An important clinical point is that new or acquired nipple inversion in an adult, as opposed to congenital inversion, may signal an underlying carcinoma or duct ectasia, and in that setting imaging and FNA or core biopsy of any mass is indicated. Yokohama categorisation is not applicable to the deformity itself.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role in congenital nipple inversion or tubular (tuberous) breast deformity. These are developmental conditions managed clinically and surgically, and any excised tissue usually shows normal or fibrotic breast tissue. The important point is clinical: acquired, recent or unilateral nipple inversion needs investigation for an underlying carcinoma or duct ectasia. In that setting the workup of any lesion follows the usual approach, including keratin and myoepithelial markers for suspected invasion and ER, PR and HER2 if carcinoma is found.

entities.variants: Juvenile (pubertal) hypertrophy; gestational gigantomastia; drug-induced (D-penicillamine)
entities.remarks: Massive diffuse enlargement; stromal and ductal proliferation without lobule formation, PASH-like stroma common.
entities.histo: Juvenile (virginal) hypertrophy is a rapid, massive, usually bilateral enlargement of the breasts around puberty that is thought to reflect end-organ hypersensitivity to normal hormones. Gestational gigantomastia occurs in pregnancy, and drug-induced forms are reported with D-penicillamine and other agents. Reduction specimens are large and composed of firm, white fibrous tissue with relatively scanty glandular elements and fat. Microscopically there is diffuse proliferation of hypocellular to moderately cellular stroma, often with pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH)-like slit-like spaces. Ducts are increased and may show gynaecomastoid or mild usual epithelial hyperplasia, but lobule formation is characteristically sparse. In gestational cases, lactational change is present. The changes are diffuse rather than forming a discrete mass. Differentials include giant (juvenile) fibroadenoma and benign phyllodes tumour, which are circumscribed masses; diffuse PASH; and hamartoma. Pathological examination is mainly to exclude these lesions and any unexpected atypia.
entities.cyto: Juvenile (virginal) hypertrophy and gigantomastia are diagnosed clinically as diffuse breast enlargement; FNA is rarely done. If aspirated, smears are hypocellular with fragments of fibrous and sometimes oedematous stroma, adipose tissue and small numbers of bland cohesive ductal cells with myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, resembling normal breast or mild fibroadenomatoid change. Features such as PASH are seen on histology. Cytology mainly serves to exclude a discrete neoplasm such as juvenile fibroadenoma or phyllodes tumour in a rapidly enlarging breast. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) when adequate.
entities.ihc: IHC has little diagnostic role in juvenile (virginal) hypertrophy or gigantomastia, which are clinical diagnoses. Histology shows non-specific stromal and ductal proliferation, often with PASH-like stroma and gynaecomastoid epithelial change. The stroma is CD34+ and may be PR-positive, and the ducts keep a normal p63/calponin-positive myoepithelial layer with heterogeneous ER and CK5/6 expression. IHC can help when a discrete mass raises the possibility of juvenile fibroadenoma or phyllodes tumour, but morphology decides. Endocrine evaluation and, in gestational or drug-induced cases (for example D-penicillamine), clinical history are more important than special stains.

entities.variants: Gross cysts (blue-domed cysts); microcysts; apocrine metaplasia; stromal fibrosis; mild (usual) hyperplasia; simple adenosis
entities.remarks: Non-proliferative breast disease; no or minimal increase in cancer risk (RR ~1).
entities.histo: Fibrocystic change is the commonest non-proliferative breast condition of women aged 20 to 50. It presents with lumpiness, cyclical pain or cysts, and confers no or minimal increase in cancer risk. Grossly there are firm fibrous tissue and cysts of varying size, including blue-domed gross cysts containing turbid fluid. Microscopically the components are cystically dilated ducts and acini (microcysts and gross cysts) lined by flattened or apocrine epithelium. Apocrine metaplasia shows eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and apical snouts, and stromal fibrosis may replace lobular stroma. Mild usual hyperplasia of two to four cell layers and simple adenosis may be present, and cyst rupture produces chronic inflammation, foamy histiocytes and fibrosis. Calcifications are common in cysts and acini. Differentials include proliferative lesions such as florid UDH, sclerosing adenosis and papilloma, which should be reported separately because of their modest risk, as well as cystic hypersecretory lesions and mucocele-like lesions. Documenting atypia, if present, is the key reporting point.
entities.cyto: Fibrocystic change yields smears of variable, usually low to moderate cellularity, with cohesive flat monolayered sheets of bland ductal cells, myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, sheets of apocrine cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, foamy macrophages and proteinaceous cyst fluid background, sometimes with fragments of fibrous stroma. Mild anisonucleosis and prominent nucleoli in apocrine cells are expected and should not be over-called. Differentials include fibroadenoma (more cellular, staghorn sheets and abundant bare nuclei) and proliferative lesions. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), with correlation with imaging (triple test).
entities.ihc: IHC isn't required for fibrocystic change, a non-proliferative condition diagnosed on morphology (cysts, apocrine metaplasia, stromal fibrosis, mild adenosis). Stains are useful only for specific mimics. Apocrine metaplasia is AR+, GCDFP-15+, and ER/PR-negative, and it shouldn't be mistaken for atypia. Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMMHC, calponin) confirm a preserved two-cell layer around cysts and adenosis when the stroma is sclerotic, and CK5/6 shows a heterogeneous, non-clonal pattern in any accompanying epithelial hyperplasia. Mammographic calcifications should be correlated with the histology, and oxalate crystals checked under polarised light.

entities.variants: Simple cyst; apocrine cyst; cyst with calcium oxalate (weddellite) crystals; ruptured cyst
entities.remarks: Lined by flattened or apocrine epithelium with myoepithelial layer; calcium oxalate crystals (birefringent) mostly in apocrine cysts.
entities.histo: Breast cysts are fluid-filled dilated terminal duct lobular units, common in perimenopausal women. They present as smooth, mobile, sometimes tender masses, and the classic gross cyst is blue-domed with turbid fluid. Simple cysts are lined by a flattened attenuated epithelium with an outer myoepithelial layer and sometimes no visible lining. Apocrine cysts are lined by eosinophilic cells with apical snouts and may show papillary apocrine change. Calcium oxalate (weddellite) crystals, which are colourless, birefringent and polyhedral, occur mainly in apocrine cysts and correlate with mammographic calcifications. Ruptured cysts provoke chronic inflammation, foamy histiocytes, cholesterol clefts and fibrosis. Cyst fluid cytology is usually not needed for simple cysts. Differentials include intracystic (encapsulated) papillary carcinoma and papilloma, which show papillary fronds; cystic hypersecretory lesions with colloid-like secretion; galactocele (milky contents); mucocele-like lesion with extravasated mucin; and epidermal inclusion cyst lined by squamous epithelium.
entities.cyto: Aspiration of a simple breast cyst yields clear, yellow, green or brown fluid, often with complete resolution of the lump. Smears are typically hypocellular, containing foamy macrophages, occasional apocrine cells and scanty ductal cells in a proteinaceous background. Many guidelines consider cytology of clear non-bloody cyst fluid unnecessary if the lump resolves, but bloody fluid, residual mass or recurrence warrant cytology and imaging, because intracystic papilloma or papillary carcinoma may present this way. Degenerated apocrine cells can look atypical. A cyst fluid with only macrophages is reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) cyst contents rather than insufficient.
entities.ihc: Benign breast cysts seldom need IHC. They're lined by flattened or apocrine epithelium with an outer myoepithelial layer, which may be attenuated. When the lining is lost or distorted, or a cyst wall is inflamed, p63, SMMHC or calponin can show residual myoepithelium, and keratin highlights surviving lining cells. Apocrine cyst lining is AR+ and GCDFP-15+, ER− and PR−, which is a normal profile rather than atypia. Cyst fluid cytology seldom requires ancillary studies. Polarisation identifies calcium oxalate (weddellite) crystals, which are typical of apocrine cysts and correlate with mammographic calcifications. Intracystic papillary lesions are worked up separately.

entities.variants: Simple apocrine metaplasia; papillary apocrine change (simple/complex); atypical apocrine metaplasia
entities.remarks: Eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, apical snouts, AR+/GCDFP-15+, ER/PR−; atypical apocrine change needs comparison with apocrine DCIS (nuclear enlargement ≥3x, necrosis).
entities.histo: Apocrine metaplasia is a frequent benign change, especially in cysts and fibrocystic change. The cells have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, apical cytoplasmic snouts and round nuclei with prominent nucleoli. They are typically AR-positive and GCDFP-15-positive, and usually ER-negative and PR-negative. Simple apocrine metaplasia forms a single layer. Papillary apocrine change ranges from simple papillae to complex anastomosing structures. Atypical apocrine metaplasia shows nuclear enlargement (about three times), pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli, and can be difficult to separate from apocrine DCIS. Apocrine DCIS shows marked nuclear enlargement, architectural complexity extending through ducts, necrosis and a larger extent. Because apocrine cells normally have large nuclei, atypia should be judged conservatively, especially on core biopsy. Differentials also include apocrine adenosis, which retains myoepithelium, invasive carcinoma with apocrine differentiation, and granular cell tumour, which is S100-positive.
entities.cyto: Apocrine metaplasia, commonly part of fibrocystic change, yields flat sheets, honeycomb groups or single cells with abundant dense granular eosinophilic (Pap orange-pink, MGG blue-grey with granules) cytoplasm, well-defined cell borders, round central nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Mild nuclear enlargement and anisonucleosis occur, and degenerated apocrine cells in cyst fluid may appear atypical. The background often contains foamy macrophages and cyst fluid. The main pitfall is over-calling apocrine atypia as apocrine carcinoma, which shows marked pleomorphism, dyscohesion and necrosis. Usually Yokohama Category 2 (Benign); Category 3 if atypia is significant.
entities.ihc: Apocrine metaplasia has a characteristic immunoprofile: AR positive, GCDFP-15 positive, and ER and PR negative or only weakly positive, with HER2 usually negative. Myoepithelial cells (p63, SMMHC, calponin) are retained around the involved glands. Because apocrine cells are ER− and CK5/6−, they can look like an 'abnormal' profile and lead to a false call of atypia or clonality. They don't follow the usual UDH pattern, so morphology is decisive. Atypical apocrine lesions are judged on nuclear enlargement (about three times normal), prominent nucleoli and necrosis rather than IHC, and Ki-67 is low in benign metaplasia.

entities.entity: Other metaplastic changes of breast epithelium
entities.variants: Squamous metaplasia (in cysts, papillomas, post-biopsy, gynaecomastia); clear cell change/metaplasia; mucinous/goblet cell metaplasia (rare); myoid metaplasia
entities.remarks: Benign; recognise to avoid over-calling carcinoma (e.g. clear cell change vs clear cell DCIS/LCIS).
entities.histo: Other metaplastic changes of breast epithelium are benign alterations that matter mainly as mimics. Squamous metaplasia is seen in cysts, papillomas, fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumours. It also occurs after biopsy or infarction, in gynaecomastia, and in subareolar ducts in SMOLD, and shows bland keratinising or non-keratinising squamous cells. It must be separated from squamous or metaplastic carcinoma by its bland cytology and confinement to pre-existing structures.
