Reactive keratinocyte atypia may also be present. Toker cells (bland CK7-positive cells) may be prominent in the epidermis. Correlation is needed with nipple adenoma, which shows florid proliferation with erosion, and with Paget disease (large atypical CK7-positive and HER2-positive cells), eczema and intraductal papilloma as causes of discharge.
entities.cyto: Other benign nipple changes, including nipple discharge without mass, hyperkeratosis and fibroepithelial polyp, are commonly assessed by nipple discharge or scrape cytology. Benign discharge shows foamy macrophages, proteinaceous debris, occasional apocrine cells, squames and sparse inflammatory cells. Bloody discharge with papillary clusters suggests papilloma, while atypical cells warrant imaging and biopsy. Nipple discharge cytology has low sensitivity, so a negative result does not exclude carcinoma or Paget disease. The Yokohama System primarily covers FNA, and nipple specimens are reported descriptively using analogous benign, atypical, suspicious or malignant terminology.
entities.ihc: IHC is seldom required for benign nipple changes such as lactiferous duct hyperplasia, nipple duct ectasia, and fissures or erosions. When there's an erosion or epidermal change, the key issue is excluding Paget disease. CK7, GATA3 and HER2 identify Paget cells. Toker cells are bland, CK7+ and HER2−. Bowen disease is p63+ and CK7−, and pagetoid melanoma is S100+, SOX10+ and Melan-A+. In duct proliferations of the nipple, myoepithelial markers and CK5/6 separate UDH and nipple adenoma from DCIS. Lactiferous duct squamous metaplasia is p63+ and CK5/6+.

entities.variants: Reactive follicular hyperplasia; silicone lymphadenopathy; dermatopathic changes
entities.remarks: Upper outer quadrant; may harbour metastasis or lymphoma; may be sentinel node.
entities.histo: Intramammary lymph nodes are found most often in the upper outer quadrant and appear on mammography as circumscribed, reniform nodules with a fatty hilum. They may be removed as a sentinel node or as an indeterminate mass. Reactive changes include follicular hyperplasia with large germinal centres, sinus histiocytosis and paracortical hyperplasia. Silicone lymphadenopathy shows sinusoidal vacuolated histiocytes and giant cells with refractile material in patients with implants. Dermatopathic changes include paracortical expansion by Langerhans and interdigitating cells with melanin-laden macrophages, in patients with skin disease. Intramammary nodes may harbour metastatic breast carcinoma, which is staged as an axillary nodal metastasis, or metastatic lobular carcinoma in the sinuses mimicking histiocytes. They may also harbour lymphoma, benign epithelial inclusions or nevus cell rests. Keratin IHC helps detect subtle metastasis. Differentials of a reactive node include lymphoma (architectural effacement, monotonous population), toxoplasmosis and cat-scratch disease.
entities.cyto: Intramammary or axillary reactive lymph node aspirates show a polymorphous lymphoid population dominated by small lymphocytes with centrocytes, centroblasts, immunoblasts, plasma cells, tingible body macrophages and lymphoglandular bodies, sometimes with follicular dendritic cell aggregates. Epithelial cells are absent. The node can mimic a breast mass radiologically. Pitfalls include metastatic carcinoma (especially lobular, which may be sparse and single-cell), lymphoma (monomorphic population requiring flow cytometry) and granulomatous lymphadenitis. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or using the Sydney System (Benign/reactive) for lymph node specimens.
entities.ihc: In a reactive intramammary lymph node, IHC mainly serves to exclude metastatic carcinoma and lymphoma. Pan-keratin (AE1/AE3), and in lobular cases E-cadherin-negative keratin-positive cells, detects metastases, while GATA3 confirms breast origin. Reactive follicles are CD10+, BCL6+ and BCL2-negative with a high Ki-67, polar and tingible-body macrophage-rich, which separates them from follicular lymphoma (BCL2+). Benign epithelial inclusions or ectopic breast tissue have a myoepithelial layer (p63, calponin), unlike metastases. In dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, S100+ and CD1a+ Langerhans and interdigitating cells are prominent. Silicone lymphadenopathy shows CD68+ vacuolated histiocytes.

entities.remarks: Benign florid sclerosing ductal proliferation in subareolar region, resembling radial scar/papilloma; myoepithelium retained; mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging.
entities.histo: Subareolar sclerosing duct hyperplasia is a rare, benign, florid proliferative lesion of the subareolar ducts, usually in middle-aged women. It presents as a firm, palpable subareolar mass with irregular margins that mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging, sometimes with nipple discharge. Microscopically, it is a poorly circumscribed lesion of ducts with florid usual-type epithelial hyperplasia, papillary areas and central sclerosis that distorts and entraps ducts. It resembles a radial scar or a sclerosing papilloma, but it is located beneath the nipple rather than at the nipple surface. Entrapped glands in sclerotic stroma can appear infiltrative, but they retain a continuous myoepithelial layer on p63, calponin and SMMHC. Apocrine metaplasia, cysts and calcifications are common. Cytological atypia is absent, and the CK5/6 pattern is mosaic. Differentials include nipple adenoma, which involves the nipple ducts and may erode the epidermis, radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, sclerosing intraductal papilloma, and invasive carcinoma, which lacks myoepithelium and lobulocentric organisation. Local excision is curative.
entities.cyto: Subareolar sclerosing duct hyperplasia is rarely described cytologically; aspirates from this subareolar mass are expected to show moderate cellularity with cohesive, sometimes crowded sheets and small angulated groups of bland ductal cells, retained myoepithelial cells, bare bipolar nuclei, apocrine cells and fragments of sclerotic stroma. Squamous cells from the nipple region may be admixed. Crowding and small tubules entrapped in sclerotic stroma can mimic tubular or low-grade invasive carcinoma, and the lesion overlaps with papilloma, nipple adenoma and radial scar. Preserved myoepithelium and bare nuclei favour benignity. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or, given clinical and radiological suspicion, Category 3 (Atypical) with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Subareolar sclerosing duct hyperplasia is a florid, sclerosing ductal proliferation under the nipple that resembles a radial scar or papilloma and can mimic carcinoma clinically and on imaging. IHC is used mainly to confirm that it is benign. Myoepithelial markers (p63 together with SMMHC or calponin) show a retained myoepithelial layer around the distorted, entrapped ducts in the sclerotic stroma, which separates it from invasive carcinoma. The proliferating epithelium shows the heterogeneous, mosaic CK5/6 and ER pattern of usual ductal hyperplasia. A monotonous, uniformly ER-positive, CK5/6-negative area would suggest ADH or DCIS. Squamous metaplasia (p63+, CK5/6+) and apocrine change (AR+) may be present. Nipple adenoma and syringomatous tumour are separated mainly on location and architecture.

entities.entity: Breast changes with gender-affirming hormone therapy (transgender breast pathology)
entities.variants: Trans-feminine (estrogen: ductal and lobular development, PASH, fibroadenoma-like changes); trans-masculine (testosterone: lobular atrophy, stromal fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia) in mastectomy specimens
entities.remarks: Recognised specimen category; carcinoma occurs rarely in both groups.
entities.histo: Breast changes with gender-affirming hormone therapy are now a recognised specimen category, most often encountered in chest-masculinising mastectomy specimens from trans-masculine individuals receiving testosterone. These show lobular atrophy with reduced or small lobules, dense stromal fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia, periductal fibrosis, mild chronic inflammation and sometimes cysts, and findings consistent with background fibrocystic change. Tissue from trans-feminine individuals receiving oestrogen with anti-androgens shows breast development resembling female puberty. This includes formation of ducts and lobules (lobular development), gynaecomastoid hyperplasia, PASH, and fibroadenoma-like or adenosis-like change, sometimes with secretory change. Pathologists should sample these specimens appropriately according to institutional policy and look specifically for atypia, lesions requiring follow-up, and incidental carcinoma, which occurs rarely in both groups. Differentials include gynaecomastia, fibrocystic change, PASH, fibroadenoma, and occult carcinoma. Reports should use respectful, accurate terminology and correlate with the clinical history and duration of therapy.
entities.cyto: Breast changes with gender-affirming hormone therapy are mostly seen in mastectomy specimens rather than cytology. In trans-feminine patients on oestrogen, aspirates of a lump may resemble normal or gynaecomastia-like breast or fibroadenoma, with cohesive bland ductal sheets, myoepithelial cells, bare bipolar nuclei and stroma, sometimes PASH-like stromal fragments. In trans-masculine patients on testosterone, aspirates are usually hypocellular with fibrous stroma, scanty atrophic ductal cells and apocrine cells. These changes are benign, and carcinoma, though rare, must still be excluded by standard criteria. Hormone history should be stated on the request. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) when adequate.
entities.ihc: In breast tissue from gender-affirming hormone therapy, IHC is seldom needed and mainly confirms benign changes. In trans-feminine (oestrogen-treated) specimens, newly formed ducts and lobules keep a normal p63/calponin-positive myoepithelial layer with heterogeneous ER/PR and CK5/6, and the PASH-like stroma is CD34+ and PR+. In trans-masculine (testosterone-treated) mastectomies, lobular atrophy, stromal fibrosis and apocrine metaplasia are seen. The apocrine cells are AR+ and GCDFP-15+, and ER is often reduced, which shouldn't be read as atypia. Incidental carcinoma is rare in both groups. It's worked up in the usual way with myoepithelial markers, E-cadherin, and ER, PR and HER2 per ASCO/CAP. AR status may be relevant.

entities.remarks: Benign clear intraepidermal cells of the nipple; CK7+, usually HER2−; key mimic of Paget disease (Toker cells are bland, with no underlying carcinoma).
entities.histo: Toker cell hyperplasia refers to an increased number of Toker cells, benign clear cells found in the nipple epidermis of a proportion of normal nipples, most often near the openings of lactiferous ducts. It is usually an incidental finding, but it is important as the key mimic of Paget disease. Microscopically, scattered single cells or small clusters with abundant pale to clear cytoplasm lie in the basal and lower epidermal layers. Their nuclei are bland, round to oval, small and uniform, with fine chromatin and small or inconspicuous nucleoli, and mitoses are absent. Clusters may form small duct-like structures, and hyperplastic Toker cells may be more numerous or show mild atypia. They are positive for CK7, CAM5.2 and often GATA3, but usually HER2-negative and negative for p63, S100 and SOX10. There is no underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma. The main differential is Paget disease, which shows large pleomorphic cells, prominent nucleoli, mitoses and HER2 positivity, with underlying carcinoma. Others are clear keratinocytes (p63-positive, CK7-negative), melanocytes and pagetoid Bowen disease.
entities.cyto: Toker cell hyperplasia is an incidental intraepidermal finding of the nipple and is not sampled by FNA. On nipple scrape or imprint, Toker cells may appear as occasional single or small groups of cells with pale or clear cytoplasm and bland, round, uniform nuclei with fine chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli, among squames. The key pitfall is Paget disease, whose cells are larger, pleomorphic, with prominent nucleoli and usually HER2 positivity; both are CK7 positive, so CK7 alone cannot separate them. Bland cells without atypia favour Toker cells, but persistent nipple changes require biopsy. Reported descriptively as benign (analogous to Yokohama Category 2).
entities.ihc: Toker cells are benign clear cells in the epidermis of the nipple. They're important mainly as a mimic of Paget disease. They are CK7 positive and CAM5.2 positive, often ER positive, and usually HER2 negative, with a low Ki-67, and they lack the nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli and mitoses of Paget cells. Paget cells are typically HER2 3+ and GATA3 positive, are atypical, and are associated with underlying DCIS or carcinoma. Because CK7 and GATA3 stain both cell types, HER2 combined with morphology is the most useful discriminator. Bowen disease (p63+, CK7−) and pagetoid melanoma in situ (SOX10+, Melan-A+) are excluded with a small panel. An underlying carcinoma should be excluded clinically and radiologically.

entities.remarks: Polyclonal lymphoid proliferation with germinal centres; exclude MALT lymphoma (light-chain restriction, clonality studies).
entities.histo: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (pseudolymphoma) of the breast is a rare, benign, polyclonal lymphoid proliferation that forms a mass or nodule and clinically or radiologically mimics carcinoma or lymphoma. Microscopically, there is a dense, sometimes nodular lymphoid infiltrate with numerous reactive follicles. The follicles have well-formed germinal centres with polarisation, tingible-body macrophages and intact mantle zones, and the interfollicular areas contain small lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes and vessels. Ducts and lobules may be surrounded or partially effaced, but true destructive lymphoepithelial lesions are absent or minimal. Germinal centres are BCL2-negative. The B and T cells are mixed, and kappa and lambda staining or ISH shows polytypic plasma cells, with no monotypic population. Clonality studies (IGH PCR) are polyclonal. It is essential to exclude MALT lymphoma, which shows marginal zone expansion, monocytoid B cells, lymphoepithelial lesions, light-chain restriction and clonality. Other differentials include intramammary lymph node, lymphocytic (diabetic) mastopathy, IgG4-related mastitis and follicular lymphoma (BCL2-positive follicles). Follow-up is advised because some cases evolve to lymphoma.
entities.cyto: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (pseudolymphoma) of breast yields cellular aspirates of a polymorphous lymphoid population, with small lymphocytes predominating together with centrocytes, centroblasts, immunoblasts, plasma cells, tingible body macrophages and lymphoglandular bodies, sometimes with follicular dendritic cell clusters. Epithelial cells are scanty or absent. The picture resembles a reactive lymph node, and the main differential is marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, which can also appear polymorphous; follicular lymphoma and lymphocytic mastitis are others. Flow cytometry showing polyclonal B cells without light-chain restriction is essential. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) when clonality is excluded, otherwise Category 3 (Atypical) with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: In reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (pseudolymphoma) of the breast, the job of IHC is to show polyclonality and exclude MALT lymphoma. Reactive germinal centres are CD10+, BCL6+ and BCL2-negative, with a high, polarised Ki-67 and tingible-body macrophages. CD21 or CD23 shows intact follicular dendritic cell meshworks. A mixture of CD20+ B cells and CD3+ T cells is present. Kappa and lambda ISH show a polytypic plasma cell population. Monotypic plasma cells, sheets of CD20+/CD43+ marginal-zone cells, or lymphoepithelial lesions highlighted by keratin favour MALT lymphoma, and IGH gene rearrangement studies are used when the result is equivocal. Lymphocytic mastopathy, IgG4-related mastitis (IgG4 counts) and an intramammary lymph node are other differentials.

entities.remarks: Rare; seen in myelofibrosis/haemoglobinopathies, or post-chemotherapy/G-CSF; megakaryocytes can mimic carcinoma cells.
entities.histo: Extramedullary haematopoiesis of the breast is rare. It occurs in myelofibrosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, in haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia, and after chemotherapy with G-CSF support. It may also be found incidentally in post-chemotherapy specimens and fibroepithelial lesions. It can present as a mass or as calcifications. Microscopically, trilineage haematopoietic cells are scattered in the stroma, around ducts and in vessels. These include erythroid precursors with round dark nuclei, myeloid precursors including eosinophilic myelocytes, and megakaryocytes. Megakaryocytes are large cells with lobulated, hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant cytoplasm, and they can mimic atypical carcinoma cells or the bizarre stromal giant cells of phyllodes tumour. IHC confirms the haematopoietic nature, with CD61 or CD42b for megakaryocytes, MPO for myeloid cells, and glycophorin or E-cadherin for erythroid cells, and keratins are negative. Differentials include metastatic or residual carcinoma after chemotherapy, myeloid sarcoma (sheets of blasts), the stromal giant cells of fibroepithelial lesions and inflammatory infiltrates. Correlation with haematological history is essential.
entities.cyto: Extramedullary haematopoiesis of the breast is rare and occurs in myelofibrosis, haemoglobinopathies, or after chemotherapy or G-CSF. Aspirates show a trilineage haematopoietic population: myeloid precursors at various stages, erythroid precursors with round dark nuclei, and large megakaryocytes with multilobated hyperchromatic nuclei, in a bloody background, sometimes with adipose tissue. Megakaryocytes can mimic pleomorphic carcinoma or tumour giant cells, which is the main pitfall, and myeloid precursors may raise concern for myeloid sarcoma. Clinical history and recognition of the mixed lineages are key; CD61 or factor VIII and MPO on cell block help. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), with clinical correlation.
entities.ihc: IHC helps identify extramedullary haematopoiesis (EMH) in the breast, especially when megakaryocytes or immature cells mimic carcinoma or lymphoma. Megakaryocytes are CD61, CD42b and factor VIII positive and keratin negative, which separates them from pleomorphic carcinoma cells. Erythroid precursors are glycophorin A/C, CD71 and E-cadherin positive (note this E-cadherin pitfall). Myeloid cells are myeloperoxidase, lysozyme and CD15 positive. The main differential is myeloid sarcoma, which shows sheets of immature blasts (CD34+, CD117+, MPO+) rather than trilineage maturing haematopoiesis. Clinical correlation with myelofibrosis, haemoglobinopathy or recent G-CSF or chemotherapy is essential. JAK2, CALR or MPL testing belongs to the systemic workup.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th: columnar cell lesion with low-grade (monomorphic) cytological atypia without architectural complexity; part of low-grade breast neoplasia family (with ADH, LN, low-grade DCIS, tubular ca); ER+, CK5/6−.
entities.histo: Flat epithelial atypia (FEA) is a columnar cell lesion in which one to several layers of epithelium show low-grade, monomorphic cytological atypia without the complex architecture of ADH or DCIS. It usually presents as mammographic microcalcifications. Acini of the terminal duct lobular unit are enlarged and dilated, often with flocculent luminal secretions and calcifications. They are lined by cuboidal to columnar cells with round, rather than oval, nuclei, an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, loss of polarity and small, often visible nucleoli, which gives a low-grade look at low power. Cells may form small mounds but no rigid bridges, arcades or micropapillae. FEA is ER-positive and CK5/6-negative. It belongs to the low-grade neoplasia family, with ADH, lobular neoplasia, low-grade DCIS and tubular carcinoma, which commonly coexist. Differentials include columnar cell change (oval nuclei oriented perpendicular to the basement membrane), ADH, clinging-type DCIS, apocrine metaplasia and cystic hypersecretory lesions. Upgrade rates on excision are low, and management is often tailored by multidisciplinary review.
entities.cyto: Flat epithelial atypia is a mammographic-calcification lesion usually diagnosed on core biopsy; it is not a cytological diagnosis. Aspirates, if obtained, may show cohesive groups of monotonous cuboidal to columnar cells with mild nuclear enlargement, round nuclei, slight loss of polarity, apical snouts and scant secretions, sometimes with calcific debris, and reduced numbers of myoepithelial cells. These features overlap with columnar cell change, low-grade ADH, low-grade DCIS and tubular carcinoma (the Rosen triad). Cytology cannot reliably separate these, so findings are reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with core biopsy or excision.
entities.ihc: Flat epithelial atypia (FEA) shows one to several layers of monotonous columnar cells with low-grade nuclear atypia. Its immunoprofile is strong, diffuse ER and PR positivity, CK5/6 and CK14 negativity, CK8/18 and CK19 positivity, and a low Ki-67, with a retained myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin). This profile is shared with columnar cell lesions without atypia, ADH and low-grade DCIS, so IHC can't separate FEA from them. The diagnosis rests on cytological atypia (rounded nuclei, loss of polarity, nucleoli). FEA is clonal (16q loss, 1q gain) and part of the low-grade neoplasia family, often with coexisting lobular neoplasia or tubular carcinoma.

entities.variants: ADH in TDLU; ADH within papilloma (atypical focus <3 mm); ADH in radial scar / fibroadenoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: monotonous cells with rigid bridges/cribriform/micropapillary architecture, qualitatively like low-grade DCIS but ≤2 mm or ≤2 membrane-bound spaces; RR ~4–5; excision usually recommended on core biopsy.
entities.histo: Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) is a clonal intraductal proliferation of monotonous, evenly spaced cells with low-grade round nuclei. It has rigid bridges, cribriform spaces, arcades or micropapillae, and so is qualitatively similar to low-grade DCIS, but it is quantitatively limited. It involves no more than two membrane-bound spaces, or measures 2 mm or less, and partial involvement of spaces with residual polarised luminal cells also favours ADH. The cells are diffusely ER-positive and CK5/6-negative, unlike the mosaic pattern of UDH. ADH within a papilloma is defined as an atypical focus under 3 mm, and ADH can also occur in radial scars and fibroadenomas. The relative risk of later carcinoma is about four to five times, in either breast. On core biopsy, surgical or vacuum excision is usually recommended because of upgrade to DCIS or invasive carcinoma. Differentials are florid UDH, low-grade DCIS, lobular neoplasia (E-cadherin loss), columnar cell lesions with FEA, and collagenous spherulosis.
entities.cyto: Atypical ductal hyperplasia cannot be reliably diagnosed or distinguished from low-grade DCIS on FNA, as the distinction is based on histological size and extent criteria. Aspirates show moderately to highly cellular smears with crowded, sometimes cribriform or rigid groups of fairly monotonous cells with mild to moderate nuclear enlargement, reduced myoepithelial cells and fewer bare nuclei, but without significant dyscohesion or necrosis. The overlap with UDH, fibroadenoma, low-grade DCIS and invasive low-grade carcinoma is substantial. Such smears are reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with core biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: IHC can support but not alone establish atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH). ADH is monotonous and clonal, with strong, diffuse ER positivity and uniform CK5/6 (CK14, 34βE12) negativity in the atypical cells. This is the opposite of the heterogeneous mosaic pattern of usual ductal hyperplasia. The ADH-5 cocktail (CK5/14, p63, CK7/18) is useful. The distinction between ADH and low-grade DCIS is quantitative (two ducts or at least 2 mm) and not resolved by IHC. Myoepithelium is retained. E-cadherin is useful when the cells are solid and monotonous, to exclude lobular neoplasia. In papillomas and radial scars, the same CK5/6 and ER pattern helps identify atypical foci.

entities.variants: Pagetoid spread into ducts
entities.remarks: WHO 5th non-invasive lobular neoplasia; discohesive monomorphic cells filling <50% of acini of a lobule without distension; E-cadherin loss / p120 cytoplasmic; RR ~4–5.
entities.histo: Atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH) belongs to non-invasive lobular neoplasia. It is usually incidental, and it does not form a mass or calcifications of its own. Acini of a lobule are partly filled by a monomorphic population of small, round, discohesive cells with uniform nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli and sometimes intracytoplasmic vacuoles or targetoid mucin. They fill less than half of the acini of a lobule without distending them, and residual lumina may persist. Pagetoid spread is common: neoplastic cells undermine the normal luminal epithelium of adjacent ducts beneath an intact luminal layer. The cells show loss of membranous E-cadherin, with cytoplasmic p120 and beta-catenin, owing to CDH1 inactivation, and are ER-positive. ALH carries a relative risk of about four to five, affecting either breast. Differentials include LCIS (more than 50% of acini filled and distended), solid low-grade DCIS (E-cadherin retained), clear cell change, and cancerisation of lobules by DCIS.
entities.cyto: Atypical lobular hyperplasia is a histological diagnosis, usually incidental, and is not diagnosed on cytology. If cells are present in an aspirate, they appear as small, uniform, loosely cohesive or single cells with round nuclei, scant cytoplasm and occasional intracytoplasmic lumina (targetoid vacuoles), resembling lobular carcinoma in situ and invasive lobular carcinoma. These cannot be distinguished on FNA, and the cells may be very few and easily overlooked or mistaken for lymphocytes. Such findings are reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) with core biopsy; adequate smears of bland ductal cells alone are Category 2.
entities.ihc: E-cadherin is the key IHC test for atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH), which shows loss of membrane E-cadherin (or aberrant, fragmented or cytoplasmic staining) in the discohesive lobular cells. p120 catenin moves from the membrane to diffuse cytoplasmic staining, and β-catenin is lost. CK8/18 shows perinuclear ring staining. The cells are ER positive and PR positive, HER2 negative, and have a low Ki-67. Myoepithelium is preserved, often with a pagetoid pattern in which ALH cells undermine the duct epithelium. The ALH versus LCIS distinction is quantitative (degree of lobular distension), not immunohistochemical. CDH1 alteration underlies the E-cadherin loss.

entities.variants: Classic LCIS (type A and B cells); florid LCIS (marked distension, confluent, may have necrosis/calcification); pleomorphic LCIS (grade 3 nuclei, may be apocrine, often necrosis)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th non-invasive lobular neoplasia; classic LCIS = risk factor & non-obligate precursor (RR ~8–10); florid and pleomorphic LCIS behave more aggressively and are managed like DCIS (clear excision); CDH1 alteration, E-cadherin negative.
entities.histo: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is non-invasive lobular neoplasia in which discohesive, monomorphic neoplastic cells fill and distend more than half of the acini of a lobule. Classic LCIS consists of type A cells, which are small and uniform with scanty cytoplasm, and type B cells, which are slightly larger with more cytoplasm and mild nuclear variation. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles and pagetoid spread along ducts are common. Classic LCIS is a risk factor and non-obligate precursor of carcinoma, with a relative risk of about 8 to 10, in either breast. Florid LCIS shows marked acinar distension with confluence, minimal intervening stroma, and frequently central necrosis or calcification. Pleomorphic LCIS shows grade 3 nuclei, often apocrine cytoplasm and necrosis, and may be HER2-positive. Florid and pleomorphic LCIS are managed like DCIS, with excision to clear margins. All forms show E-cadherin loss due to CDH1 alteration. Differentials include solid DCIS (E-cadherin retained, cohesive cells), especially for florid and pleomorphic forms, and collagenous spherulosis involved by LCIS.
entities.cyto: Lobular carcinoma in situ, classic type, cannot be distinguished from atypical lobular hyperplasia or invasive lobular carcinoma on cytology. Aspirates usually show low to moderate cellularity with loosely cohesive small groups and single, uniform, small to intermediate cells with round eccentric nuclei, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli and intracytoplasmic lumina, sometimes with signet ring forms. Pleomorphic and florid LCIS show larger pleomorphic nuclei and may mimic high-grade DCIS or invasive carcinoma. Since invasion cannot be assessed, findings are generally reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or 4 (Suspicious), with core biopsy and E-cadherin on histology.
entities.ihc: Lobular carcinoma in situ is characterised by loss of E-cadherin, with p120 catenin moved to diffuse cytoplasmic staining and β-catenin lost. This separates it from solid low-grade DCIS (membrane E-cadherin and p120). About 15% of lobular lesions keep aberrant, fragmented E-cadherin staining, so p120 is a useful addition. Classic LCIS is ER+, PR+, HER2−, Ki-67 low. Florid and pleomorphic LCIS may be ER-positive or negative, with HER2 overexpression, higher Ki-67 and p53 positivity in some, and need excision. Myoepithelial markers confirm that the lesion is in situ. CK5/6 is negative, which can mislead toward DCIS, so E-cadherin is the deciding stain.

entities.variants: Nuclear grade: low, intermediate, high. Architecture: cribriform, micropapillary, solid, papillary, flat (clinging), comedo (central necrosis). Cytological variants: apocrine, signet-ring/mucinous, neuroendocrine, spindle cell, squamous, clear cell, cystic hypersecretory DCIS. DCIS involving sclerosing adenosis/papilloma/radial scar/fibroadenoma
entities.remarks: Non-invasive (pTis) clonal neoplastic proliferation confined to ductal-lobular system; non-obligate precursor of invasive carcinoma. Report grade, necrosis, size/extent, margins, ER (± HER2 in some settings); low-grade DCIS ≥2 mm; myoepithelial layer present.
entities.histo: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a clonal neoplastic epithelial proliferation confined to the duct-lobular system with an intact myoepithelial layer and basement membrane. It is a non-obligate precursor of invasive carcinoma and is staged pTis. It usually presents as mammographic calcifications. Nuclear grade is low (uniform small nuclei, even spacing), intermediate, or high (large pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, mitoses). Low-grade DCIS must involve at least two ducts or measure more than 2 mm to separate it from ADH. Architectural patterns include cribriform, micropapillary, solid, papillary and flat or clinging, and comedo DCIS shows central necrosis with calcification. Rare cytological variants include apocrine, signet-ring or mucinous, neuroendocrine, spindle cell, squamous, clear cell and cystic hypersecretory. DCIS may involve sclerosing adenosis, papillomas, radial scars and fibroadenomas, mimicking invasion. Reports should give grade, necrosis, architecture, size or extent, margins and ER status. Differentials include ADH, UDH, LCIS (E-cadherin loss), and invasion, which is assessed with myoepithelial markers.
entities.cyto: Ductal carcinoma in situ cannot be distinguished from invasive carcinoma on FNA because invasion is a histological feature. High-grade DCIS yields cellular smears with dyscohesive groups and single cells showing marked pleomorphism, coarse chromatin and nucleoli, in a background of necrotic debris (comedonecrosis) and calcifications, often reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, with a comment that invasion cannot be assessed. Low-grade DCIS shows cohesive, monotonous cells, cribriform or micropapillary groups and few bare nuclei, overlapping with ADH and often reported as Category 3 or 4. Core biopsy is required to assess invasion.
entities.ihc: In DCIS, IHC confirms the in-situ nature and characterises the lesion. Myoepithelial markers (p63 with SMMHC or calponin) are preserved around involved ducts, and their absence is assessed carefully to exclude microinvasion. E-cadherin is positive and separates it from LCIS, notably solid low-grade DCIS from LCIS. Low-grade DCIS is uniformly ER-positive and CK5/6-negative, unlike UDH. High-grade DCIS can be ER-negative, HER2-positive or basal-like (CK5/6+). ER is routinely reported because it guides endocrine therapy, and HER2 testing is optional, or used in trials. Ki-67 isn't standard. Assess for microinvasion with keratin and myoepithelial stains.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th: atypical monotonous proliferation within papilloma measuring ≥3 mm (<3 mm = papilloma with ADH); high-grade atypia = DCIS regardless of size.
entities.histo: Intraductal papilloma with DCIS is defined in WHO 5th edition as a papilloma, with its myoepithelium-lined fibrovascular cores, partly colonised by an atypical monotonous epithelial proliferation. That proliferation is cytologically and architecturally identical to low- or intermediate-grade DCIS and measures 3 mm or more. A similar focus under 3 mm is classified as papilloma with ADH. Any high-grade atypia, in the form of large pleomorphic nuclei, necrosis or mitoses, is diagnosed as DCIS regardless of size. The atypical areas show solid, cribriform or micropapillary architecture with monotonous cells that are diffusely ER-positive and CK5/6-negative. They contrast with the mosaic CK5/6 pattern of the benign residual papilloma and of UDH. Myoepithelium is retained in the uninvolved papilloma and at the duct periphery. Differentials include papilloma with florid UDH, papillary DCIS (lacking a benign papilloma background), encapsulated papillary carcinoma and solid papillary carcinoma. Excision with assessment of margins and surrounding tissue for additional DCIS is recommended.
entities.cyto: Intraductal papilloma with DCIS cannot be reliably diagnosed on FNA. Aspirates show features of papilloma, such as papillary clusters with fibrovascular cores, foamy macrophages, apocrine cells and sometimes haemorrhage, together with areas of more monotonous, crowded epithelial cells with reduced myoepithelial cells. Distinguishing atypical from benign papillary epithelium is unreliable, and the IAC Yokohama System recommends that papillary lesions be reported as at least Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious) when atypia is present, with excision or core biopsy for definitive classification.
entities.ihc: In an intraductal papilloma with DCIS, IHC delineates the atypical area and confirms that the lesion is in situ. The background papilloma shows heterogeneous CK5/6 and ER staining, with a myoepithelial layer along the fibrovascular cores and at the periphery (p63, SMMHC, calponin, CK5/6). The DCIS component is monotonous, uniformly ER-positive and CK5/6-negative, and usually lacks myoepithelium within it. WHO 5th edition grades it by size: an atypical focus under 3 mm is papilloma with ADH, and 3 mm or more is papilloma with DCIS (any size if high grade). E-cadherin excludes lobular neoplasia colonising the papilloma. Peripheral myoepithelium is retained.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th: DCIS with true fibrovascular cores lacking myoepithelial cells within papillae, but myoepithelium retained at duct periphery; often multiple ducts, usually low/intermediate grade.
entities.histo: Papillary ductal carcinoma in situ is DCIS with papillary architecture, often involving several adjacent ducts rather than forming a single cystic lesion. Neoplastic epithelium covers thin, delicate true fibrovascular cores. The cores lack myoepithelial cells, but a myoepithelial layer persists around the periphery of the involved ducts. The epithelium is monotonous, usually of low or intermediate nuclear grade, and stratified columnar or solid, often with cribriform or micropapillary areas between papillae and sometimes dimorphic cells. It is uniformly ER-positive and CK5/6-negative. The lesion is staged and managed as DCIS. Differentials include intraductal papilloma with DCIS, in which a benign papilloma with myoepithelium-lined cores is partly involved; encapsulated papillary carcinoma, which is a single cystic nodule with a fibrous capsule and usually no peripheral myoepithelium; solid papillary carcinoma; and micropapillary DCIS, whose fronds lack fibrovascular cores. Myoepithelial IHC with p63, calponin and SMMHC is essential for this distinction.
entities.cyto: Papillary DCIS yields cellular smears with papillary and three-dimensional clusters, often with fibrovascular cores, numerous single intact columnar epithelial cells with mildly to moderately atypical, monotonous, elongated nuclei, and absent or scanty myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei. A haemorrhagic or cystic background with haemosiderin-laden macrophages is common. Distinction from benign papilloma, papilloma with atypia, encapsulated papillary carcinoma and invasive papillary carcinoma is not possible on cytology. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 3 (Atypical), papillary lesion, with excision recommended.
entities.ihc: Papillary DCIS is a DCIS with papillary architecture, in which the fibrovascular cores are covered by monotonous neoplastic cells and lack myoepithelial cells along the papillae. A peripheral myoepithelial layer at the duct wall is retained. p63, SMMHC and calponin show this pattern, which separates it from a benign papilloma (myoepithelium along cores and periphery) and from encapsulated papillary carcinoma (often no peripheral myoepithelium). The neoplastic cells are typically strongly ER+ and PR+, CK5/6− and HER2−, and E-cadherin positive. A uniform ER-positive, CK5/6-negative profile confirms clonality. Keratin can help assess whether there's an invasive component.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th: solid nodules with delicate fibrovascular cores, often neuroendocrine differentiation (synaptophysin/chromogranin) and extracellular mucin; ER+; staged as in situ (pTis) when nodules are rounded even if myoepithelium is absent at periphery; invasive when jigsaw/geographic pattern (see Malignant).
entities.histo: Solid papillary carcinoma in situ consists of circumscribed, expansile, rounded solid nodules that fill ducts in older women and may present with bloody nipple discharge or a mass. The nodules are composed of monotonous, low- to intermediate-grade epithelial cells, often spindled and streaming, around delicate fibrovascular cores, so the papillary nature can be subtle. Neuroendocrine differentiation is frequent, with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 positivity, and intracellular or extracellular mucin. The tumour is strongly ER-positive and HER2-negative, and CK5/6 is negative. A myoepithelial layer may be absent at the periphery of the nodules. WHO 5th edition nevertheless considers solid papillary carcinoma with rounded, smooth-contoured nodules to be in situ (pTis). When the nodules form irregular, jigsaw or geographic shapes infiltrating stroma, or when mucinous or NST carcinoma accompanies them, the lesion is solid papillary carcinoma with invasion, staged on the invasive component. Differentials include florid UDH, solid DCIS, encapsulated papillary carcinoma and neuroendocrine tumour.
entities.cyto: Solid papillary carcinoma in situ yields cellular smears with many single cells and loosely cohesive solid groups of uniform cells with round to oval, sometimes plasmacytoid nuclei, fine granular salt-and-pepper chromatin and moderate granular cytoplasm, around delicate capillaries; extracellular or intracellular mucin may be present. Bare nuclei and myoepithelial cells are scanty. Neuroendocrine differentiation (synaptophysin, chromogranin on cell block) is common. The monotony may suggest a low-grade neoplasm and mimic papilloma, mucinous carcinoma or neuroendocrine tumour. Invasion cannot be assessed. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or 5 (Malignant), with histology for invasion.
entities.ihc: Solid papillary carcinoma in situ is typically strongly ER+ and PR+, HER2−, CK5/6−, and has a low Ki-67. Neuroendocrine markers are often positive: synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 in about half of cases. Intracellular or extracellular mucin is common. Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMMHC, calponin) may be present, reduced or absent at the periphery of the expansile nodules. If they're absent but the contour is smooth and rounded, WHO 5th edition treats it as in situ, staged as Tis. A jagged, geographic contour means invasive SPC. Separate it from UDH (CK5/6 heterogeneous) and from TCCRP (ER−, IDH2 R172 mutation).

entities.remarks: Cystic hypersecretory lesion with nuclear atypia/micropapillary proliferation, short of cystic hypersecretory DCIS.
entities.histo: Atypical cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia is part of the cystic hypersecretory spectrum, intermediate between cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia without atypia and cystic hypersecretory DCIS. Cysts and dilated ducts are filled with dense, homogeneous, eosinophilic colloid-like secretion that shows retraction and cracks, resembling thyroid follicles. The epithelial lining shows nuclear enlargement, mild to moderate pleomorphism, crowding and focal micropapillary or tufted proliferation. However, the extent or degree of atypia falls short of a confident diagnosis of DCIS, which shows more extensive micropapillary growth and higher-grade atypia. The secretions are PAS-positive and thyroglobulin-negative, and the epithelium is GATA3-positive. Because the lesions are uncommon and may be associated with DCIS or invasive carcinoma elsewhere, excision with generous sampling is generally advised. Differentials include cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia without atypia, cystic hypersecretory DCIS, metastatic thyroid carcinoma (TTF-1 and thyroglobulin positive), secretory carcinoma (S100-positive, ETV6::NTRK3) and pseudolactational hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Atypical cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia is rarely diagnosed on FNA. Aspirates show abundant dense, colloid-like secretion with cracking artefact, foamy macrophages and groups of ductal cells showing mild to moderate nuclear atypia, crowding and occasional micropapillary architecture. Distinction from cystic hypersecretory change without atypia and from cystic hypersecretory carcinoma (DCIS) is not possible cytologically, and the colloid-like material may mimic thyroid colloid or mucin. Smears showing atypical cells with this secretion are reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or 4 (Suspicious), with excision recommended.
entities.ihc: Atypical cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia is diagnosed on morphology: thyroid-like colloid secretion in cystically dilated ducts, with mild atypia, micropapillary tufts or crowding. IHC is supportive. The epithelium is GATA3+ and CK7+, and TTF-1 and thyroglobulin negative, which excludes thyroid metastasis. Myoepithelium is retained (p63, SMMHC, calponin). Atypical areas tend toward a more uniform, CK5/6-negative pattern, and ER may be variable. The distinction from cystic hypersecretory DCIS rests on morphology, and these lesions are associated with invasive carcinoma, often high grade or ER-negative, so complete excision and careful sampling are needed.

entities.variants: Classic MGA; atypical microglandular adenosis; MGA-associated carcinoma (see Malignant)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th adenosis entity; haphazard infiltrative small round glands with eosinophilic secretions, single epithelial layer lacking myoepithelium but with basement membrane (laminin/collagen IV); S100+, ER−/PR−/HER2−. Considered a non-obligate precursor of triple-negative carcinoma (incl. acinic cell carcinoma) — complete excision advised.
entities.histo: Microglandular adenosis (MGA) is a rare, infiltrative proliferation of small round glands distributed haphazardly in fibrous stroma and fat, without lobulocentricity. The glands have open lumina containing eosinophilic, PAS-positive secretions and are lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland round nuclei. They lack myoepithelial cells, which are negative for p63, calponin and SMMHC, but are surrounded by a basement membrane that stains for laminin and collagen IV. The cells are S100-positive and negative for ER, PR and HER2. Atypical MGA shows more complex, crowded or back-to-back glands, nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli and mitoses. MGA is a non-obligate precursor of triple-negative carcinoma, including acinic cell carcinoma, and shares TP53 mutations with it, so complete excision is advised. Differentials include tubular carcinoma (angulated glands, ER-positive, apical snouts, no basement membrane), sclerosing adenosis (myoepithelium present), and acinic cell carcinoma with zymogen-like granules.
entities.cyto: Microglandular adenosis and atypical MGA are rarely sampled by FNA and have no reliable cytological criteria. Aspirates may show small, round, cohesive acinar groups of cuboidal cells with clear or vacuolated cytoplasm and round, mildly atypical nuclei, without myoepithelial cells (MGA lacks a myoepithelial layer), sometimes with eosinophilic secretion. The absence of myoepithelial cells makes it closely mimic tubular or low-grade invasive carcinoma, a significant pitfall. Atypical MGA shows more crowding and nuclear atypia. Findings are reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or 4 (Suspicious), with core biopsy; MGA is S100 positive and ER/PR negative on histology.
entities.ihc: Microglandular adenosis (MGA) has a distinctive profile. Small round glands with eosinophilic, PAS-positive secretions lack a myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin negative) but are surrounded by a basement membrane (laminin and collagen IV positive). The epithelial cells are S100 positive, ER, PR and HER2 negative, and EMA negative. Atypical MGA and MGA-associated carcinoma share this triple-negative, S100-positive profile and a high Ki-67, and often have TP53 mutations. They can be mistaken for tubular carcinoma (ER+, no basement membrane) or acinic cell carcinoma (lysozyme+, α1-ACT+, DOG1+). The basement membrane is the key distinguishing finding.

entities.variants: Central (large duct, solitary) papilloma; peripheral (multiple) papillomas / papillomatosis; sclerosing papilloma; infarcted papilloma; papilloma with UDH, apocrine/squamous metaplasia, collagenous spherulosis; papilloma with ADH (atypical focus <3 mm)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th papillary neoplasm; arborising fibrovascular cores lined by epithelium and myoepithelium (p63, CK5/6 mosaic). Central: nipple discharge; peripheral: higher association with atypia/carcinoma. Papilloma with ADH carries increased risk (also see Preneoplastic for papilloma with DCIS).
entities.histo: Intraductal papilloma is a benign papillary neoplasm with arborising fibrovascular cores covered by a luminal epithelial layer and an underlying myoepithelial layer. Central (large duct) papillomas are solitary subareolar lesions presenting with serous or bloody nipple discharge. Peripheral papillomas arise in terminal duct lobular units, are often multiple (papillomatosis) and are more often associated with atypia or carcinoma. Variants include sclerosing papilloma, with fibrosis entrapping glands that mimics invasion, and infarcted papilloma, often in pregnancy. Papillomas may show UDH, apocrine or squamous metaplasia, collagenous spherulosis, or an atypical monotonous focus under 3 mm (papilloma with ADH), which increases risk. IHC shows a continuous myoepithelial layer on p63, calponin or SMMHC within the cores, with mosaic CK5/6 and heterogeneous ER in the epithelium. Differentials include papilloma with DCIS (3 mm or more, or high grade), papillary DCIS and encapsulated papillary carcinoma, which lack myoepithelium in the cores, and nipple adenoma. Excision is advised for atypical lesions and for discordant core biopsies.
entities.cyto: Intraductal papilloma aspirates or bloody nipple discharge show moderate to high cellularity with papillary clusters, sometimes with fibrovascular cores, cohesive staghorn or three-dimensional groups, columnar cells, apocrine cells, foamy and haemosiderin-laden macrophages and myoepithelial cells, in a haemorrhagic or cystic background. Single columnar cells may be seen. Cytology cannot reliably separate benign papilloma from atypical papilloma or papillary carcinoma. The Yokohama System advises that papillary lesions be reported as Category 3 (Atypical) for most papillary aspirates, or Category 2 only when clearly benign, with core biopsy or excision recommended.
entities.ihc: Intraductal papilloma (central or peripheral) shows a two-cell-type pattern. A continuous myoepithelial layer runs along the fibrovascular cores and the duct periphery (p63, SMMHC, calponin, CK5/6, CK14), and the epithelial proliferation is heterogeneous for CK5/6 and ER. Areas of usual hyperplasia show mosaic CK5/6 staining. This contrasts with papillary DCIS and encapsulated papillary carcinoma (myoepithelium absent along the cores, uniform ER+, CK5/6−). Atypical foci in a papilloma are uniformly ER-positive and CK5/6-negative, and are graded by size (under 3 mm ADH). Apocrine metaplasia is AR+ and ER−. Sclerosis can entrap epithelium, and retained myoepithelium separates this from invasion.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th adenoma; well-circumscribed, closely packed uniform tubules with two-cell layer and scant stroma; young women; may merge with fibroadenoma.
entities.histo: Tubular adenoma is a benign, well-circumscribed epithelial tumour, typically in young women, that presents as a mobile mass resembling a fibroadenoma. Grossly it is a firm, tan-yellow, homogeneous, sharply demarcated nodule. Microscopically it consists of closely packed, uniform, small round tubules lined by a single luminal epithelial layer with an outer myoepithelial layer, set in scant, delicate, vascular stroma. Sometimes the lumina contain eosinophilic secretion. There is no compression of ducts into slits as in a fibroadenoma, and the stroma is not cellular. Cytological atypia and necrosis are absent, and mitoses are rare. Tubular adenoma can merge with a fibroadenoma, and it may show lactational change in pregnancy, which forms a lactating adenoma. Differentials include fibroadenoma (prominent stroma), lactating adenoma, tubular carcinoma (angulated tubules, single cell layer, desmoplasia, infiltrative edge) and microglandular adenosis (no myoepithelium, infiltrative). Myoepithelial IHC confirms the two-cell layer.
entities.cyto: Tubular adenoma aspirates are cellular with numerous tightly cohesive, small tubular and acinar clusters of uniform, bland cuboidal cells with round nuclei, admixed with myoepithelial cells, many bare bipolar nuclei and scanty stromal fragments. The appearance overlaps with fibroadenoma, which shows larger staghorn sheets and more stroma, and the tubular arrangement may mimic tubular carcinoma, though bare nuclei and myoepithelial cells favour benignity. Lactating adenoma is a related lesion. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), consistent with a benign epithelial or fibroepithelial lesion.
entities.ihc: Tubular adenoma rarely needs IHC. It's a well-circumscribed nodule of closely packed small tubules with sparse stroma. Each tubule keeps an inner luminal layer (CK7, CK8/18) and an outer myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin), and the luminal cells show heterogeneous ER positivity. The intact myoepithelium separates it from tubular carcinoma, which lacks myoepithelial cells. When lactational change is present (lactating adenoma or lactational nodule), the vacuolated hobnail cells are still surrounded by myoepithelium. Ki-67 is low. Fibroadenoma is separated by its stromal component, and microglandular adenosis by the absence of myoepithelium.

entities.variants: Lactational nodule (lactational change in tubular adenoma/fibroadenoma)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th adenoma; pregnancy/lactation; lobulated, secretory hobnail cells; may infarct.
entities.histo: Lactating adenoma presents during pregnancy or lactation as a rapidly growing, mobile, well-circumscribed, lobulated mass that may raise concern for pregnancy-associated carcinoma. Grossly it is tan-grey, soft, lobulated and sometimes contains infarcts. Microscopically there are lobules of closely packed acini lined by cuboidal cells with vacuolated or foamy cytoplasm and hobnail nuclei projecting into lumina that contain secretion, with an attenuated myoepithelial layer. The stroma is scant and the fibrous septa delicate. Nuclei can show reactive enlargement and prominent nucleoli, but they are uniform. Infarction is common and may cause pain and alarming necrosis. The term lactational nodule covers lactational change superimposed on a tubular adenoma, fibroadenoma or normal lobules, and some lesions likely represent nodular lactational hyperplasia rather than true neoplasms. Differentials include tubular adenoma, fibroadenoma with lactational change, secretory carcinoma, invasive carcinoma in pregnancy and infarcted lesions. Preserved lobular architecture and myoepithelium distinguish it from carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Lactating adenoma arises in pregnancy or lactation and yields cellular smears with loosely cohesive acinar clusters, many single cells and stripped nuclei, with abundant fragile vacuolated cytoplasm, enlarged round nuclei, prominent nucleoli and a frothy, lipid-rich proteinaceous background. Infarction may cause necrosis and atypical degenerated cells. The nuclear enlargement, nucleoli and dyscohesion are a well-known pitfall for false-positive diagnosis of carcinoma; awareness of pregnancy and the bubbly background is essential. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), consistent with lactational change or lactating adenoma, or Category 3 if atypia is concerning.
entities.ihc: Lactating adenoma, or lactational nodule, is lactational change in a tubular adenoma or fibroadenoma. The secretory, vacuolated, hobnail cells keep a myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin), which separates them from secretory carcinoma (no myoepithelium, S100+, mammaglobin+, SOX10+, ETV6-NTRK3), acinic cell carcinoma (no myoepithelium, lysozyme+) and clear-cell carcinoma. Proliferation can be high in pregnancy, so Ki-67 isn't reliable. The cells are S100 positive and α-lactalbumin positive in many cases. Infarction is common and can make morphology difficult, and keratin and myoepithelial markers may still be retained in the ghost architecture.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th adenoma; well-circumscribed glandular proliferation within a duct with sclerotic wall, often apocrine metaplasia; regarded by some as sclerosed papilloma; must not be mistaken for invasive carcinoma (myoepithelium retained).
entities.histo: Ductal adenoma is a benign, well-circumscribed glandular proliferation within a dilated duct with a thick, sclerotic fibrous wall, typically in middle-aged women. It may be palpable, sometimes with nipple discharge. Microscopically the nodule contains compressed and distorted glands, tubules and cords in dense central hyalinised fibrosis, often with apocrine metaplasia, which can show nuclear enlargement. The surrounding duct wall is thick, and residual papillary areas are sometimes present, so many regard it as a sclerosed papilloma. Glands at the periphery can appear to infiltrate the sclerotic wall, mimicking invasive carcinoma, but they retain a myoepithelial layer on p63, calponin and SMMHC. Calcifications and haemosiderin may be present. Differentials include invasive carcinoma (no myoepithelium, infiltrative beyond the duct, desmoplasia), sclerosing papilloma, nipple adenoma (location), pleomorphic adenoma and complex sclerosing lesion. Recognising the low-power circumscribed, duct-bound architecture is the key to avoiding overdiagnosis.
entities.cyto: Ductal adenoma is a rare well-circumscribed intraductal lesion, considered a variant of sclerosed papilloma. Aspirates may show cohesive groups and small tubules of bland epithelial cells, apocrine cells, myoepithelial cells, bare nuclei and fragments of sclerotic stroma, sometimes with foamy macrophages. Pseudo-infiltrative tubules in sclerotic stroma can mimic invasive carcinoma histologically, and on cytology the apocrine atypia may raise concern. Cytology cannot provide a specific diagnosis; the overlap with papilloma, fibroadenoma and adenosis means it is reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 3 (Atypical), with histology.
entities.ihc: Ductal adenoma is a well-circumscribed, often sclerosed, adenomatous lesion within a duct. Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMMHC, calponin, CK5/6) show a myoepithelial layer around the compressed glands and at the periphery. This is the key test in separating it from invasive carcinoma, because the sclerosis and entrapped glands are pseudoinfiltrative. The epithelium shows heterogeneous ER and CK5/6 staining and may show apocrine metaplasia (AR+, GCDFP-15+). Some regard it as a sclerosed papilloma, which has the same IHC pattern. Atypical areas are assessed with CK5/6 and ER. Pleomorphic adenoma-like areas are rare.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th epithelial-myoepithelial tumour; rare in breast (often subareolar, near papilloma); epithelial/myoepithelial cells with chondromyxoid stroma; PLAG1/HMGA2 rearrangements; mimic of metaplastic carcinoma.
entities.histo: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumour) is rare in the breast. It usually occurs in the subareolar region of older women, often in association with an intraductal papilloma, and may calcify or ossify, simulating carcinoma on mammography. Grossly it is a well-circumscribed, firm, lobulated, grey-white nodule, sometimes gritty. Microscopically it is biphasic. Ducts and tubules are lined by luminal epithelial cells and surrounded by myoepithelial cells, which merge with plasmacytoid, spindled or stellate myoepithelial cells in chondromyxoid stroma, sometimes with cartilage or bone. Cytological atypia is minimal and mitoses are rare. PLAG1 or HMGA2 rearrangements may be present, and PLAG1 IHC can help. Myoepithelial cells are positive for p63, SOX10, calponin and S100. The main differential is matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma, which is infiltrative, has high-grade cytology, merges directly with matrix without a myoepithelial interface, and is triple-negative. Others include adenomyoepithelioma, mucinous carcinoma, fibroadenoma with myxoid stroma and chondrolipoma.
entities.cyto: Pleomorphic adenoma of the breast is rare and usually subareolar. As in salivary gland, aspirates show a biphasic picture: cohesive clusters of bland ductal epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells (plasmacytoid, spindle or stellate) embedded in or intimately mixed with fibrillary, metachromatic chondromyxoid stroma that stains bright magenta on MGG. Cartilage or squamous metaplasia may be present. The chondromyxoid matrix can be misinterpreted as mucin, raising mucinous carcinoma, or as the matrix of matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma, which is the major pitfall. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or 2, with excision advised.
entities.ihc: Breast pleomorphic adenoma resembles its salivary counterpart. The ductal component is CK7+ and CK8/18+, and the myoepithelial and modified myoepithelial component in the chondromyxoid stroma is p63+, SMA+, calponin+, CK5/6+, CK14+, S100+, and often GFAP+. PLAG1 immunohistochemistry is positive in many cases and HMGA2 in some, reflecting PLAG1 or HMGA2 rearrangements that FISH can confirm. ER and PR are variable. The main differential is metaplastic carcinoma with chondroid differentiation, which is a high-grade, infiltrative, triple-negative carcinoma lacking an organised two-cell pattern and showing p53 aberrant staining and a high Ki-67. Fibroadenoma with myxoid stroma lacks a myoepithelial matrix.

entities.variants: Spindle cell; tubular; lobulated; mixed patterns; ER-positive and ER-negative types; with atypia
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; biphasic proliferation of luminal epithelial and abluminal myoepithelial cells (p63, calponin, SMMHC, CK5/6); ER-negative AMEs frequently HRAS Q61 hotspot ± PIK3CA/PIK3R1 mutations and higher risk of malignant transformation; may recur locally.
entities.histo: Adenomyoepithelioma is a biphasic tumour of luminal epithelial cells and abluminal myoepithelial cells, typically a well-circumscribed or lobulated mass in older women. The luminal cells line tubules and glands, are CK7-positive and CK8/18-positive, and are often ER-positive. The myoepithelial cells are polygonal, clear, eosinophilic or spindled, sometimes plasmacytoid, and are positive for p63, calponin, SMMHC, SMA and CK5/6. The growth patterns are spindle cell, tubular, lobulated (myoepithelial nests separated by fibrous septa) and mixed, and some lesions have a papillary or intraductal origin. ER-positive tumours are often PIK3CA or AKT1 mutated. ER-negative tumours frequently harbour HRAS Q61 hotspot mutations, often with PIK3CA or PIK3R1, and have a greater risk of malignant transformation. Atypical features include nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses, necrosis and infiltrative borders, which require careful sampling. Local recurrence is possible after incomplete excision. Differentials include adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma, pleomorphic adenoma, intraductal papilloma, adenoid cystic carcinoma and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Adenomyoepithelioma yields cellular smears with a biphasic population of cohesive epithelial clusters and numerous myoepithelial cells that may be clear, epithelioid, plasmacytoid or spindled, together with bare nuclei and sometimes hyaline or myxoid stromal material. Mild nuclear atypia may be seen. The lesion overlaps cytologically with fibroadenoma, papilloma, pleomorphic adenoma and myoepithelial-rich carcinomas, and malignant transformation cannot be excluded on FNA. Immunocytochemistry on cell block (p63, SMA, CK) can highlight the biphasic nature. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with excision for definitive diagnosis.
entities.ihc: Adenomyoepithelioma is a biphasic tumour with a luminal component (CK7+, CK8/18+, EMA+) and a proliferating abluminal myoepithelial component that is p63+, SMMHC+, calponin+, SMA+, CK5/6+, CK14+ and often S100 positive. ER-positive tumours are often PIK3CA or AKT1 mutated. ER-negative tumours frequently carry HRAS Q61 mutations, which are associated with a higher risk of malignant transformation. The main differentials are intraductal papilloma with myoepithelial hyperplasia, pleomorphic adenoma (chondromyxoid matrix, PLAG1), and metaplastic or adenoid cystic carcinoma (MYB). Ki-67 and atypia in either component help identify adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma.

entities.variants: Usual (intracanalicular, pericanalicular patterns); cellular fibroadenoma; complex fibroadenoma (cysts >3 mm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, papillary apocrine change); juvenile fibroadenoma (cellular stroma, pericanalicular, gynaecomastoid epithelium; adolescents; may be giant); myxoid fibroadenoma (Carney complex association); fibroadenoma with infarction; fibroadenomatosis/fibroadenomatoid change; fibroadenoma with LCIS/DCIS/invasive carcinoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th fibroepithelial tumour; commonest benign tumour of young women; MED12 exon 2 mutations frequent; cellular fibroadenoma vs benign phyllodes is the main differential (leaf-like architecture, periductal stromal condensation favour phyllodes).
entities.histo: Fibroadenoma is the commonest benign tumour of young women. It is a well-circumscribed, mobile, rubbery mass with a grey-white, bulging, lobulated cut surface showing slit-like spaces. It is a biphasic fibroepithelial tumour, and MED12 exon 2 mutations are frequent. In the intracanalicular pattern, the stroma compresses ducts into curvilinear slits. In the pericanalicular pattern, the stroma surrounds round, open ducts. Both have a two-cell epithelial layer with uniformly distributed, bland, low-cellularity stroma. Cellular fibroadenoma shows increased stromal cellularity without leaf-like fronds or periductal condensation. Complex fibroadenoma contains cysts over 3 mm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications or papillary apocrine change. Juvenile fibroadenoma in adolescents shows cellular stroma, a pericanalicular pattern and gynaecomastoid epithelial hyperplasia, and it can become giant. Myxoid fibroadenoma is associated with Carney complex. Infarction occurs in pregnancy, and LCIS, DCIS or invasive carcinoma may rarely arise within. The main differential is benign phyllodes tumour, which has leaf-like architecture, periductal stromal condensation and stromal heterogeneity.
entities.cyto: Fibroadenoma aspirates are typically cellular with large, cohesive, monolayered branching (staghorn or antler-like) sheets of bland ductal epithelial cells with intermixed myoepithelial cells, numerous bare bipolar nuclei in the background, and fragments of fibromyxoid stroma that is metachromatic on MGG and of low cellularity. Foamy macrophages and apocrine cells may be present. Pitfalls include mild atypia or crowding in cellular fibroadenoma mimicking carcinoma, and overlap with benign phyllodes tumour (cellular stroma, spindle cells). The triad of staghorn sheets, bare nuclei and stroma supports the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), consistent with fibroadenoma.
entities.ihc: Fibroadenoma, including the cellular and juvenile types, rarely needs IHC. The epithelial component keeps its myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin) and shows heterogeneous ER and CK5/6 staining, while the stroma is CD34-positive and often PR-positive. No IHC marker reliably separates cellular fibroadenoma from benign phyllodes tumour. Stromal Ki-67 tends to be lower and stromal CD34 is retained, but these are only supportive, and the diagnosis rests on morphology (leaf-like architecture, periepithelial stromal condensation). MED12 exon 2 mutations are common in both fibroadenoma and phyllodes, and TERT promoter mutations favour phyllodes. Lobular neoplasia or carcinoma within a fibroadenoma is worked up separately.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; leaf-like architecture with periductal stromal hypercellularity; well-defined border, mild stromal cellularity/atypia, mitoses <2.5/mm² (<5/10 HPF), no stromal overgrowth; may recur locally; MED12, TERT promoter mutations.
entities.histo: Benign phyllodes tumour is a fibroepithelial neoplasm, usually in women around 40 to 50, presenting as a rapidly enlarging, well-circumscribed mass. Grossly it is firm, bulging and lobulated, with curved clefts. Microscopically there are leaf-like (phyllodes) architecture formed by elongated cleft-like spaces lined by two-layered epithelium and broad, club-shaped stromal fronds projecting into them. The stroma is hypercellular, condenses beneath the epithelium (periductal or subepithelial stromal condensation) and shows mild cellularity and mild nuclear atypia. Mitoses are fewer than 2.5 per mm², about fewer than 5 per 10 HPF. The border is well defined and pushing, and there is no stromal overgrowth, defined as stroma without epithelium in a low-power field. Adipocytic or other benign heterologous elements may occur. Local recurrence occurs, especially with positive margins, and MED12 and TERT promoter mutations are common. The main differential is cellular or juvenile fibroadenoma. Borderline phyllodes shows more atypia, more mitoses and focally permeative borders, and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma must also be considered, especially on core biopsy.
entities.cyto: Benign phyllodes tumour aspirates show features of a fibroepithelial lesion: staghorn epithelial sheets, myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, together with abundant, hypercellular stromal fragments and numerous single spindle stromal cells with mild atypia. Cystic spaces and leaf-like patterns may be suggested by fragments. Separation from cellular fibroadenoma is often impossible cytologically, but large hypercellular stromal fragments, single spindle cells and stromal-to-epithelial dominance favour phyllodes tumour. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), fibroepithelial lesion with cellular stroma, with excision recommended.
entities.ihc: Benign phyllodes tumour has stromal cells that are typically CD34+, often BCL2+, with variable SMA and desmin, a low Ki-67, and patchy or negative p53. Keratins are negative in the stroma, though focal keratin can occur. Myoepithelial markers confirm the benign epithelial component. No marker reliably separates it from cellular fibroadenoma. The diagnosis rests on stromal cellularity, leaf-like architecture and periepithelial condensation, with MED12 mutations shared by both. TERT promoter mutations favour phyllodes. In any spindle-cell lesion with atypia, broad-spectrum keratins and p63 should be done to exclude metaplastic carcinoma, which is diffusely keratin- and p63-positive.

entities.variants: Adenolipoma; myoid hamartoma (smooth muscle); chondrolipoma / chondroid hamartoma; hamartoma with PASH
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; well-circumscribed mass of disorganised normal breast components ('breast within a breast'); Cowden syndrome association when multiple.
entities.histo: Mammary hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma) is a well-circumscribed, often encapsulated mass composed of disorganised but otherwise normal breast components. It is described as a breast within a breast, and on mammography it appears as a circumscribed lesion with mixed fat and soft-tissue density surrounded by a thin radiolucent rim. Grossly it resembles normal breast tissue sharply demarcated from the surrounding parenchyma. Microscopically, lobules and ducts with a two-cell layer are distributed in variable proportions of fibrous stroma and fat, often lacking the normal interlobular-intralobular relationship. Fibrous stroma frequently extends into lobules, and pseudocapsule formation is common. Adenolipoma is fat-rich. Myoid hamartoma contains smooth muscle bundles, chondrolipoma contains cartilage, and hamartoma with PASH contains pseudoangiomatous stroma. Multiple hamartomas raise the possibility of Cowden (PTEN) syndrome. Core biopsy may look normal, so radiological correlation is essential. Differentials include fibroadenoma, lipoma, PASH, phyllodes tumour, normal breast tissue and fibrocystic change.
entities.cyto: Hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma) of the breast lacks distinctive cytological features. Aspirates show a mixture of normal breast components: bland cohesive ductal cell groups with myoepithelial cells, bare bipolar nuclei, fragments of fibrous stroma and abundant mature adipose tissue, sometimes with smooth muscle (myoid hamartoma) or cartilage. The appearance resembles normal breast, fibroadenoma or fibrocystic change. The diagnosis is primarily radiological (well-circumscribed mass with a breast-within-a-breast appearance) and histological. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) with a comment that the findings are compatible with a benign lesion and need radiological correlation.
entities.ihc: Hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma) is a well-circumscribed mass of disorganised but normal breast elements: ducts, lobules, fibrous stroma and fat, sometimes with smooth muscle (myoid hamartoma) or cartilage (chondrolipoma). IHC isn't needed. The epithelial elements keep their myoepithelial layer (p63, calponin), and the stroma is often CD34+ with PASH. Myoid hamartomas contain SMA-positive and desmin-positive smooth muscle bundles. HMGA2 rearrangements have been reported in some cases, but testing isn't routine. Distinguishing it from fibroadenoma, lipoma and phyllodes tumour depends on the imaging and gross circumscription.

entities.variants: Sclerosing papillomatosis pattern; papillomatosis pattern; adenosis pattern; mixed patterns (synonyms: florid papillomatosis of nipple, erosive adenomatosis)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; benign proliferation of collecting ducts of nipple with retained myoepithelium; serous/bloody discharge, erosion mimicking Paget disease; may coexist with carcinoma rarely.
entities.histo: Nipple adenoma (florid papillomatosis of the nipple, erosive adenomatosis) is a benign proliferation of the collecting ducts in the nipple, typically in middle-aged women. It presents with serous or bloody discharge, erythema, crusting or erosion that mimics Paget disease, or as a palpable nodule. Grossly there is an ill-defined firm nodule beneath the nipple skin. Microscopically, several patterns may coexist. The sclerosing papillomatosis pattern shows florid UDH-like ductal proliferation with papillae and sclerosis distorting ducts. The papillomatosis pattern is predominantly papillary, and the adenosis pattern shows proliferating, compressed glands that can appear infiltrative in stromal desmoplasia. The proliferation often extends to and replaces the surface epidermis, causing erosion, and squamous cysts may be present near the surface. Myoepithelium is retained around glands. Differentials include invasive carcinoma and DCIS, syringomatous tumour of the nipple (comma-shaped tubules, deep infiltration), intraductal papilloma, Paget disease and low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma. Rare associated carcinomas are reported, so complete excision is advised.
entities.cyto: Nipple adenoma (florid papillomatosis of the nipple) can present with erosion and discharge, mimicking Paget disease. Aspirates or scrapes are cellular, with cohesive and papillary groups of ductal cells with myoepithelial cells, apocrine cells, bare bipolar nuclei, keratinous squames and inflammatory cells. Crowding and mild atypia, plus occasional dyscohesive cells, may lead to misinterpretation as carcinoma. The presence of myoepithelial cells, bare nuclei and squamous cells from the nipple surface favour benignity. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 3 (Atypical), with biopsy to exclude carcinoma or Paget disease.
entities.ihc: In nipple adenoma, IHC confirms a preserved myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin, CK5/6) around the compact tubules and papillary proliferations, including those in the sclerotic stroma. This separates it from invasive carcinoma and syringomatous tumour. The epithelium shows heterogeneous CK5/6 and ER staining, often with florid UDH. Areas of squamous metaplasia near the skin are p63+. Erosion of the nipple skin can mimic Paget disease clinically, but the intraepidermal cells aren't HER2- or GATA3-positive Paget cells. DCIS arising within a nipple adenoma (uniform ER+, CK5/6−) is rare and is assessed with the same panel.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th (formerly syringomatous adenoma); infiltrative small comma/tadpole-shaped squamoid tubules and nests in nipple stroma, ER/PR−, p63+ outer cells; locally aggressive/recurs, does not metastasise — differential: low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma, tubular carcinoma.
entities.histo: Syringomatous tumour of the nipple (formerly syringomatous adenoma) is a rare, locally infiltrative but non-metastasising neoplasm of the nipple and areola. It presents as a firm subareolar mass, sometimes with nipple inversion. Microscopically, small, branching or comma- and tadpole-shaped tubules, cords and solid squamoid nests infiltrate the nipple stroma, smooth muscle bundles and nerves. Some tubules contain keratin cysts. The tubules are lined by two layers, an inner luminal layer and outer cells that are p63-positive and CK5/6-positive, and they lie in a desmoplastic or cellular stroma. Cytological atypia is minimal and mitoses are rare. ER and PR are negative. The tumour resembles cutaneous syringoma and microcystic adnexal carcinoma, but arises in the nipple. Incomplete excision leads to local recurrence, so clear margins are needed. Differentials include low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma (deep breast parenchyma, similar histology, ER-negative), tubular carcinoma (ER-positive, single layer, no squamous change), nipple adenoma (retained myoepithelium, not infiltrative), and squamous cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Syringomatous tumour of the nipple is a locally infiltrative benign neoplasm that is rarely aspirated and has no well-defined cytological criteria. Aspirates may show small, tightly cohesive, angulated or comma-shaped clusters and tubules of bland basaloid or squamoid cells, keratin cysts and fragments of desmoplastic stroma. The small tubules may closely mimic tubular carcinoma or low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma, and diagnosis requires histology showing infiltrating tubules and cords with squamous differentiation in the nipple stroma. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: Syringomatous tumour of the nipple is an infiltrative, locally aggressive proliferation of small comma-shaped tubules and squamous nests in the nipple stroma. IHC is supportive. The tumour is ER, PR and HER2 negative, which separates it from low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma (also ER−) and tubular carcinoma (ER+). The outer cells are p63+, CK5/6+ and CK14+, and the inner luminal cells are CK7 positive, mimicking a two-cell pattern. Its histology overlaps with low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma, and the distinction is mainly by location (nipple versus parenchyma). Nipple adenoma has a well-organised myoepithelial layer. Ki-67 is low.

entities.variants: Perilobular haemangioma (microscopic, incidental); cavernous; capillary; venous; complex; anastomosing haemangioma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th vascular tumour; well-circumscribed, no endothelial atypia, no dissection of lobules — key differential from well-differentiated angiosarcoma.
entities.histo: Haemangiomas of the breast are benign vascular tumours, either incidental microscopic lesions or small palpable or mammographically detected masses, and they may calcify. Perilobular haemangioma is a microscopic cluster of thin-walled, congested capillaries around lobules, usually under 2 mm. Cavernous, capillary and venous haemangiomas are well-circumscribed lesions in subcutis or parenchyma, with dilated or small capillary vessels, and complex haemangiomas show mixed vessel types. Anastomosing haemangioma shows sinusoidal, anastomosing channels with hobnail endothelium, and may have GNAQ-type mutations. The endothelium is flat and bland, there are no multilayering, mitoses or endothelial tufts, and lesions do not dissect through lobules or fat. Thrombosis or papillary endothelial hyperplasia may occur. The key differential is well-differentiated angiosarcoma, which is usually larger, infiltrative and dissecting through lobules and fat, with anastomosing channels and endothelial atypia. Others include PASH, angiolipoma and atypical vascular lesion after radiotherapy. Small core biopsies of vascular lesions often require excision for full assessment.
entities.cyto: Breast haemangioma aspirates are typically bloody with low cellularity, consisting mainly of blood, occasional small clusters of bland endothelial cells with elongated nuclei, small capillary fragments and haemosiderin-laden macrophages, sometimes with stromal fragments. Epithelial cells are absent unless the needle traverses normal breast. Cytology is usually non-diagnostic because the findings are indistinguishable from a bloody aspirate.
