Well-differentiated angiosarcoma, which can be deceptively bland, is the most important differential, so imaging correlation and core or excision biopsy are needed. Usually reported as Yokohama Category 1 (Insufficient) or Category 3 (Atypical) with a descriptive comment.
entities.ihc: Haemangiomas of the breast (perilobular, cavernous, capillary) are positive for CD31, ERG and CD34, with a continuous SMA-positive pericyte layer around the vessels. Their main mimic is low-grade angiosarcoma. Haemangiomas are small (usually under 2 cm), well circumscribed, and don't dissect fat or lobules with anastomosing channels. IHC can't reliably make this distinction, because both are CD31+ and ERG+. MYC amplification or IHC is negative in haemangiomas and in primary angiosarcoma, but positive in post-radiation angiosarcoma. Ki-67 is low. Atypical vascular lesions are separated by context. GLUT1 is positive in infantile haemangioma.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; diffuse proliferation of well-formed vascular channels involving large area of breast, surrounding but not invading lobules; rare; may recur.
entities.histo: Angiomatosis of the breast is a rare, benign, diffuse proliferation of well-formed vascular channels involving a large area of breast tissue, usually in young women. It presents as a diffuse, soft mass or swelling, sometimes with skin discolouration, and may recur after incomplete excision. Microscopically, thin-walled, variably sized, dilated capillary, venous and lymphatic-type channels with bland flat endothelium extend extensively through interlobular stroma and fat. They surround but do not invade or dissect lobules, and the lobules remain intact with preserved intralobular stroma. Endothelial atypia, multilayering, papillary tufts and mitoses are absent. Larger thick-walled vessels and fat may be part of the lesion. The main differential is low-grade angiosarcoma, which shows dissection into lobules and fat with anastomosing channels, endothelial atypia and hyperchromasia, and occasional solid areas and blood lakes. Other differentials are haemangioma (localised, circumscribed), lymphangioma, PASH and vascular malformation. Wide excision is required.
entities.cyto: Angiomatosis is a rare diffuse vascular proliferation involving breast parenchyma, and FNA yields mainly blood with a few fragments of bland endothelial cells, stromal tissue and normal breast elements, findings that are non-specific. The lesion is important because it must be distinguished from low-grade angiosarcoma, which can be equally bland in aspirates; this cannot be done reliably on cytology. Imaging shows an ill-defined lesion. A bloody aspirate from such a lesion should be reported as non-diagnostic or Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with core or excisional biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: Angiomatosis is a diffuse, benign vascular proliferation involving a large area of breast tissue. Its vessels are CD31+, ERG+ and CD34+, with a variable SMA-positive pericyte layer, and D2-40 may highlight a lymphatic component. Its main significance is the differential with low-grade angiosarcoma, which also forms diffuse, infiltrative vascular channels in fat. IHC doesn't separate them, because endothelial markers are positive in both and MYC is negative in primary angiosarcoma. The distinction relies on morphology: angiomatosis lacks endothelial atypia, multilayering, anastomosing channels and mitoses. Ki-67 is low in angiomatosis and higher in angiosarcoma.

entities.entity: Lymphangioma / lymphatic malformation and other benign vascular lesions
entities.variants: Lymphangioma (cystic hygroma); pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) of nipple/breast skin; venous malformation
entities.remarks: Rare in breast parenchyma; mainly skin/subcutis of breast.
entities.histo: Lymphangioma (lymphatic malformation) and other benign vascular lesions involve the breast rarely, mainly in the skin and subcutis rather than the parenchyma. Cystic lymphangioma (cystic hygroma) may extend from the axilla or chest wall. It shows large, thin-walled, endothelial-lined cystic spaces containing proteinaceous lymph and lymphocytes, with walls containing smooth muscle and lymphoid aggregates, and the lining cells are D2-40-positive and PROX1-positive. Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) of the nipple or breast skin is an exophytic, ulcerated polypoid lesion with lobules of capillaries in oedematous, inflamed stroma, separated by fibrous septa and with an epidermal collarette. Venous malformations show large, thick-walled, irregular veins with uneven smooth muscle and thrombi or phleboliths. The differentials include angiosarcoma, atypical vascular lesion (post-radiation), angiomatosis, haemangioma and Kaposi sarcoma, which shows HHV8 positivity and spindle cells with slit-like vessels.
entities.cyto: Lymphangioma or lymphatic malformation and other benign vascular lesions such as angiolipoma-like and capillary lesions yield aspirates of clear to milky lymphatic fluid or blood, containing mature lymphocytes, few histiocytes and occasional flat endothelial cells, without epithelial cells. The findings are non-specific, and the differential includes lymph node, chylous cysts and low-grade vascular neoplasms. Lymphocyte-rich fluid can mimic lymphoma, requiring flow cytometry if a monotonous population is seen. Cytology cannot confirm the lesion, and radiological correlation is needed. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 1 when non-representative.
entities.ihc: Lymphangioma and related benign vascular lesions (pyogenic granuloma, venous haemangioma) are diagnosed on morphology. In lymphangiomas the lining is D2-40 (podoplanin) and PROX1 positive, with CD31 and ERG positivity and weak or absent CD34. Pyogenic granuloma shows lobules of capillaries that are CD31+ and ERG+ with a pericyte layer. The main differential remains angiosarcoma and, after radiotherapy, an atypical vascular lesion. MYC is negative in these benign lesions. Ki-67 is generally low, though it can be higher in pyogenic granuloma. Lymphangioma circumscriptum and acquired lymphatic lesions after breast radiotherapy belong in the context of atypical vascular lesions.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; self-limited clonal myofibroblastic proliferation (USP6 rearrangement, MYH9::USP6); tissue-culture-like spindle cells, extravasated RBCs, myxoid stroma; rapid growth.
entities.histo: Nodular fasciitis of the breast is a rapidly growing, often tender, self-limited myofibroblastic proliferation, usually under 3 cm, in the subcutis or parenchyma. The rapid growth and core biopsy findings may suggest sarcoma or metaplastic carcinoma. Grossly it is a circumscribed but unencapsulated nodule with a myxoid to fibrous cut surface. Microscopically, plump, uniform spindle myofibroblasts are arranged in short, irregular fascicles and S-shaped or storiform patterns in a loose, myxoid, tissue culture-like stroma. Extravasated red cells, lymphocytes, osteoclast-like giant cells and microcysts are present, and older lesions are more collagenous. Mitoses can be frequent but are not atypical, and necrosis is absent. The cells are SMA-positive and desmin-negative, and negative for keratins, p63, beta-catenin (nuclear) and S100. USP6 rearrangement, such as MYH9::USP6, confirms the diagnosis. Differentials include spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin and p63 positive), fibromatosis, myofibroblastoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, scar and sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Nodular fasciitis in the breast yields cellular smears of plump, bland spindle and stellate myofibroblasts arranged singly and in loose clusters in a myxoid background, with mitoses, lymphocytes, extravasated red cells and occasional osteoclast-like giant cells, resembling tissue culture fibroblasts. Ductal cells are absent or incidental. The rapid growth and cellularity can mimic sarcoma, metaplastic carcinoma or phyllodes tumour; lack of nuclear pleomorphism and atypical mitoses favours fasciitis. USP6 rearrangement can be confirmed molecularly. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion, with core biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: Nodular fasciitis is a rapidly growing, self-limited myofibroblastic proliferation with a 'tissue culture' appearance. The cells are SMA positive (tram-track pattern), calponin positive, desmin usually negative, and negative for keratins, p63, CD34, S100, β-catenin (nuclear) and ALK. This keratin and p63 negativity separates it from spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma, which is the most important mimic in the breast. Desmoid fibromatosis shows nuclear β-catenin, and IMT is ALK positive. The key molecular hint is USP6 rearrangement (often MYH9-USP6), which FISH or RNA sequencing can confirm in difficult cases. Ki-67 may be high despite benign behaviour.

entities.variants: Classic; collagenised/fibrous; epithelioid; cellular; infiltrative; lipomatous; myxoid; deciduoid; palisaded/schwannian-like; with atypia (atypical/pleomorphic)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; men and older women; bland spindle cells in short fascicles with thick hyalinised collagen bands; CD34+, desmin+, ER/PR/AR+; RB1 (13q14) loss — same family as spindle cell lipoma and cellular angiofibroma.
entities.histo: Myofibroblastoma is a benign stromal tumour that occurs in men and older women as a well-circumscribed, mobile, slow-growing mass. Grossly it is firm, rubbery and grey-pink, sometimes containing fat. Microscopically, classic lesions consist of bland spindle cells in short, haphazard fascicles separated by thick, hyalinised, eosinophilic collagen bands, with no mammary ducts or lobules within the tumour. Adipose tissue and mast cells are common. The variants are collagenised or fibrous, epithelioid (which mimics invasive lobular carcinoma), cellular, infiltrative, lipomatous, myxoid, deciduoid, palisaded or schwannian-like, and atypical or pleomorphic, with degenerative nuclear atypia. The cells are positive for CD34, desmin, ER, PR, AR and often BCL2, with variable SMA. Loss of RB1 (13q14) places myofibroblastoma in the same family as spindle cell lipoma and cellular angiofibroma. Differentials include epithelioid myofibroblastoma versus lobular carcinoma (keratin-negative), PASH, solitary fibrous tumour (STAT6), desmoid fibromatosis (infiltrative, beta-catenin), spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, and leiomyoma.
entities.cyto: Myofibroblastoma, common in the male breast, yields aspirates of moderate cellularity with bland spindle to oval cells singly and in loose clusters, with fine chromatin, small nucleoli and scant cytoplasm, mixed with fragments of thick collagen bundles, and sometimes adipocytes and mast cells. Epithelial cells are absent. Epithelioid variants may mimic lobular carcinoma. Cell block immunochemistry shows CD34, desmin, ER and PR positivity with loss of RB1. Differentials include spindle cell lipoma, solitary fibrous tumour, metaplastic carcinoma and nodular fasciitis. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), bland spindle cell lesion, with excision.
entities.ihc: Myofibroblastoma is made of bland spindle cells in short fascicles separated by collagen bands. They are CD34+, desmin+ and ER+, PR+ and AR+ in many cases, often BCL2+ and CD99+, with variable SMA. Keratins, p63 and S100 are negative. The key finding is loss of nuclear RB1 expression, reflecting 13q14 deletion (shared with spindle-cell lipoma and cellular angiofibroma). This helps confirm the diagnosis, especially in epithelioid variants that mimic invasive lobular carcinoma (keratin+, E-cadherin−). In men and older women it's important to separate it from spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin+, p63+) and from PASH or fibromatosis.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; S100+, SOX10+, CD68+ (granular cytoplasm, lysosomes), inhibin+; infiltrative and hard; important clinical/radiological mimic of carcinoma; rarely malignant.
entities.histo: Granular cell tumour of the breast is a schwannian neoplasm that occurs in the subcutis or parenchyma, often in the upper inner quadrant. It forms a hard, fixed, infiltrative, stellate mass that closely mimics carcinoma clinically, radiologically and even grossly. The cut surface is firm and white-tan to yellow. Microscopically, sheets, nests and cords of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic, coarsely granular cytoplasm and small, round, central, bland nuclei infiltrate the stroma and fat and often surround ducts and nerves. The granules are lysosomes and are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. The overlying skin may show pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. The cells are positive for S100, SOX10, CD68, inhibin, calretinin and TFE3, and negative for keratins and ER. Malignant granular cell tumour is rare and is recognised by necrosis, marked pleomorphism, spindling, increased mitoses and a high Ki-67. Differentials include apocrine carcinoma and histiocytoid lobular carcinoma (keratin-positive), fat necrosis and histiocytic lesions, and metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Granular cell tumour of the breast can mimic carcinoma clinically and radiologically. Aspirates show single and loosely cohesive cells and syncytial groups with abundant, fragile, finely granular eosinophilic or grey-blue cytoplasm, ill-defined borders, small round bland nuclei with small nucleoli and a background of free granules from disrupted cells. Stripped nuclei may be seen. Pitfalls include apocrine carcinoma, histiocytic lesions and lipid-rich carcinoma. Cell block immunostaining shows S100, SOX10, CD68 and inhibin positivity with cytokeratin negativity. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 2 with a comment suggesting granular cell tumour and recommending excision.
entities.ihc: Granular cell tumour has cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm that infiltrate stroma and can mimic invasive carcinoma clinically and histologically. IHC is decisive. The cells are S100 positive (strong, nuclear and cytoplasmic), SOX10 positive, CD68 positive (granular), calretinin positive, inhibin positive and TFE3 positive in some cases, and negative for keratins, EMA, ER, PR and GATA3. This separates it from apocrine carcinoma (keratin+, AR+, GCDFP-15+) and from histiocytic lesions (CD68+, S100−). PAS with diastase shows the granules. Malignant variants show necrosis, mitoses and a high Ki-67, but these are exceptionally rare in the breast.

entities.variants: Conventional; cellular; plexiform; ancient
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; Antoni A/B, Verocay bodies; S100/SOX10 diffuse.
entities.histo: Schwannoma of the breast is a rare, benign nerve sheath tumour arising from small cutaneous or intramammary nerves. It presents as a well-circumscribed, slow-growing, mobile mass, often tender. Grossly it is an encapsulated, firm, tan-yellow nodule, sometimes with cystic or haemorrhagic change. Microscopically, conventional schwannoma shows alternating cellular Antoni A areas, with fascicles of spindle cells, tapering wavy nuclei and nuclear palisading forming Verocay bodies, and hypocellular, loose, myxoid Antoni B areas. It also has thick-walled hyalinised vessels. Cellular schwannoma consists predominantly of Antoni A with fascicles and may show mitoses. Plexiform schwannoma has multinodular growth. Ancient schwannoma shows degenerative nuclear atypia, hyalinisation, cyst formation and calcification, without mitotic activity. The cells show diffuse strong S100 and SOX10 positivity, and an EMA-positive capsule. Differentials include neurofibroma (less cellular, CD34-positive fibroblasts, axons), myofibroblastoma, spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, leiomyoma, phyllodes tumour, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour.
entities.cyto: Schwannoma in the breast is rare and yields aspirates of variable cellularity with cohesive fragments of bland spindle cells with wavy, tapering, buckled nuclei, fibrillary cytoplasm and occasional nuclear palisading (Verocay-like), with scattered degenerate atypical nuclei in ancient schwannoma. Epithelial cells are absent. Aspiration may be painful. Differentials include neurofibroma, myofibroblastoma, leiomyoma, phyllodes stroma and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma. Cell block S100 and SOX10 positivity supports the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion, or Category 2 with a comment, with histology for confirmation.
entities.ihc: Schwannoma of the breast shows Antoni A and B areas and Verocay bodies. On IHC it is diffusely and strongly positive for S100 and SOX10, with a collagen IV- and laminin-positive basement membrane around individual cells, and calretinin positive in many cases. It is keratin negative, SMA negative, desmin negative and CD34 positive only in capsular or Antoni B areas. Neurofilament shows few or no axons, which separates it from neurofibroma. The main differentials are spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin+, p63+), myofibroblastoma (CD34+, desmin+, RB1 loss), and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (patchy S100, H3K27me3 loss).

entities.variants: Localised; diffuse; plexiform (NF1)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; NF1 association; NF1 patients have increased breast cancer risk.
entities.histo: Neurofibroma of the breast is uncommon. It occurs sporadically as a localised cutaneous or subcutaneous lesion, or in neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) as diffuse or plexiform lesions, and nipple-areolar involvement is common in NF1. Grossly localised neurofibromas are soft, gelatinous, poorly circumscribed or unencapsulated nodules, while plexiform lesions form tortuous, thickened nerve bundles. Microscopically, loosely arranged spindle cells with wavy, buckled nuclei are set in a myxoid to collagenous stroma, described as shredded carrot collagen, with mast cells, residual axons and fibroblasts. The cells show patchy S100 and SOX10 positivity, CD34-positive fibroblastic network and neurofilament-positive axons. Diffuse neurofibromas infiltrate dermis and fat around adnexa, and plexiform neurofibromas expand multiple nerve fascicles, with a risk of transformation to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour. Women with NF1 have an increased risk of breast cancer, so they need screening. Differentials include schwannoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (CD34-positive, storiform), myxoid fibroadenoma, nodular fasciitis and MPNST.
entities.cyto: Neurofibroma of the breast, often in neurofibromatosis type 1 and involving skin or nipple, yields hypocellular aspirates with loosely cohesive bland spindle cells with wavy, comma-shaped nuclei in a fibrillary or myxoid background, mast cells and scattered collagen fibres. Epithelial cells are absent. The cytology is non-specific and overlaps with schwannoma, myofibroblastoma and other bland spindle cell lesions; S100 and SOX10 on cell block support neural origin. In NF1, increased cellularity and atypia may suggest malignant transformation. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), bland spindle cell lesion, or Category 2 with clinical correlation.
entities.ihc: Neurofibroma is a mixed tumour: S100 and SOX10 positive Schwann cells (patchy staining of only part of the population), CD34-positive fibroblasts arranged in a fingerprint-like network, neurofilament-positive axons running through the lesion, and EMA-positive perineurial cells at the periphery. It is keratin negative, SMA negative and desmin negative. This mixed pattern separates it from schwannoma (diffuse S100). H3K27me3 is retained, and loss favours malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour. NF1-associated plexiform neurofibromas carry a risk of malignant transformation, and patients with NF1 have an increased risk of breast carcinoma, so check for germline NF1.

entities.variants: Nipple-areolar (dartoic) leiomyoma; parenchymal leiomyoma; angioleiomyoma; Cutaneous leiomyoma (WHO 5th lists cutaneous leiomyoma and leiomyoma of the nipple and areola)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; most arise in nipple-areolar complex; SMA/desmin/h-caldesmon+.
entities.histo: Leiomyomas of the breast are uncommon benign smooth muscle tumours. Most arise in the nipple-areolar complex from the dartos smooth muscle, forming small, firm, sometimes painful nodules. Parenchymal leiomyomas are rare, circumscribed masses deeper in the breast. Angioleiomyomas are subcutaneous, painful, well-circumscribed nodules composed of thick-walled vessels with concentric smooth muscle. Grossly, leiomyomas are firm, whorled and grey-white. Microscopically, interlacing fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm, perinuclear vacuoles and blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei show no significant atypia, necrosis or mitoses. Nipple leiomyomas are less circumscribed and merge with the normal dartos muscle. IHC shows positivity for SMA, desmin and h-caldesmon, and negativity for keratins, S100 and CD34. Differentials include leiomyosarcoma (atypia, mitoses, necrosis), myofibroblastoma (CD34-positive, desmin-positive, collagen bands), myoid hamartoma, spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin and p63 positive), phyllodes tumour with smooth muscle differentiation, and schwannoma.
entities.cyto: Leiomyoma of the breast, usually near the nipple-areola, yields aspirates of low cellularity with cohesive fascicles of bland spindle cells with blunt-ended cigar-shaped nuclei, eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm and occasional perinuclear vacuoles, without epithelial cells. Spindle cells may be difficult to aspirate because of the firm consistency. Differentials include myofibroblastoma, schwannoma, phyllodes stroma, myoepithelial lesions and leiomyosarcoma, which shows atypia, mitoses and necrosis. Cell block desmin and SMA support smooth muscle. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion, with histology.
entities.ihc: Breast leiomyoma, usually arising in the nipple-areolar complex, is made of fascicles of bland smooth muscle cells that are SMA positive, desmin positive, h-caldesmon positive and SMMHC positive, often ER and PR positive. It's negative for keratins, p63, S100 and CD34. Leiomyosarcoma is separated by atypia, necrosis and mitoses (with a higher Ki-67 and often aberrant p53), not by IHC. Myoepithelial tumours share SMA and calponin positivity but are also p63+ and keratin (CK5/6, CK14) positive. Spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma must be excluded with broad-spectrum keratins and p63, as must myofibroblastoma (CD34+, desmin+, RB1 loss).

entities.variants: Conventional lipoma; spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (RB1 loss); chondroid lipoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; distinguish from hamartoma (adenolipoma) and fat necrosis.
entities.histo: Lipomas of the breast are common benign adipocytic tumours. They form soft, mobile, encapsulated masses that are radiolucent on mammography. Grossly they are thinly encapsulated, yellow and greasy, with a lobulated cut surface. Conventional lipomas consist of mature, univacuolated adipocytes of uniform size, with small eccentric nuclei and delicate fibrous septa, and they do not contain ducts or lobules. Spindle cell and pleomorphic lipomas, which are more common in men, contain bland CD34-positive spindle cells, rope-like collagen, mast cells and, in pleomorphic lipomas, floret giant cells. These lipomas show RB1 loss and overlap with myofibroblastoma. Chondroid lipoma contains lipoblast-like cells in a chondromyxoid matrix. Differentials include hamartoma or adenolipoma (contains ducts and lobules), fat necrosis, atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical stromal cells, MDM2 amplification), angiolipoma, and normal fatty breast tissue sampled from a fatty mass. On core biopsy, correlation with imaging confirms that the lesion was sampled.
entities.cyto: Lipoma of the breast yields greasy aspirates composed of mature adipose tissue fragments with uniform univacuolated adipocytes, small eccentric bland nuclei and delicate capillaries, without epithelial cells. The cytological features are indistinguishable from normal breast fat, so correlation with a discrete fatty lesion on imaging is essential to accept the sample as representative. Pitfalls include aspirating fat around a missed lesion and well-differentiated liposarcoma, which may show atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells or lipoblasts. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), adipose tissue consistent with lipoma when concordant, or Category 1 if not representative.
entities.ihc: Lipoma of the breast usually needs no IHC. Adipocytes are S100 positive. Spindle-cell and pleomorphic lipomas show CD34-positive spindle cells and loss of nuclear RB1 (13q14 deletion). The main differentials are hamartoma (glandular elements present), fat necrosis (histiocytes, CD68+) and atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma. In large, deep or atypical lesions, MDM2 amplification by FISH, or MDM2 and CDK4 nuclear IHC, should be done: amplification favours ALT/WDL and its absence supports lipoma. Angiolipoma has a vascular component.

entities.variants: Conventional; cellular angiolipoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; vascular component with fibrin thrombi; cellular angiolipoma mimics angiosarcoma (well-circumscribed, capsule, thrombi favour angiolipoma).
entities.histo: Angiolipoma is a benign adipocytic tumour with a vascular component that occurs in the breast subcutis or parenchyma, often as small, sometimes tender or multiple nodules. It may be detected on mammography or ultrasound as a hyperechoic mass. Grossly the nodule is well-circumscribed, encapsulated and yellow, with a reddish tinge. Microscopically, mature adipose tissue is mixed with clusters of small capillary-sized vessels, often concentrated at the periphery, and these frequently contain fibrin thrombi, a diagnostic clue. The endothelium is flat and bland. Cellular angiolipoma is composed predominantly of vascular channels with little fat, and the dense proliferation of capillaries and spindle cells can closely mimic angiosarcoma. Its circumscription, fibrous capsule, fibrin microthrombi, absence of endothelial atypia and absence of dissection into breast lobules favour angiolipoma. Other differentials include haemangioma, lipoma, Kaposi sarcoma (HHV8-positive) and spindle cell lipoma, so careful examination of the borders is important in core biopsies.
entities.cyto: Angiolipoma yields aspirates similar to lipoma, with mature adipose tissue fragments plus small capillary fragments, occasional bland endothelial cells and sometimes fibrin microthrombi, without epithelial cells. It is often tender. The vascular component may be scanty or appear more prominent in cellular angiolipoma, which can mimic a vascular tumour such as angiosarcoma. Cytology cannot reliably separate angiolipoma from lipoma or normal fat, and imaging correlation is required. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) when concordant, or Category 3 if the vascular component is cellular and atypical, with excision.
entities.ihc: Angiolipoma shows mature adipocytes with clusters of capillaries containing fibrin microthrombi. The capillary endothelium is CD31, CD34 and ERG positive. It can be mistaken for angiosarcoma, especially cellular angiolipoma, but it lacks infiltrative, anastomosing channels in breast lobules and endothelial atypia, and it's MYC negative with a low Ki-67. Adipocytes are S100 positive. MDM2 amplification is absent, which excludes atypical lipomatous tumour. The diagnosis is mainly morphological, and IHC is used to confirm vascular differentiation and exclude malignancy.

entities.entity: Other benign soft-tissue tumours of breast (rare)
entities.variants: Benign fibrous histiocytoma (dermatofibroma) of breast skin; glomus tumour; soft-tissue chondroma; benign fibrous lesions of skin
entities.remarks: Rare; classify per WHO Soft Tissue & Bone Tumours (5th ed).
entities.histo: Other benign soft-tissue tumours of the breast are rare and should be classified according to WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours (5th edition). Benign fibrous histiocytoma (dermatofibroma) of the breast skin shows a dermal proliferation of spindle cells in a storiform pattern, with collagen trapping at the periphery, overlying epidermal hyperplasia with basal pigmentation, and FXIIIa positivity. It is separated from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans by being CD34-negative and lacking deep infiltration of fat. Glomus tumour shows uniform round cells with sharp borders around vessels, positive for SMA and collagen IV, and is often painful. Soft-tissue chondroma shows lobules of mature hyaline cartilage, often calcified, and must be separated from chondroid metaplastic carcinoma and from the cartilage of phyllodes tumours or hamartomas. Other benign skin fibrous lesions include scars and keloids. For any mesenchymal-looking lesion in the breast, metaplastic carcinoma and phyllodes tumour must first be excluded by keratin, p63 IHC and adequate sampling for epithelial elements.
entities.cyto: Other rare benign soft tissue tumours of the breast, such as solitary fibrous tumour, spindle cell lipoma, fibromatosis-like lesions and benign fibrous histiocytoma, yield aspirates of variable cellularity with bland spindle cells, collagen, adipose tissue, myxoid stroma or mast cells, without epithelial cells. The cytological features are non-specific and overlap with phyllodes tumour stroma, myofibroblastoma, nodular fasciitis and metaplastic carcinoma. Cell block immunochemistry (for example STAT6, CD34, beta-catenin, cytokeratin) helps narrow the differential. Definitive classification requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion, with core or excision biopsy.
entities.ihc: Rare benign soft tissue tumours of the breast are classified as in the WHO soft tissue volume, using entity-specific IHC. Dermatofibroma is factor XIIIa positive and CD34 negative, unlike DFSP (CD34+, COL1A1-PDGFB). Solitary fibrous tumour is STAT6 nuclear positive and CD34 positive (NAB2-STAT6). Hibernoma is S100 positive. Benign PEComa is HMB-45, Melan-A and SMA positive. Glomus tumour is SMA positive, h-caldesmon positive and collagen IV positive. In every spindle-cell lesion of the breast, broad-spectrum keratins and p63 should be done first to exclude metaplastic carcinoma, which is far more common than primary mesenchymal tumours.

entities.entity: Benign adnexal tumours of breast/nipple skin
entities.variants: Hidradenoma; syringoma; eccrine spiradenoma; pilomatricoma; seborrhoeic keratosis; hidradenoma papilliferum (ectopic)
entities.remarks: Arise from skin of breast; classify per WHO Skin Tumours; hidradenoma of breast may mimic carcinoma (CRTC1::MAML2).
entities.histo: Benign adnexal tumours of the breast and nipple skin arise from cutaneous hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, and are classified according to WHO Skin Tumours. Hidradenoma forms a dermal nodule with clear, poroid and squamoid cells and cystic spaces, and harbours a CRTC1::MAML2 fusion. When it is deep in breast tissue, it can mimic carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Syringoma shows small comma-shaped ducts in a sclerotic dermis and must be differentiated from syringomatous tumour of the nipple and microcystic adnexal carcinoma. Eccrine spiradenoma consists of blue balls of basaloid cells with lymphocytes. Pilomatricoma shows basaloid cells, ghost (shadow) cells and calcification. Seborrhoeic keratosis shows basaloid acanthosis with horn cysts. Hidradenoma papilliferum can arise in ectopic mammary-like glands. These lesions are located in the dermis or subcutis with no relationship to breast ducts, and their adnexal differentiation is helpful. Differentials include primary breast carcinoma, metastatic carcinoma, and syringomatous tumour of the nipple.
entities.cyto: Benign adnexal tumours of breast or nipple skin, such as pilomatrixoma, hidradenoma, syringoma and cylindroma, are sometimes aspirated as superficial nodules. Pilomatrixoma shows basaloid cells, ghost (shadow) cells, keratinous debris, calcification and giant cells; hidradenoma shows clusters of cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyaline stroma. These features may mimic carcinoma, especially when basaloid cells are numerous, or adenoid cystic carcinoma when hyaline globules are present. The superficial dermal location on imaging is key. Findings are reported descriptively, often as Yokohama Category 2 or 3 depending on cellularity and atypia, with excision.
entities.ihc: Benign adnexal tumours of the breast and nipple skin (hidradenoma, syringoma, spiradenoma, pilomatricoma) are classified per the WHO skin tumour volume, and IHC is used mainly to separate them from mammary carcinoma. Adnexal tumours are often p63 positive and CK5/6 positive, with luminal CEA and EMA, and are frequently ER and GATA3 positive, which overlaps with breast tumours. Morphology and location (dermis versus parenchyma) are key. Pilomatricoma shows nuclear β-catenin (CTNNB1 mutations), and hidradenoma often carries CRTC1-MAML2 fusions. Syringoma in the nipple should be separated from syringomatous tumour of the nipple.

entities.remarks: Listed by WHO 5th under adenosis and benign sclerosing lesions; well-circumscribed nodular adenosis/adenoma made of apocrine cells with myoepithelium retained.
entities.histo: Apocrine adenoma is a rare, benign, well-circumscribed nodular lesion listed in WHO 5th edition among adenosis and benign sclerosing lesions. It can be regarded as nodular adenosis or an adenoma composed of apocrine cells. It presents as a palpable or imaging-detected circumscribed mass. Microscopically, closely packed tubules and glands are lined by apocrine cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, apical snouts, round nuclei and prominent nucleoli, set in scant stroma. A preserved, continuous myoepithelial layer is present on p63, calponin and SMMHC. Cysts and papillary apocrine change may be seen, but significant atypia, necrosis and mitoses are absent. The cells are AR-positive and GCDFP-15-positive, and ER-negative. Differentials include apocrine adenosis (lobulocentric, sclerosing, not a discrete adenoma), tubular adenoma with apocrine change, ductal adenoma, apocrine DCIS (marked atypia, necrosis, no benign glandular pattern), and invasive apocrine carcinoma, which is infiltrative and lacks myoepithelium. Complete excision is curative.
entities.cyto: Apocrine adenoma is a rare circumscribed nodular lesion composed of apocrine cells. Aspirates would be expected to show cohesive sheets, acini and honeycomb groups of apocrine cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, round central nuclei and prominent nucleoli, admixed with myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, often with foamy macrophages. The cytology overlaps with apocrine metaplasia, apocrine adenosis and fibrocystic change, and nucleoli inherent to apocrine cells may cause concern for apocrine carcinoma, which is dyscohesive and pleomorphic, sometimes necrotic. A specific diagnosis requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign), or Category 3 if atypia is present.
entities.ihc: Apocrine adenoma is a well-circumscribed nodular adenosis or adenoma made of apocrine cells. Its IHC matches benign apocrine metaplasia: the luminal cells are AR positive and GCDFP-15 positive, ER and PR negative or weak, and HER2 negative, with a low Ki-67. A retained myoepithelial layer (p63, SMMHC, calponin) around every gland is the key finding separating it from invasive apocrine carcinoma, which lacks myoepithelium and is often HER2-positive or AR-positive triple-negative. Apocrine DCIS within adenosis shows marked nuclear atypia and a higher Ki-67, with myoepithelium preserved. The ER-negative, CK5/6-negative profile of apocrine cells mustn't be mistaken for clonal atypia. Granular cell tumour (S100+, keratin−) is a morphological mimic.

entities.remarks: Not separately classified by WHO 5th (PathologyOutlines 'other carcinoma subtypes, not WHO classified'); purely myoepithelial benign tumour (spindle/plasmacytoid cells; p63, SMA, calponin, S100+); part of the adenomyoepithelial spectrum.
entities.histo: Myoepithelioma of the breast is a rare benign tumour composed purely, or almost purely, of myoepithelial cells, without the ductal epithelial component of adenomyoepithelioma. WHO 5th edition does not classify it separately, and it is regarded as part of the adenomyoepithelial spectrum. It presents as a well-circumscribed, firm mass. Microscopically, it shows sheets, nests or fascicles of bland spindle, epithelioid, plasmacytoid or clear myoepithelial cells in a collagenous or myxoid stroma, sometimes with hyalinisation. Nuclear atypia is minimal, mitoses are rare and necrosis is absent. The cells are positive for p63, SMA, calponin, SMMHC, S100 and CK5/6 (often with keratin positivity), and negative for ER. The main differential is myoepithelial carcinoma, which shows infiltrative borders, nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and necrosis. Others include spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, adenomyoepithelioma, myoepithelial hyperplasia, myofibroblastoma (CD34-positive and desmin-positive), leiomyoma and schwannoma (S100-positive but p63-negative). Complete excision with clear margins is advised because of the risk of local recurrence.
entities.cyto: Myoepithelioma of the breast is rare, and cytological descriptions are limited. Aspirates would be expected to show a monophasic population of myoepithelial cells, spindle, plasmacytoid, epithelioid or clear, singly and in loose clusters, with bland oval nuclei, sometimes with hyaline or myxoid stromal material, and without a luminal epithelial component. The differentials include adenomyoepithelioma, pleomorphic adenoma, spindle cell lesions such as myofibroblastoma and schwannoma, and spindle cell metaplastic or myoepithelial carcinoma. Cell block positivity for p63, SMA, calponin and S100 supports myoepithelial differentiation. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with excision for definitive classification.
entities.ihc: Myoepithelioma is a benign tumour made purely of myoepithelial cells, often spindle-shaped or plasmacytoid, and sits in the adenomyoepithelial spectrum. The tumour cells are p63 positive, SMA positive, calponin positive, SMMHC positive, CK5/6 and CK14 positive, and often S100 positive, with variable GFAP. They are ER and PR negative, have a low Ki-67, and lack a significant CK7/CK8-18-positive luminal component, which separates them from adenomyoepithelioma. The key differentials are myoepithelial carcinoma and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma, which share the same markers. These are recognised by infiltrative growth, atypia, necrosis, mitoses and a high Ki-67, so IHC alone can't decide. Myofibroblastoma (CD34+, desmin+, p63−) and leiomyoma (keratin−, p63−) are excluded with a small panel.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; invasive focus/foci each ≤1 mm (pT1mi) usually associated with high-grade DCIS; multiple foci not summed; confirm absence of myoepithelium (p63/SMMHC).
entities.histo: Microinvasive carcinoma is invasive carcinoma with one or more foci of invasion, each measuring 1 mm or less, staged pT1mi. It usually arises in a background of extensive, high-grade DCIS, frequently with comedonecrosis, or in lobular neoplasia. Microscopically, small irregular clusters or single tumour cells lie in the stroma beyond the basement membrane, without a surrounding myoepithelial layer, often with a desmoplastic or lymphocytic stromal response next to involved ducts. Multiple foci are not added together, but their number should be reported, and the largest focus is the one measured. Confirmation requires myoepithelial IHC, such as p63, calponin, SMMHC or CK5/6, and sometimes keratin to highlight single cells. Pitfalls include tangential sectioning of DCIS-involved ducts, DCIS in sclerosing adenosis or radial scars, cancerisation of lobules, crush and cautery artefact, and displaced epithelium after biopsy. Nodal metastases are uncommon, and sentinel node biopsy is often performed, depending on the extent of DCIS. ER, PR and HER2 may be tested on the in situ or invasive component.
entities.cyto: Microinvasive carcinoma (invasion 1 mm or less) is a histological diagnosis that cannot be made on cytology. Aspirates reflect the in situ component, typically high-grade DCIS with cellular smears, dyscohesive pleomorphic cells, coarse chromatin, nucleoli and necrotic debris, and are reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant) carcinoma, or Category 4 (Suspicious) if low-grade or limited. The cytology report should state that in situ and invasive carcinoma cannot be distinguished. Core biopsy and excision with careful histological sampling are required to identify foci of microinvasion.
entities.ihc: IHC is essential for diagnosing microinvasive carcinoma, defined as invasive foci each 1 mm or less, usually in a background of high-grade DCIS. Myoepithelial markers, ideally two of them (p63 plus SMMHC or calponin) and a basement membrane marker, show that the suspicious cells or clusters lack myoepithelium. Pan-keratin highlights small foci in inflamed or cancerised stroma. Pitfalls include tangential sectioning, cancerisation of lobules, sclerosing adenosis involved by DCIS, and crush artefact, which can falsely suggest invasion. ER, PR and HER2 testing on the microinvasive focus is often not possible and is typically performed on the DCIS. Ki-67 isn't routine.

entities.entity: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NST)
entities.variants: Special morphological patterns (WHO 5th): medullary pattern (formerly medullary/atypical medullary carcinoma — now IBC-NST with medullary pattern, TIL-rich, often BRCA1/TNBC); oncocytic carcinoma; lipid-rich carcinoma; glycogen-rich clear cell carcinoma; sebaceous carcinoma; carcinoma with osteoclast-like stromal giant cells; pleomorphic carcinoma; carcinoma with choriocarcinomatous features; carcinoma with melanocytic features; carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation (<90% NE). Mixed types: IBC-NST with special-type component (10–90% special type); mixed ductal-lobular; Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma pattern; WHO wording 'basal-like and medullary pattern'; HER2-low / HER2-ultralow are biomarker categories (not morphological variants)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: commonest type (~70–75%); diagnosed when no special-type pattern or special type <10%; pure special type requires ≥90% of the pattern; 10–90% special type = mixed carcinoma. Nottingham (Elston-Ellis) grade 1–3; report ER, PR, HER2 (incl. HER2-low), Ki-67; TILs recommended in TNBC/HER2+. Molecular intrinsic subtypes: luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like.
entities.histo: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NST) accounts for about 70 to 75% of breast cancers. It is diagnosed when no special-type pattern is present or a special pattern makes up less than 10% of the tumour. Grossly it is a firm, grey-white, stellate, gritty mass. Microscopically, tumour cells form sheets, nests, cords, trabeculae and glands in desmoplastic stroma, with variable pleomorphism and mitoses. Nottingham grading combines tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic count. Special morphological patterns include a medullary pattern (circumscribed, syncytial, TIL-rich, often BRCA1-associated and triple-negative), oncocytic, lipid-rich, glycogen-rich clear cell, sebaceous, osteoclast-like stromal giant cells, pleomorphic, choriocarcinomatous, melanocytic and neuroendocrine differentiation under 90%. Tumours with 10 to 90% of a special type are reported as mixed, including mixed ductal-lobular carcinoma. Reports should give grade, size, LVI, margins, ER, PR, HER2 including HER2-low, Ki-67, and TILs in triple-negative or HER2-positive disease. Differentials include ILC (E-cadherin loss), metastases (GATA3 and TRPS1 positive in breast) and DCIS with tangential sectioning.
entities.cyto: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type yields cellular smears with dyscohesive groups and numerous single intact atypical epithelial cells with enlarged, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear membranes, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli and variable cytoplasm, often with intracytoplasmic lumina. Myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei are absent or scanty. Necrosis may be present in high-grade tumours. Low-grade tumours may be deceptively bland. Cell block allows ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 testing. In situ and invasive disease cannot be separated. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, consistent with ductal carcinoma NST.
entities.ihc: In invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NST), IHC is above all predictive. ER and PR are reported per ASCO/CAP (1% or more positive, with 1–10% reported as ER-low positive), and HER2 is scored 0, 1+, 2+ or 3+, with ISH for 2+ cases. HER2-low and HER2-ultralow categories are now reported for trastuzumab deruxtecan eligibility. Ki-67 is reported with its method. These define the surrogate subtypes. Diagnostically, E-cadherin separates it from lobular carcinoma, and myoepithelial markers confirm invasion. Special patterns have their own markers: medullary-pattern tumours are triple-negative with dense TILs and BRCA1 association, and tumours with osteoclast-like giant cells contain CD68-positive giant cells. PD-L1 (22C3, CPS 10 or more) applies to TNBC.

entities.variants: Classic; solid; alveolar; pleomorphic (grade 3 nuclei, may have apocrine/histiocytoid features); tubulolobular; signet-ring cell (histiocytoid) pattern; mixed lobular (non-classic combinations); Lobular carcinoma with extracellular mucin (rare)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; ~10–15%; discohesive cells in single files/targetoid pattern; E-cadherin loss (CDH1 inactivation) with cytoplasmic p120; ER+ mostly (pleomorphic may be HER2+/AR+); multifocal/bilateral; unusual metastatic sites (peritoneum, GI tract, ovary, meninges, bone marrow).
entities.histo: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) makes up about 10 to 15% of breast cancers. It is often multifocal or bilateral and clinically or radiologically subtle, with ill-defined thickening rather than a discrete mass. Classic ILC shows small, uniform, discohesive cells with round nuclei and intracytoplasmic vacuoles infiltrating singly and in single files, often surrounding ducts in a targetoid pattern with little desmoplasia. Solid ILC forms sheets, alveolar ILC forms nests of 20 or more cells, and tubulolobular ILC combines small tubules with lobular single files. Pleomorphic ILC has grade 3 nuclei, often apocrine or histiocytoid features, and may be HER2-positive or AR-positive. Signet-ring cell ILC shows prominent intracytoplasmic mucin. Mixed non-classic patterns also occur. Loss of E-cadherin from CDH1 inactivation, with cytoplasmic p120, confirms the lobular phenotype, and most tumours are ER-positive. Metastases favour unusual sites such as the peritoneum, gastrointestinal tract, ovary, meninges and bone marrow, and can mimic primary tumours. Differentials include IBC-NST, histiocytes, lymphoma, signet-ring metastases from the stomach, and epithelioid myofibroblastoma.
entities.cyto: Invasive lobular carcinoma aspirates are often of low to moderate cellularity because of dyscohesive infiltrative growth in dense stroma. Smears show small, uniform, single cells and short chains or Indian files of cells with round to eccentric nuclei, scant cytoplasm, intracytoplasmic lumina and signet ring forms; pleomorphic ILC has larger, more atypical cells. The bland, sparse cells are easily missed or mistaken for lymphocytes or histiocytes, a major cause of false-negative results. E-cadherin loss on cell block supports the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), or Category 3 or 4 when cells are scanty.
entities.ihc: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) shows loss of E-cadherin, which is the key diagnostic marker, with p120 catenin moved to diffuse cytoplasmic staining and β-catenin lost. About 15% of cases retain aberrant or fragmented E-cadherin, which is why p120 is a useful addition. Classic ILC is ER+, PR+ (often), HER2−, and has a low Ki-67. Pleomorphic ILC may be ER-negative, HER2-positive or apocrine (AR+, GCDFP-15+), and has a higher Ki-67. Single-file cells can hide in stroma, nodes or margins, so keratin (AE1/AE3) helps. Metastatic ILC to the GI tract, peritoneum or ovary is GATA3+ and ER+. CDH1 mutation or loss underlies it, and CDH1 germline variants occur in some patients.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; >90% open angulated tubules with single layer of low-grade cells, apical snouts, desmoplastic/elastotic stroma; ER+/PR+, HER2−; excellent prognosis; often with FEA/ADH/low-grade DCIS/LN (low-grade family).
entities.histo: Tubular carcinoma is a special type of invasive carcinoma with an excellent prognosis, often found on screening as a small spiculated mass under 1 to 2 cm. More than 90% of the tumour must consist of open, angulated, oval or teardrop-shaped tubules. The tubules are lined by a single layer of low-grade, uniform cuboidal to columnar cells with apical snouts, arranged haphazardly in cellular desmoplastic or elastotic stroma, and they lack a myoepithelial layer. Nuclear pleomorphism and mitoses are minimal. Tubular carcinoma is strongly ER-positive and PR-positive, HER2-negative and has a low Ki-67. It is frequently accompanied by members of the low-grade breast neoplasia family, such as flat epithelial atypia, ADH, low-grade DCIS, lobular neoplasia and tubulolobular carcinoma. Nodal metastasis is uncommon. Differentials include radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, sclerosing adenosis and microglandular adenosis, which have rounded glands with a basement membrane but no myoepithelium and are ER-negative and S100-positive. Low-grade IBC-NST with tubules under 90% and tubular adenoma must also be excluded.
entities.cyto: Tubular carcinoma is a common cause of false-negative breast FNA. Aspirates are of low to moderate cellularity with small, rigid, angulated, comma-shaped or tubular groups of uniform cuboidal cells with mild nuclear atypia, few single cells and absent or scanty myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei; stromal fragments with elastosis may be present. The bland cells overlap with fibroadenoma, sclerosing adenosis and radial scar. Angulated tubules without myoepithelial cells are a clue. Usually reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or 4 (Suspicious), rarely Category 5, with core biopsy for confirmation.
entities.ihc: Tubular carcinoma has open, angulated tubules with single-layered epithelium, apical snouts and no myoepithelial layer. p63, SMMHC and calponin are negative around the tubules, and this is the key finding against sclerosing adenosis, radial scar and microglandular adenosis (S100+, ER−, basement membrane present). It is strongly ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, and has a low Ki-67, a luminal A-like profile. E-cadherin is positive. It's often associated with flat epithelial atypia, low-grade DCIS and lobular neoplasia (the 'Rosen triad'). The diagnosis requires more than 90% tubular morphology, and tubular-pattern areas within NST are reported as mixed.

entities.variants: Pure (>90%); mixed with tubular carcinoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; invasive cribriform islands of low-grade cells; ER+; excellent prognosis; differential: cribriform DCIS, adenoid cystic carcinoma, collagenous spherulosis.
entities.histo: Invasive cribriform carcinoma is a special type of low-grade invasive carcinoma with an excellent prognosis, similar to tubular carcinoma. More than 90% of the tumour is composed of invasive, irregular, angulated islands of low-grade, uniform cells with sieve-like (cribriform) spaces, set in desmoplastic stroma. The lumina are sharply punched-out and may contain secretions or microcalcifications. A component of tubular carcinoma is often present, and tumours with mixed tubular and cribriform patterns are classified as invasive cribriform carcinoma when the cribriform pattern predominates. Osteoclast-like giant cells occur in some tumours. The tumour is ER-positive and PR-positive, and HER2-negative. Differentials include cribriform DCIS, which has rounded, duct-shaped nests surrounded by myoepithelium, and adenoid cystic carcinoma, which has dual luminal and basaloid cells, basement membrane material, CD117 and MYB positivity and is triple-negative. Collagenous spherulosis shows myoepithelial-lined spherules. Other differentials are IBC-NST with a cribriform component, and metastatic prostatic or salivary carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Invasive cribriform carcinoma is a low-grade tumour that yields cellular smears with cohesive cribriform and tubular groups of uniform cells with mild nuclear atypia, few single cells and scanty or absent myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei, sometimes with osteoclast-like giant cells. The bland cells overlap with fibroadenoma, low-grade DCIS and adenoid cystic carcinoma, which can also have a cribriform pattern but shows hyaline globules and basaloid cells. Invasion cannot be assessed. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant) when atypia and cellularity are sufficient, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Invasive cribriform carcinoma is strongly ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, and has a low Ki-67, a luminal A-like profile. Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMMHC, calponin) are absent around the invasive cribriform islands, which separates it from cribriform DCIS (myoepithelium retained) and from collagenous spherulosis. The main mimic is adenoid cystic carcinoma, which has true basement membrane-filled pseudolumina and a biphasic luminal and myoepithelial population (CD117+, p63+, CK5/6+), is ER-negative, and carries MYB-NFIB fusion or MYB overexpression. E-cadherin is positive. More than 90% cribriform morphology is required, and tubular admixture is allowed.

entities.variants: Type A (paucicellular, classic); type B (hypercellular, often neuroendocrine differentiation); mixed (with NST); Mucinous carcinoma with micropapillary features (micropapillary mucinous carcinoma)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; >90% clusters of tumour cells floating in extracellular mucin pools; ER+/HER2−; favourable prognosis; older women.
entities.histo: Mucinous carcinoma is a special type of carcinoma with a favourable prognosis, usually in older women, presenting as a soft, circumscribed mass with a gelatinous, glistening cut surface. More than 90% of the tumour consists of clusters, nests, trabeculae or cribriform groups of tumour cells floating in pools of extracellular mucin, separated by thin fibrous septa containing capillaries. Type A (paucicellular, classic) has abundant mucin with small, scattered groups of cells. Type B (hypercellular) has larger sheets of cells, often with neuroendocrine differentiation (granular cytoplasm, synaptophysin positivity), and overlaps with solid papillary carcinoma. Tumours with 10 to 90% mucinous carcinoma and NST carcinoma are mixed tumours with a less favourable prognosis. Pure mucinous carcinoma is ER-positive and PR-positive, HER2-negative and rarely metastasises to nodes. A micropapillary pattern within mucinous carcinoma, with reversed polarity, represents a variant with more frequent nodal involvement. Differentials include mucocele-like lesions (epithelial strips with myoepithelium), myxoid fibroadenoma, metaplastic carcinoma with matrix production, and metastatic mucinous carcinoma from the gastrointestinal tract or ovary.
entities.cyto: Mucinous carcinoma aspirates are gelatinous and show abundant extracellular mucin, often with branching capillaries, in which float numerous cohesive three-dimensional balls, sheets and single intact epithelial cells with mild to moderate nuclear atypia and moderate cytoplasm; neuroendocrine-type plasmacytoid cells may be seen. Myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei are absent. The main differentials are mucocele-like lesion (scanty bland cells, myoepithelium) and mixed mucinous carcinoma with an NST component. Mucin may be mistaken for stroma on MGG. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), consistent with mucinous carcinoma, or Category 4 when cellularity is low.
entities.ihc: Mucinous carcinoma (type A paucicellular and type B hypercellular) is typically ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, and has a low Ki-67. Type B often shows neuroendocrine differentiation, with synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity. Clusters floating in mucin lack a myoepithelial layer, which separates them from mucocele-like lesions (myoepithelium-bearing epithelial strips). In metastatic settings, GATA3 positivity, CK7 positivity, CK20 negativity, CDX2 negativity and SATB2 negativity help separate breast primary from colorectal or appendiceal mucinous carcinoma, and WT1 and PAX8 negativity help with ovarian tumours. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma and micropapillary-pattern mucinous carcinoma (MUC1 inside-out) are distinct. HER2 is rarely positive.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; rare; cysts lined by tall columnar cells with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin, resembling ovarian/pancreatic counterpart; usually ER/PR/HER2 negative but favourable outcome; exclude metastasis.
entities.histo: Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is a rare primary breast carcinoma, mainly in postmenopausal women. It presents as a large, cystic, well-circumscribed mass, and the cut surface shows cysts filled with mucinous fluid. Microscopically, cysts of varying size are lined by tall columnar epithelium with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin and basal nuclei, closely resembling mucinous cystic tumours of the ovary or pancreas. Cytological atypia ranges from low to high grade, and papillary or stratified areas and stromal invasion around cysts are present. Extracellular mucin is less prominent than in classic mucinous carcinoma. The cells are CK7-positive and usually CK20-negative and CDX2-negative. ER, PR and HER2 are generally negative, but the prognosis is reportedly favourable. Because of its resemblance to extramammary mucinous neoplasms, metastases from the ovary, pancreas, appendix and gastrointestinal tract must be excluded clinically, radiologically and immunohistochemically. The presence of an associated in situ component, GATA3 positivity and the CK7/CK20 profile support a breast origin. Other differentials are mucinous carcinoma and mucocele-like lesion.
entities.cyto: Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is a rare primary breast tumour that resembles its ovarian and pancreatic counterparts. Aspirates would be expected to show abundant mucin with tall columnar cells containing intracytoplasmic mucin, in papillary or sheet-like groups with variable nuclear atypia, sometimes with necrotic debris. Cytological descriptions are limited. The key differentials are metastatic mucinous carcinoma from ovary, pancreas or gastrointestinal tract, and mucinous carcinoma of the breast. Immunochemistry on cell block (CK7, ER, PR, GATA3, CK20, CDX2) and clinical evaluation help exclude metastasis. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), mucinous adenocarcinoma, with a comment on excluding metastasis.
entities.ihc: Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is rare. Its cysts are lined by tall columnar mucinous cells that resemble pancreatic or ovarian counterparts. Unlike conventional mucinous carcinoma it is usually ER−, PR− and HER2−, but CK7 positive and GATA3 positive. It is CK20 negative, CDX2 negative, SATB2 negative, PAX8 negative and WT1 negative, and this profile is key to excluding metastasis from the ovary, pancreas or appendix, together with clinical and imaging correlation. Myoepithelium is absent in the invasive areas. PIK3CA mutations have been reported. Mucocele-like lesions and mucinous DCIS are separated on morphology and by the presence of myoepithelium.

entities.variants: Pure (>90%); mixed with NST
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; hollow/morula-like clusters in clear stromal spaces with 'inside-out' (reverse) polarity (EMA/MUC1 on stromal surface); high propensity for LVI and nodal metastasis; micropapillary pattern in mucinous carcinoma is a variant of mucinous.
entities.histo: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma is defined by small, hollow or morula-like clusters of tumour cells without fibrovascular cores. The clusters lie within clear stromal spaces that resemble lymphatics but lack an endothelial lining. The cells show inside-out (reverse) polarity, with the apical surface facing the stroma, which is shown by EMA or MUC1 staining on the outer stromal surface of the clusters. The nuclei are usually intermediate to high grade, and psammomatous calcifications may occur. Pure tumours have more than 90% micropapillary pattern, but mixed tumours with NST carcinoma are more common, and the proportion should be reported because even small components matter. The tumour has a high propensity for lymphovascular invasion and nodal metastasis, often presenting with extensive nodal disease. It is usually ER-positive, with variable HER2 positivity. A micropapillary pattern can occur within mucinous carcinoma, where it is classified as a variant of mucinous carcinoma. Differentials include IBC-NST with retraction artefact (no reversed polarity), true LVI, which is D2-40-positive, and metastatic micropapillary carcinoma from the ovary, lung or bladder.
entities.cyto: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma yields cellular smears with numerous small, tight, three-dimensional clusters and morules of cells without fibrovascular cores, showing reversed polarity with a scalloped or knobby outer border, moderate to marked nuclear atypia and dense cytoplasm, along with single cells. Psammoma bodies and mucin may occasionally be seen. Differentials include papillary lesions, mucinous carcinoma with micropapillary features and metastatic serous carcinoma of the ovary or micropapillary carcinoma of lung or bladder, which require cell block immunochemistry (WT1, PAX8, GATA3, ER). Lymph node metastasis is frequent. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with micropapillary features.
entities.ihc: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma is defined morphologically, and the key IHC finding is reversed polarity, with 'inside-out' apical staining of EMA or MUC1 on the outer (stroma-facing) surface of the clusters. It is usually ER+ (often strongly) and PR+, with HER2 positivity more frequent than in NST, so HER2 per ASCO/CAP is important. Ki-67 is often intermediate to high. It has a high rate of lymphovascular invasion and nodal metastasis, and D2-40 or CD31 helps separate true lymphovascular invasion from the retraction artefact typical of the tumour. In metastases, GATA3 and ER separate it from micropapillary carcinoma of the lung, bladder and ovary.

entities.variants: Apocrine carcinoma (ER−/PR−/AR+ molecular apocrine); apocrine features in ER+ carcinoma; histiocytoid apocrine
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; >90% apocrine cells (abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli); AR+, GCDFP-15+; often HER2+ or triple-negative 'molecular apocrine' subtype.
entities.histo: Carcinoma with apocrine differentiation is defined in WHO 5th edition by more than 90% of tumour cells showing apocrine features. The cells have abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, distinct borders, large round nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and sometimes vacuolated or foamy cytoplasm. The architecture varies from sheets to glands, and an apocrine DCIS component is often present. The cells are AR-positive and GCDFP-15-positive. Molecular apocrine carcinomas are typically ER-negative and PR-negative and AR-positive, and they are either HER2-positive or triple-negative. Apocrine features may also be seen in otherwise ER-positive carcinomas. Histiocytoid apocrine carcinoma has foamy cytoplasm resembling histiocytes, can be lobular-like and is E-cadherin-negative. AR expression may be relevant for clinical trials or therapy. Differentials include granular cell tumour (S100-positive, keratin-negative), oncocytic carcinoma (mitochondria-rich, AR variable), apocrine adenosis with myoepithelium, histiocytic lesions and fat necrosis (CD68-positive), and metastatic tumours such as renal cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Carcinoma with apocrine differentiation yields cellular smears of dyscohesive groups and single large cells with abundant, granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm, large round to pleomorphic nuclei with prominent macronucleoli and coarse chromatin, sometimes with necrosis. Myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei are absent. Benign apocrine metaplasia, apocrine adenosis and granular cell tumour are the key differentials; benign apocrine cells are cohesive, uniform and lack necrosis. Cell block immunochemistry typically shows androgen receptor and GCDFP-15 positivity, often ER and PR negative. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with apocrine features, or Category 4 when atypia is less marked.
entities.ihc: Carcinoma with apocrine differentiation shows an apocrine profile: AR positive, GCDFP-15 positive, and typically ER and PR negative. These are 'molecular apocrine' tumours, and many are HER2 positive. AR-positive triple-negative tumours correspond to the luminal androgen receptor TNBC subtype. Report ER, PR and HER2 per ASCO/CAP, and AR if it's relevant to trials. FOXA1 is positive. PIK3CA mutations are frequent. The differentials include apocrine DCIS and apocrine adenosis, which keep their myoepithelium (p63, SMMHC), and granular cell tumour (S100+, keratin−). Histiocytoid lobular carcinoma (E-cadherin−) and oncocytic carcinoma (mitochondria-rich, GCDFP-15 negative) are separated by IHC.

entities.variants: Low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma; fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma; spindle cell carcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma (incl. acantholytic, cystic); metaplastic carcinoma with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation (chondroid, osseous, rhabdomyoid, other); mixed metaplastic carcinoma; Matrix-producing carcinoma (direct transition to chondromyxoid/osteoid matrix); carcinosarcoma (historical term)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; mostly triple-negative (basal-like/claudin-low), poor chemosensitivity except low-grade forms. Spindle-cell lesions of breast: keratins (HMW CK, AE1/AE3, CK5/6, 34βE12) and p63 positivity favour metaplastic carcinoma over sarcoma/phyllodes. Low-grade adenosquamous and fibromatosis-like types behave indolently (local recurrence).
entities.histo: Metaplastic carcinoma is a heterogeneous group in which tumour cells differentiate towards squamous or mesenchymal-looking (spindle, chondroid, osseous) elements. Most are triple-negative, basal-like or claudin-low, and respond poorly to chemotherapy. Low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma shows small glands and squamoid nests in a cellular stroma and has an indolent course. Fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma shows bland spindle cells in a collagenous stroma with scattered keratin-positive cells, and tends to recur locally. Spindle cell carcinoma shows atypical spindle cells. Squamous cell carcinoma, which may be acantholytic or cystic, shows keratinising cells and must be distinguished from a skin primary or metastasis. Metaplastic carcinoma with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation contains chondroid, osseous, rhabdomyoid or other elements, and mixed forms also occur. For spindle cell lesions of the breast, keratin positivity (AE1/AE3, HMW keratins, CK5/6, 34betaE12) and p63 strongly favour metaplastic carcinoma over sarcoma or malignant phyllodes tumour, and an associated DCIS component supports it. Differentials include phyllodes tumour, desmoid fibromatosis (nuclear beta-catenin), nodular fasciitis, myoepithelial carcinoma and primary sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Metaplastic carcinoma shows varied cytology depending on the component. Smears may contain malignant epithelial cells in groups, keratinising or non-keratinising malignant squamous cells, atypical spindle cells singly and in fascicles, chondromyxoid or osteoid matrix, and osteoclast-like giant cells, frequently with necrosis. Low-grade spindle cell (fibromatosis-like) variants are deceptively bland. Pitfalls include phyllodes tumour, sarcoma, nodular fasciitis and pleomorphic adenoma. Cell block cytokeratin (high-molecular-weight) and p63 support epithelial origin, and the tumours are usually triple negative. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant) or Category 4, depending on atypia and sampling.
entities.ihc: Metaplastic carcinoma is mostly triple-negative and basal-like. Diagnosis requires a broad keratin panel (AE1/AE3, MNF116, CK5/6, 34βE12, CK14), because keratin can be focal in spindle cells, and p63 (positive in most spindle-cell variants). Sarcomatoid tumours with no keratin or p63 staining in a breast mass should still be considered metaplastic carcinoma rather than sarcoma or malignant phyllodes, so sample widely. GATA3 is often weak or negative, and SOX10 is often positive. Variants include low-grade adenosquamous and fibromatosis-like carcinoma, spindle-cell, squamous, and carcinoma with heterologous differentiation. EGFR is often positive. PD-L1 is relevant for TNBC therapy. PIK3CA and TP53 mutations are common.

entities.remarks: Clinical diagnosis (erythema/oedema/peau d'orange ≥1/3 of breast, cT4d); dermal lymphatic tumour emboli commonly but not required; any histological type, often high-grade NST; poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Inflammatory carcinoma is a clinicopathological entity rather than a histological type. It is defined clinically by rapid onset of diffuse erythema, oedema and peau d'orange involving at least one third of the breast, with or without an underlying palpable mass, and it is staged cT4d. Biopsy confirms invasive carcinoma, usually high-grade IBC-NST, often HER2-positive or triple-negative, although any histological type may occur. A skin punch biopsy commonly shows dermal lymphatic tumour emboli, which cause the skin changes through lymphatic obstruction. However, dermal lymphatic emboli are not required for the diagnosis, and their presence without the clinical features does not establish inflammatory carcinoma. Microscopically there is little inflammatory infiltrate despite the name. Reports should state the histological type, grade, receptor status and the presence or absence of dermal lymphovascular invasion. The prognosis is poor, and treatment is multimodal, with neoadjuvant systemic therapy, modified radical mastectomy and radiotherapy. Differentials include acute mastitis or abscess and locally advanced neglected carcinoma (cT4b).
entities.cyto: Inflammatory carcinoma is a clinicopathological entity defined by diffuse erythema and oedema due to dermal lymphatic tumour emboli; the underlying carcinoma is usually high-grade NST. FNA of the underlying mass shows cellular smears of dyscohesive pleomorphic malignant cells with prominent nucleoli and sometimes necrosis, reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant). Cytology cannot establish the clinical diagnosis or dermal lymphatic involvement, which requires skin punch biopsy. The main clinical mimic is acute mastitis or abscess; inflammatory cells in the aspirate are not typical of inflammatory carcinoma, so a purely inflammatory aspirate should not reassure when the clinical picture is suspicious.
entities.ihc: Inflammatory carcinoma is a clinical diagnosis (erythema, oedema, peau d'orange) supported by dermal lymphatic tumour emboli, which are not required for diagnosis. IHC shows tumour emboli in dermal lymphatics, which are D2-40 positive. The tumour is usually high grade NST, often ER-negative and HER2-positive or triple-negative, with a high Ki-67. ER, PR and HER2 testing per ASCO/CAP on the core biopsy is essential before neoadjuvant therapy. Pan-keratin highlights emboli and isolated cells. Mastitis is the main clinical mimic, so a biopsy with keratin staining is warranted in persistent inflammatory change. PD-L1 testing applies in TNBC.

entities.remarks: Usually triple-negative carcinoma (NST, acinic cell, matrix-producing metaplastic) arising in MGA; shares TP53 alterations with associated MGA.
entities.histo: Carcinoma arising in microglandular adenosis is a rare carcinoma that develops in association with MGA or atypical MGA, typically in middle-aged women. Its morphology is variable. Most cases are triple-negative IBC-NST, but acinic cell carcinoma with zymogen-like granules and matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma are also seen, and in situ carcinoma may arise within the MGA glands. The MGA component shows small round glands without myoepithelium, with eosinophilic secretions, surrounded by basement membrane, and is S100-positive and ER-negative and PR-negative. Atypical MGA shows more complex, crowded glands and cytological atypia, forming a transition to carcinoma. The carcinoma shows loss of the basement membrane, solid or nested growth, high-grade nuclei and increased mitoses, and it often shares TP53 mutations and copy-number alterations with the associated MGA, supporting a precursor relationship. Treatment follows triple-negative breast cancer protocols, and complete excision of the MGA is recommended. Differentials include tubular carcinoma, which is ER-positive, sclerosing adenosis (myoepithelium present), and triple-negative carcinoma without MGA.
entities.cyto: Carcinoma arising in microglandular adenosis cannot be specifically diagnosed on cytology. Aspirates show features of invasive carcinoma, often triple negative, with cellular smears of dyscohesive groups and single cells showing moderate to marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli and sometimes clear or vacuolated cytoplasm, possibly with background small acinar groups representing MGA. The relationship to MGA is established only histologically. Cell block immunochemistry may show S100 positivity and ER, PR and HER2 negativity. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, or Category 4 (Suspicious) when cellularity or atypia are limited.
entities.ihc: Carcinoma arising in microglandular adenosis (MGA) is usually triple-negative and shares the S100-positive profile of MGA: ER, PR and HER2 negative, S100 positive, with variable EMA. It lacks myoepithelium (p63, SMMHC, calponin negative). Background MGA keeps a laminin- and collagen IV-positive basement membrane, which is lost in invasive carcinoma. Ki-67 is high. The carcinoma can be NST, acinic cell-like (lysozyme+, α1-antichymotrypsin+, DOG1+), metaplastic or matrix-producing. TP53 mutations are common and shared with the adjacent MGA, supporting MGA as a precursor. PD-L1 testing applies to triple-negative disease.

entities.variants: Without invasion; with invasion (invasive component beyond capsule, usually NST)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; cystic papillary lesion with fibrous capsule, myoepithelium absent within papillae and usually at periphery; low/intermediate grade, ER+; staged as pTis when no invasion beyond capsule (stage invasive component only); excellent prognosis.
entities.histo: Encapsulated papillary carcinoma is a cystic papillary neoplasm, usually in older women, presenting as a circumscribed mass that is often subareolar and may cause bloody discharge. Grossly it is a cystic lesion containing friable, haemorrhagic papillary tissue within a fibrous capsule. Microscopically, a thick fibrous capsule surrounds a cyst filled with delicate fibrovascular cores covered by monotonous, low- to intermediate-grade neoplastic epithelium arranged in solid, cribriform or stratified patterns. Myoepithelial cells are absent within the papillae and usually also at the periphery of the capsule. The tumour is ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative. Without invasion beyond the capsule it behaves as in situ disease, with an excellent prognosis, and it is staged pTis. When frank invasive carcinoma, usually IBC-NST, infiltrates beyond the capsule, only the invasive component is measured and staged. Entrapped epithelium in the capsule and biopsy-related displacement are pitfalls. Differentials include intraductal papilloma (myoepithelium-lined cores), papilloma with DCIS, solid papillary carcinoma and invasive papillary carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Encapsulated papillary carcinoma yields cellular, often haemorrhagic or cystic aspirates with papillary clusters with fibrovascular cores, numerous single intact columnar cells with low to intermediate grade, monotonous, elongated nuclei, haemosiderin-laden macrophages and absent or very few myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei. The cytology overlaps with intraductal papilloma, papillary DCIS and solid papillary carcinoma, and the distinction, as well as assessment of the capsule and invasion, requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 when atypia and cellularity are marked, papillary lesion, with excision recommended.
entities.ihc: Encapsulated papillary carcinoma is a cystic papillary lesion with a fibrous capsule. IHC typically shows no myoepithelial cells either along the fibrovascular cores or at the periphery (p63, SMMHC, calponin negative), though a minority keep partial peripheral myoepithelium. Despite this, WHO 5th edition stages pure EPC as in situ (Tis) when there's no frank invasion beyond the capsule. The cells are strongly ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, CK5/6 negative, and have a low Ki-67. Invasion beyond the capsule is staged on the size of the invasive component. High-grade or triple-negative EPC is staged as invasive. Separate it from papilloma (myoepithelium along cores).

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; invasive SPC — irregular, jigsaw/geographic nests infiltrating stroma; stage on invasive component; neuroendocrine & mucinous differentiation common.
entities.histo: Solid papillary carcinoma with invasion refers to invasive solid papillary carcinoma, in which the tumour nodules lose their rounded, smooth contours and infiltrate the stroma as irregular, jigsaw-like or geographic nests, or when there is an associated invasive carcinoma, usually mucinous or NST. The nests are composed of monotonous low- to intermediate-grade epithelial cells, often spindled, with delicate fibrovascular cores, and they frequently show neuroendocrine differentiation (synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 positive), with intracellular and extracellular mucin. The tumour is ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative, and the Ki-67 is low. Only the invasive component, defined by the irregular jigsaw nests or the conventional carcinoma, is measured and staged. Rounded nodules without peripheral myoepithelium are treated as in situ. The prognosis is generally favourable. Differentials include solid papillary carcinoma in situ, mucinous carcinoma type B (more abundant mucin), neuroendocrine tumour (90% or more NET morphology), florid UDH and solid DCIS, and encapsulated papillary carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Solid papillary carcinoma with invasion has cytology similar to solid papillary carcinoma in situ: cellular smears with numerous single and loosely cohesive monotonous cells with round to oval, eccentric plasmacytoid nuclei, salt-and-pepper chromatin, granular cytoplasm and delicate capillaries, often with mucin. Neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) are frequently positive on cell block. Invasion cannot be assessed cytologically. Differentials include neuroendocrine tumour, mucinous carcinoma and lobular carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with solid papillary and possible neuroendocrine features, or Category 4 when cells are bland.
entities.ihc: Invasive solid papillary carcinoma has irregular, jigsaw or geographic nests without myoepithelium (p63, SMMHC, calponin negative). It is strongly ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, and has a low Ki-67. Neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) are frequently positive, and mucin is common. The distinction from SPC in situ is architectural: smooth, rounded nodules even without myoepithelium are considered in situ.
