It must be distinguished from NET of the breast (90% or more neuroendocrine), invasive NST with neuroendocrine features, and TCCRP (ER−, CK5/6+, IDH2 R172 mutations, calretinin+). Report the invasive size.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; extremely rare; invasive carcinoma with >90% papillary architecture (fibrovascular cores) in the invasive component; exclude metastasis (lung, ovary, thyroid) and EPC/SPC.
entities.histo: Invasive papillary carcinoma is extremely rare and is restricted to invasive carcinomas in which more than 90% of the invasive component shows papillary architecture with true fibrovascular cores. The cores lack myoepithelial cells within the papillae and at the periphery, and the papillary structures infiltrate stroma beyond any capsule or duct. The nuclei are usually low to intermediate grade, and the tumour is mostly ER-positive. Many lesions previously called invasive papillary carcinoma are now classified as encapsulated papillary carcinoma, solid papillary carcinoma, invasive micropapillary carcinoma or papillary DCIS, so strict criteria apply. Most importantly, metastasis from papillary carcinomas of the lung, ovary (serous), thyroid and other sites must be excluded clinically and by IHC. GATA3, TRPS1 and ER support a breast origin, whereas TTF-1, PAX8, WT1 and thyroglobulin point to an extramammary primary. Differentials also include tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity, intraductal papilloma with entrapment, and IBC-NST with papillary areas, which constitutes a mixed carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Invasive papillary carcinoma is rare and yields cellular aspirates with papillary fragments with fibrovascular cores, three-dimensional clusters and many single intact columnar or polygonal atypical cells with moderate nuclear atypia, without myoepithelial cells or bare nuclei, in a haemorrhagic or cystic background. Cytology cannot distinguish it from papillary DCIS, encapsulated papillary carcinoma or benign papilloma with certainty, and metastatic papillary carcinoma from ovary, lung or thyroid must be excluded on clinical and immunochemical grounds. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), papillary carcinoma, depending on atypia.
entities.ihc: Invasive papillary carcinoma, defined as invasive carcinoma with more than 90% papillary architecture, is extremely rare, and most 'papillary' invasive tumours are invasive SPC, invasive EPC, or invasive micropapillary carcinoma. IHC confirms the absence of myoepithelial cells (p63, SMMHC, calponin negative) along the papillae and at the infiltrating periphery. It is usually ER+ and PR+ and HER2 negative. Metastatic papillary carcinoma from the ovary (PAX8+, WT1+), lung (TTF-1+, napsin A+) or thyroid (TTF-1+, thyroglobulin+, PAX8+) must be excluded with GATA3 and organ-specific markers. Micropapillary carcinoma is separated by its reverse polarity (EMA/MUC1 inside-out).

entities.remarks: WHO 5th rare/salivary gland-type; serous acinar differentiation with zymogen-like granules (lysozyme, α1-antichymotrypsin, EMA, S100); triple-negative; frequently associated with MGA; genomically TNBC-like (TP53).
entities.histo: Acinic cell carcinoma of the breast is a rare salivary-gland-type triple-negative carcinoma showing serous acinar differentiation. It presents as a mass in middle-aged women. Microscopically, tumour cells grow in solid, microglandular, microcystic and nested patterns. They have abundant, granular, amphophilic to eosinophilic cytoplasm with coarse, bright red zymogen-like granules, or clear or vacuolated cytoplasm, and round nuclei with nucleoli. The cells are positive for lysozyme, alpha-1-antichymotrypsin, EMA and S100, and sometimes for amylase. They are negative for ER, PR and HER2. The tumour is frequently associated with microglandular adenosis and is often considered part of the MGA-related neoplastic spectrum. Unlike its salivary counterpart, which has NR4A3 rearrangements, breast acinic cell carcinoma is genomically similar to triple-negative breast carcinoma, with TP53 mutations. Its behaviour is variable, and some tumours metastasise. Differentials include microglandular adenosis, secretory carcinoma (S100-positive, ETV6::NTRK3), granular cell tumour (keratin-negative), apocrine carcinoma (AR-positive) and IBC-NST.
entities.cyto: Acinic cell carcinoma of the breast is rare and yields cellular aspirates with acinar groups, sheets and single cells with abundant granular, vacuolated or clear cytoplasm (zymogen-type granules, PAS-diastase positive), round nuclei with mild to moderate atypia and small nucleoli, sometimes with many stripped nuclei. Myoepithelial cells are absent. Differentials include microglandular adenosis, lactational change, secretory carcinoma, granular cell tumour and apocrine carcinoma. Cell block immunochemistry shows lysozyme, DOG1 and S100 positivity, and the tumour is often ER and PR negative. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with acinic cell features.
entities.ihc: Acinic cell carcinoma of the breast shows serous acinar differentiation with zymogen-type granules. IHC is positive for lysozyme, α1-antichymotrypsin, amylase, DOG1, S100 and EMA, with variable SOX10. It is usually triple-negative (ER, PR, HER2 negative) and lacks myoepithelial cells. GCDFP-15 is often negative. The cytoplasmic granules are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. It overlaps with microglandular adenosis and MGA-associated carcinoma, which also stain with S100 and lack myoepithelium, and some regard these as a spectrum. TP53 mutations are frequent. Unlike the salivary type, NR4A3 rearrangements aren't characteristic. Secretory carcinoma (mammaglobin+, ETV6-NTRK3) is a differential.

entities.variants: Classic; solid-basaloid; adenoid cystic carcinoma with high-grade transformation
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; dual luminal (CK7, CD117) and myoepithelial/basaloid (p63, SMA, CK5/6) cells; true lumina and pseudolumina with basement membrane material; MYB::NFIB fusion t(6;9) or MYBL1 rearrangement; triple-negative but classic type has favourable prognosis.
entities.histo: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast is a rare salivary-gland-type triple-negative carcinoma that typically presents as a circumscribed subareolar mass in older women. Classic adenoid cystic carcinoma shows cribriform, tubular and trabecular patterns with two cell types. Luminal epithelial cells line true small lumina and are CK7-positive, CD117-positive and EMA-positive. Basaloid or myoepithelial cells surround pseudolumina filled with basophilic mucoid or eosinophilic basement membrane material, and are positive for p63, SMA, calponin and CK5/6. Perineural invasion is less frequent than in salivary tumours. The solid-basaloid variant consists of solid nests of basaloid cells with more atypia and mitoses and a worse prognosis, and high-grade transformation also occurs. MYB::NFIB fusion, t(6;9), or MYB or MYBL1 rearrangement is characteristic, with MYB IHC positivity. Despite the triple-negative phenotype, classic tumours have a favourable prognosis with rare nodal metastases. Differentials include invasive cribriform carcinoma (ER-positive, single cell type), cribriform DCIS, collagenous spherulosis and basal-like IBC-NST.
entities.cyto: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast yields cellular smears with cohesive clusters of small, uniform basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, arranged around or alongside acellular hyaline globules and cylinders that stain bright magenta on MGG and pale on Pap. Myoepithelial cells are part of the tumour. The main differentials are collagenous spherulosis (benign), pleomorphic adenoma, cribriform carcinoma and solid basaloid variants that mimic small cell carcinoma. Cell block shows a dual population (CD117 and CK7 luminal, p63 and SMA abluminal); MYB rearrangement may be detected. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant).
entities.ihc: Adenoid cystic carcinoma has a dual cell population. The luminal (ductal) cells are CK7+, CK8/18+, EMA+ and CD117 (c-kit) positive. The basaloid or myoepithelial cells are p63+, SMMHC+, calponin+, CK5/6+ and CK14+, and the pseudolumina contain basement membrane material (collagen IV and laminin positive). It is typically triple-negative, yet has a favourable prognosis in the classic form. MYB-NFIB fusion, MYB rearrangement or MYB overexpression (IHC) is the key molecular hint. The solid-basaloid variant is more aggressive. The differentials include cribriform carcinoma (ER+, no myoepithelial pseudolumina), collagenous spherulosis and cribriform DCIS.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; microcystic, solid and tubular architecture with eosinophilic/bubbly secretions; S100+, mammaglobin+, SOX10+; ETV6::NTRK3 fusion t(12;15) (pan-TRK IHC+); any age including children; indolent; NTRK inhibitors.
entities.histo: Secretory carcinoma is a rare carcinoma that occurs at any age, including in children and men. It presents as a slowly growing, circumscribed mass, often subareolar. Microscopically, the architecture is microcystic or honeycomb, solid and tubular, with abundant intracellular and extracellular eosinophilic to bubbly, PAS-positive and diastase-resistant secretions. The cells have pale, vacuolated or granular cytoplasm and uniform, low-grade round nuclei with small nucleoli. The tumour is S100-positive, mammaglobin-positive and SOX10-positive, typically triple-negative or weakly ER-positive, and has a low Ki-67. It is defined by the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion resulting from t(12;15), with pan-TRK IHC positivity, and NTRK inhibitor therapy is relevant for advanced disease. Its behaviour is indolent, with occasional nodal metastasis and late recurrence. Differentials include acinic cell carcinoma (zymogen granules, no fusion), pseudolactational or cystic hypersecretory lesions, apocrine carcinoma and IBC-NST with clear or vacuolated cells. Molecular testing (FISH or NGS) confirms the diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Secretory carcinoma yields cellular smears with clusters, acini and single cells with abundant, vacuolated, bubbly or clear cytoplasm, intracytoplasmic and extracellular secretions that are eosinophilic or magenta, and round, mild to moderately atypical nuclei with small nucleoli. Myoepithelial cells are absent. Differentials include lactational change, lactating adenoma, acinic cell carcinoma and lipid-rich or apocrine carcinoma. Cell block immunochemistry typically shows S100, mammaglobin and pan-TRK positivity; ETV6-NTRK3 fusion confirms the diagnosis and has therapeutic relevance. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with secretory features.
entities.ihc: Secretory carcinoma has microcystic, solid and tubular patterns with bubbly secretions. IHC shows S100 positivity, mammaglobin positivity, SOX10 positivity, and often CK5/6, EGFR and GATA3 positivity. ER, PR and HER2 are usually negative or weak, so it's 'triple-negative' with a favourable prognosis. Pan-TRK IHC shows nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity in most cases. The key molecular finding is ETV6-NTRK3 fusion from t(12;15), confirmed by FISH, RT-PCR or NGS, which predicts response to TRK inhibitors (larotrectinib, entrectinib). Myoepithelial markers are negative. It's separated from acinic cell carcinoma (lysozyme+, DOG1+), lactational change (myoepithelium retained), and other triple-negative carcinomas.

entities.variants: Low-grade; intermediate; high-grade
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; mucinous, intermediate and epidermoid cells; CRTC1::MAML2 fusion in subset (esp. low grade); typically triple-negative.
entities.histo: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the breast is a rare salivary-gland-type carcinoma composed of a mixture of mucinous (mucus-secreting), intermediate and epidermoid (squamoid) cells. The mucin-producing cells are mucicarmine-positive and PAS-positive, and the squamoid cells form solid nests without much keratinisation. Low-grade tumours have a cystic component, abundant mucinous cells, mild atypia and few mitoses. Intermediate- and high-grade tumours are more solid, with predominantly epidermoid and intermediate cells, marked atypia, necrosis and mitoses. A CRTC1::MAML2 fusion is found in a subset, especially low-grade cases, and supports the diagnosis. The tumour is typically triple-negative, but low-grade tumours have a good prognosis. Squamoid and intermediate cells are p63-positive and CK5/6-positive. Differentials include metaplastic carcinoma with squamous differentiation and mucinous areas (often high-grade, no fusion), adenosquamous carcinoma and hidradenoma (also CRTC1::MAML2-positive, but dermal and benign). Other differentials are mucinous carcinoma and metastatic mucoepidermoid carcinoma from salivary or lung primaries, which must be clinically excluded.
entities.cyto: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the breast is rare. Aspirates show a mixed population of epidermoid (squamoid) cells with dense cytoplasm, intermediate cells and mucin-secreting cells with vacuolated cytoplasm, in a background of extracellular mucin and sometimes cyst contents; keratinisation is usually absent. Low-grade tumours may have bland cells and be under-called, while high-grade tumours mimic squamous or metaplastic carcinoma. Mucicarmine or PAS-diastase stains identify mucin; MAML2 rearrangement supports the diagnosis. Differentials include metaplastic carcinoma, mucinous carcinoma and metastatic mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant).
entities.ihc: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma has epidermoid, intermediate and mucinous cells. The epidermoid and intermediate cells are p63 positive, p40 positive and CK5/6 positive. Mucinous cells are CK7 positive and mucicarmine and PAS-D positive. It is usually ER, PR and HER2 negative. MAML2 rearrangement, usually CRTC1-MAML2 and less often CRTC3-MAML2, is found in most low-grade breast cases and confirms the diagnosis. Myoepithelial markers other than p63 (SMMHC, calponin) are negative. The differentials are metaplastic carcinoma with squamous differentiation (no MAML2 fusion, often high grade) and low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma. Ki-67 rises with grade.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; extremely rare in breast; cytologically uniform cells in variable architecture (solid, cribriform, single files, targetoid); resembles salivary counterpart.
entities.histo: Polymorphous adenocarcinoma of the breast is an extremely rare salivary-gland-type carcinoma resembling its counterpart in minor salivary glands. Microscopically, cytologically uniform cells with round to oval, vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm grow in a striking variety of architectural patterns. These include solid nests, cribriform areas, tubules, trabeculae, single-file cords and targetoid (concentric) arrangements around ducts or nerves, often in a hyalinised or myxoid stroma. The infiltrative periphery may show single-file Indian-file growth that resembles invasive lobular carcinoma, but E-cadherin is retained. The cells are positive for keratins, S100 and BCL2, and usually negative or weakly positive for ER and PR. The p63 pattern is variable, without a true myoepithelial layer. PRKD1, PRKD2 or PRKD3 alterations have been reported in some cases. Because of its rarity, the behaviour is uncertain, and metastases have been reported. Differentials include adenoid cystic carcinoma (MYB fusion, dual cell type), ILC (E-cadherin loss), IBC-NST and metastatic salivary carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Polymorphous adenocarcinoma of the breast is extremely rare, and cytological descriptions are limited. Aspirates would be expected to show cellular smears with uniform, round to oval, bland cells with pale chromatin and small nucleoli in varied architectural patterns, including solid, cribriform, tubular and single-file arrangements, sometimes with hyaline or myxoid stromal material. The bland cytology may cause it to be under-called, and it overlaps with adenoid cystic carcinoma, lobular carcinoma and low-grade NST carcinoma. Definitive diagnosis requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 3 (Atypical), with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Polymorphous adenocarcinoma of the breast is extremely rare and resembles its salivary counterpart, with cytologically uniform cells in varied architectural patterns. IHC shows positivity for CK7, BCL2 and S100, variable positivity for p63 (often without p40 and SMMHC, so no true myoepithelial layer), and variable CD117. It is ER, PR and HER2 negative. PRKD1 hotspot mutation (E710D) is the key molecular hint in classic salivary cases, and PRKD1-3 rearrangements are reported in the cribriform type. It must be separated from adenoid cystic carcinoma (MYB-NFIB, biphasic CD117+ and p63+), invasive lobular carcinoma (E-cadherin−, ER+), and NST.

entities.entity: Tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity
entities.remarks: WHO 5th (formerly solid papillary carcinoma with reverse polarity / breast tumour resembling tall cell variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma); solid papillary nests of columnar cells with apical nuclei, nuclear grooves/inclusions; IDH2 R172 hotspot ± TET2; mostly ER−; TTF1/thyroglobulin negative; indolent.
entities.histo: Tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity is a rare low-grade tumour, previously called solid papillary carcinoma with reverse polarity or breast tumour resembling the tall cell variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Microscopically there are circumscribed solid and papillary nests with fibrovascular cores, composed of tall columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Their nuclei are located at the apical (luminal) pole rather than the base, which gives the reversed polarity, and show grooves, intranuclear pseudoinclusions and vesicular chromatin resembling papillary thyroid carcinoma. Colloid-like secretions and foamy histiocytes may be present. Myoepithelial cells are absent. The tumour is usually ER-negative or weakly positive, and HER2-negative. It is positive for CK7, calretinin and GATA3, and negative for TTF-1 and thyroglobulin. Recurrent IDH2 R172 hotspot mutations, often with TET2 or PIK3CA mutations, are characteristic, and IDH1/2 mutant-specific IHC can support the diagnosis. Its behaviour is indolent. Differentials include metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma, solid papillary carcinoma (ER-positive, neuroendocrine), encapsulated papillary carcinoma and secretory carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity is a rare low-grade tumour with very limited cytological descriptions. Aspirates may show papillary or solid clusters of tall columnar cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apically placed nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions, resembling papillary thyroid carcinoma (tall cell variant). Myoepithelial cells are absent. The thyroid-like nuclear features may lead to misdiagnosis of metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; thyroglobulin and TTF-1 negativity on cell block, together with IDH2 mutation, support a breast primary. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity (TCCRP) resembles the tall cell variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma. IHC shows CK7 positivity, CK5/6 positivity (often), calretinin positivity, and ER, PR and HER2 negative or only weakly positive. TTF-1 and thyroglobulin are negative, which excludes thyroid metastasis. GATA3 is variable. Myoepithelial markers are usually absent around the nests. The key molecular hint is IDH2 R172 hotspot mutation (often with PIK3CA mutation). IDH1/2 R132/R172 mutant-specific IHC can support the diagnosis. The differentials are SPC (ER+, neuroendocrine) and papillary or metastatic thyroid carcinoma.

entities.variants: Malignant transformation of epithelial, myoepithelial or both components (includes myoepithelial carcinoma / carcinoma arising in AME)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; carcinoma arising in AME; often ER-negative, HRAS Q61 mutations; may metastasise haematogenously (lung, bone).
entities.histo: Adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma, also called malignant adenomyoepithelioma, is a carcinoma arising in an adenomyoepithelioma. The malignant transformation may affect the epithelial component, the myoepithelial component (myoepithelial carcinoma) or both. Grossly the tumour is a mass, often with an infiltrative portion, necrosis or haemorrhage. Microscopically a residual benign or atypical biphasic AME is present, adjacent to areas of carcinoma that show nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses, necrosis and infiltrative growth, sometimes spindle cell or matrix-producing. The epithelial component may form IBC-NST or other carcinomas, and the myoepithelial component may form sheets of atypical myoepithelial cells positive for p63, calponin, SMA and CK5/6. These tumours are often ER-negative and frequently harbour HRAS Q61 hotspot mutations, often with PIK3CA or PIK3R1 alterations. They tend to metastasise haematogenously to the lung, bone and brain rather than to lymph nodes. Differentials include benign AME with atypia, spindle cell and matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma and epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma. Thorough sampling is essential.
entities.cyto: Adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma (malignant adenomyoepithelioma) shows a biphasic population of epithelial and myoepithelial cells, as in benign adenomyoepithelioma, together with cells showing frank malignant features: nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, mitoses and necrosis, affecting either or both components. Spindled or clear myoepithelial cells may dominate. Distinction from benign adenomyoepithelioma with atypia, metaplastic carcinoma and myoepithelial carcinoma is difficult on cytology. Cell block immunochemistry (p63, SMA, cytokeratin) highlights the biphasic population. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), with excision.
entities.ihc: Adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma (malignant adenomyoepithelioma) is a carcinoma arising in an adenomyoepithelioma, in the epithelial component, the myoepithelial component or both. IHC delineates the two populations: luminal cells are CK7+ and CK8/18+, and myoepithelial cells are p63+, SMMHC+, calponin+, CK5/6+, CK14+ and often S100 positive. The malignant component shows atypia, necrosis, infiltration and a high Ki-67. These tumours are often ER-negative, and HRAS Q61 mutations (frequently with PIK3CA or PIK3R1) are a key molecular finding associated with ER-negative and malignant AMEs. Separate from metaplastic carcinoma, which is triple-negative and lacks an organised biphasic background, and from epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; biphasic malignant tumour with inner luminal ductal cells and outer clear myoepithelial cells; resembles salivary EMC; HRAS mutations reported.
entities.histo: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma of the breast is a rare, biphasic malignant tumour resembling its salivary gland counterpart. Microscopically, duct-like structures are lined by an inner layer of luminal ductal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, which are CK7-positive and EMA-positive. These are surrounded by an outer layer, often multilayered, of clear myoepithelial cells, which are positive for p63, SMA, calponin and CK5/6, and the structures are encased by basement membrane. The tumour grows in nodules and sheets with infiltrative borders and may have papillary or cystic areas. Nuclear atypia is usually mild to moderate, but necrosis and mitoses increase in higher-grade lesions. The tumour overlaps with adenomyoepithelioma and malignant adenomyoepithelioma, and some authors consider it part of that spectrum. HRAS mutations have been reported, as in salivary EMC. ER and PR are usually negative. Differentials include adenomyoepithelioma (benign, circumscribed), adenoid cystic carcinoma (MYB fusion, cribriform pseudolumina), clear cell IBC-NST, metastatic renal cell carcinoma and myoepithelial carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma of the breast is very rare. Aspirates would be expected to show a biphasic population of small cohesive ductal epithelial cells and larger myoepithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, sometimes with hyaline basement membrane-like material, with mild to moderate nuclear atypia. Cytological features overlap with adenomyoepithelioma, adenoid cystic carcinoma and clear cell carcinomas. The diagnosis requires histology showing infiltrative bilayered tubules, and immunochemistry (CK7 luminal, p63 and SMA abluminal). Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), with excision.
entities.ihc: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma is biphasic, with inner luminal cells (CK7+, CK8/18+, EMA+) and outer clear myoepithelial cells (p63+, SMMHC+, calponin+, SMA+, CK5/6+, often S100+). It is usually ER, PR and HER2 negative. HRAS Q61 mutations have been described, linking it to the ER-negative adenomyoepithelioma and AME-with-carcinoma spectrum. The differentials are adenomyoepithelioma (lacks infiltrative growth and atypia), adenoid cystic carcinoma (CD117+, MYB-NFIB fusion), and clear-cell variants of other carcinomas. Ki-67 and atypia help assess malignancy. Metastatic salivary or renal clear-cell carcinoma (PAX8+) should be considered clinically.

entities.variants: NET grade 1; NET grade 2 (Nottingham grading)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; invasive tumour with ≥90% well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology and uniform strong synaptophysin/chromogranin/INSM1 expression; ER+ usually; exclude metastatic NET (lung, GI). Distinct from IBC-NST with NE differentiation and mucinous type B/SPC with NE features.
entities.histo: Neuroendocrine tumour (NET) of the breast is defined in WHO 5th edition as an invasive tumour in which 90% or more shows well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology. This consists of solid nests, trabeculae, rosettes or ribbons of uniform cells with granular cytoplasm and salt-and-pepper chromatin, separated by delicate vascular stroma. There is uniform, strong expression of neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1. Grading uses the Nottingham system, giving grade 1 or grade 2 NETs. Most tumours are ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative, and GATA3-positive, and an associated DCIS component supports a breast primary. NETs are distinct from IBC-NST with neuroendocrine differentiation (under 90%, focal or patchy markers), from mucinous carcinoma type B, and from solid papillary carcinoma with neuroendocrine features. Metastatic NET from the lung or gastrointestinal tract must be excluded, because ER and GATA3 negativity together with TTF-1 or CDX2 positivity and multiple lesions favour metastasis. Other differentials include lobular carcinoma (E-cadherin loss) and paraganglioma.
entities.cyto: Neuroendocrine tumour of the breast yields cellular smears of dyscohesive monotonous cells, singly and in loose clusters or rosette-like groups, with round to oval eccentric plasmacytoid nuclei, salt-and-pepper chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli and moderate granular cytoplasm, sometimes with mucin. Cell block shows synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 positivity, usually with ER positivity. The key differential is metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour from the gastrointestinal tract or lung, which may need clinical evaluation and markers such as CDX2 and TTF-1, and also solid papillary carcinoma and lobular carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma with neuroendocrine features.
entities.ihc: Neuroendocrine tumour (NET) of the breast requires neuroendocrine differentiation in 90% or more of the tumour. IHC is positive for synaptophysin and/or chromogranin, and INSM1 is very sensitive. These tumours are typically ER+ and PR+, HER2 negative, and GATA3 positive, which helps separate a breast primary from metastatic well-differentiated NET of the lung (TTF-1 variable), GI tract or pancreas (CDX2, ISL1, PAX6). Breast NET is graded with the Nottingham system, not Ki-67, though Ki-67 is reported. It must be separated from SPC and mucinous carcinoma type B, which often show neuroendocrine differentiation, and from invasive NST with neuroendocrine features. Report ER, PR and HER2.

entities.variants: Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; poorly differentiated, high-grade NE carcinoma; often ER−; exclude metastasis from lung; may have associated DCIS/NST component supporting breast primary.
entities.histo: Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) of the breast is a rare, poorly differentiated, high-grade carcinoma with neuroendocrine morphology and immunophenotype. Small cell NEC shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei with fine chromatin, nuclear moulding and crush artefact, frequent mitoses and necrosis. Large cell NEC shows large cells with moderate cytoplasm, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, a nested or trabecular architecture with peripheral palisading and rosettes, numerous mitoses and necrosis. The cells are positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1 and CD56, the Ki-67 is high and dot-like keratin staining is common. ER is often negative, although some tumours are ER-positive. Metastasis, particularly from small cell carcinoma of the lung, must be excluded by imaging. An associated DCIS or IBC-NST component, GATA3 positivity and ER positivity support a primary breast origin. TTF-1 can be expressed in primary breast small cell carcinoma and is not discriminatory. Differentials include lymphoma, Merkel cell carcinoma (CK20-positive), basal-like IBC-NST, ILC and melanoma. The prognosis is poor.
entities.cyto: Neuroendocrine carcinoma (small cell or large cell) of the breast yields cellular smears with dyscohesive single cells and loose clusters of small to intermediate (small cell) or large (large cell) cells with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear moulding, finely granular chromatin, crush artefact and necrosis, apoptosis and mitoses. Cell block confirms neuroendocrine marker expression. Metastatic small cell carcinoma from lung must be excluded clinically, and lymphoma, which lacks moulding and expresses CD45, is a differential. A coexisting DCIS component favours a breast primary on histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), neuroendocrine carcinoma.
entities.ihc: Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) of the breast (small cell and large cell types) is positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1 and CD56, with a high Ki-67 (often above 50%), dot-like keratin, and often aberrant p53 with Rb loss. It's frequently ER-negative or ER-low, though some are ER+, and HER2 negative. GATA3 is variable. The key differential is metastatic small cell carcinoma from the lung (TTF-1 positive in both, so TTF-1 can't be used) or elsewhere, and the presence of in-situ carcinoma or a GATA3-positive, ER-positive component favours a breast primary. Merkel cell carcinoma (CK20 paranuclear dot, MCPyV) and lymphoma (CD45) should be excluded.

entities.variants: With underlying DCIS; with underlying invasive carcinoma; without detectable underlying carcinoma (rare); anaplastic/pigmented variants (melanin-laden, mimic melanoma)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; intraepidermal large clear-cytoplasm adenocarcinoma cells in nipple epidermis; CK7+, HER2+ (often), GATA3+, CAM5.2+, ER variable; S100/SOX10/HMB45− and p63− (vs melanoma, Bowen/SCC in situ, Toker cells — Toker cells CK7+ but bland, HER2−).
entities.histo: Mammary Paget disease is an intraepidermal adenocarcinoma of the nipple and areola. It presents with eczematous erythema, scaling, crusting, erosion or ulceration, sometimes with discharge, and is usually unilateral. Microscopically, large tumour cells with abundant pale or clear cytoplasm, large pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli are distributed singly and in small clusters throughout the epidermis, especially along the basal layer. They may form gland-like spaces and contain intracytoplasmic mucin. Most cases are associated with underlying DCIS, which is often high grade and HER2-positive, with or without invasive carcinoma. A small number lack a detectable underlying carcinoma despite sampling of the lactiferous ducts. The pigmented variant contains melanin and mimics melanoma, and the anaplastic variant shows marked pleomorphism. The Paget cells are positive for CK7, CAM5.2, GATA3 and often HER2, with variable ER, and negative for S100, SOX10, HMB45 and p63. Differentials include melanoma in situ (SOX10 and Melan-A positive), Bowen disease (p63-positive, keratinocytic), Toker cells (bland, HER2-negative), clear keratinocytes and eczema.
entities.cyto: Mammary Paget disease is diagnosed cytologically by nipple scrape or touch imprint rather than FNA. Smears show large atypical Paget cells singly or in small groups among anucleate and nucleated squames, with abundant pale or vacuolated cytoplasm, large pleomorphic nuclei with prominent nucleoli and sometimes intracytoplasmic mucin or melanin pigment, in an inflammatory background. Differentials include melanoma in situ, Bowen disease (pagetoid squamous cell carcinoma in situ) and reactive keratinocytes in eczema. Immunochemistry (CK7, HER2, GATA3 positive; S100, HMB45 negative) helps. A negative scrape does not exclude Paget disease. Positive scrapes are reported as malignant (analogous to Category 5).
entities.ihc: Mammary Paget disease consists of large intraepidermal cells with clear cytoplasm. IHC is positive for CK7, CAM5.2, EMA, GATA3, often HER2 (3+ in most cases, reflecting an underlying HER2-positive DCIS) and often AR, with ER and PR often negative. It's separated from Bowen disease (p63+, p40+, CK5/6+, CK7 negative), pagetoid melanoma in situ (S100+, SOX10+, Melan-A+, HMB-45+, keratin negative) and Toker cells (bland, CK7+, HER2 negative). The underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma should be sought and is tested for ER, PR and HER2. Note that CK7 is also positive in Toker cells, so morphology matters.

entities.variants: With heterologous malignant elements (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, pleomorphic liposarcoma); with stromal overgrowth
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; all: marked stromal cellularity & atypia, ≥5 mitoses/mm² (≥10/10 HPF), stromal overgrowth, permeative border — OR presence of malignant heterologous elements (note: well-differentiated liposarcoma/ALT component alone is no longer sufficient for malignant designation); haematogenous metastasis (lung, bone) in up to ~25%; TERT promoter, TP53, EGFR, NF1 alterations.
entities.histo: Malignant phyllodes tumour is a fibroepithelial neoplasm in which the stromal component shows malignant features, usually in women around 45 to 55, presenting as a large, rapidly growing mass. Grossly it is fleshy and bulging, with haemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, it is defined by a combination of marked stromal hypercellularity and nuclear atypia, 5 or more mitoses per mm² (about 10 or more per 10 HPF), stromal overgrowth (a low-power field of stroma devoid of epithelium) and a permeative, infiltrative border. The presence of a malignant heterologous element alone is sufficient for the diagnosis. Such elements include osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and pleomorphic liposarcoma. In WHO 5th edition, a well-differentiated liposarcoma or atypical lipomatous tumour component alone no longer qualifies a tumour as malignant. Haematogenous metastases to the lung and bone occur in up to about a quarter of cases, while nodal spread is rare. Genetic alterations include TERT promoter, TP53, EGFR, NF1 and RB1 changes. Differentials include spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin and p63 positive), primary sarcoma (no epithelial component after thorough sampling) and borderline phyllodes tumour.
entities.cyto: Malignant phyllodes tumour aspirates are cellular and dominated by a stromal component of pleomorphic spindle and polygonal cells with marked nuclear atypia, mitoses and sometimes heterologous elements (liposarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous, osteosarcomatous), occasionally with necrosis. Epithelial elements may be scanty or absent, so the biphasic nature may not be appreciated. Differentials include metaplastic carcinoma (cytokeratin and p63 positive), primary sarcoma and borderline phyllodes tumour. The presence of benign epithelial sheets with malignant stroma suggests phyllodes tumour. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), malignant spindle cell neoplasm, or Category 4, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Malignant phyllodes tumour is defined morphologically (marked stromal atypia, 10 or more mitoses per 10 HPF, permeative borders, stromal overgrowth or malignant heterologous elements). No IHC marker is diagnostic. Supportive findings are a high stromal Ki-67, diffuse p53 positivity, loss of CD34, and increased stromal EGFR, CD117, CD10 and nuclear β-catenin. The key differential is metaplastic carcinoma, which needs a broad keratin panel and p63: diffuse positivity favours carcinoma, and focal keratin occurs in phyllodes. Molecular findings include MED12 and TERT promoter mutations, plus TP53, RB1, NF1, PIK3CA and EGFR alterations in malignant tumours. Heterologous elements stain like the corresponding sarcoma (MDM2-negative liposarcoma, myogenin+ rhabdomyosarcoma).

entities.variants: Cutaneous ± parenchymal; well, moderately, poorly differentiated; Epithelioid angiosarcoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; arises in skin/breast after radiotherapy for breast cancer (median ~5–7 years); high-level MYC amplification (MYC IHC diffuse nuclear) — distinguishes from atypical vascular lesion; poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Post-radiation angiosarcoma arises in the skin and sometimes the underlying breast parenchyma after radiotherapy for breast carcinoma, usually after a latency of about five to seven years or more. It presents as violaceous, bruise-like patches, plaques or nodules in the irradiated field, often multifocal. Microscopically, an infiltrative, dermal-based proliferation of anastomosing, irregular vascular channels dissects collagen and subcutaneous fat. The channels are lined by atypical, hyperchromatic, multilayered endothelial cells forming papillary tufts. They range from well-differentiated, sinusoidal vessels to poorly differentiated, solid sheets of epithelioid or spindle cells with blood lakes, necrosis and frequent mitoses. The cells are positive for CD31, ERG and CD34, and may express keratin in epithelioid forms. High-level MYC amplification, shown by diffuse nuclear MYC IHC or FISH, is characteristic. MYC amplification distinguishes this tumour from atypical vascular lesion, which is circumscribed, superficial and MYC-negative. Differentials also include recurrent carcinoma, which is keratin-positive and ERG-negative, haemangioma and Stewart-Treves syndrome. The prognosis is poor.
entities.cyto: Postradiation angiosarcoma usually arises in the skin of the irradiated breast and is often sampled by punch biopsy. Aspirates are typically bloody with variable cellularity, showing single and clustered atypical epithelioid or spindle endothelial cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, prominent nucleoli and occasional intracytoplasmic vacuoles containing red cells, sometimes forming vasoformative structures. Well-differentiated areas may be bland. Differentials include atypical vascular lesion, radiation atypia and recurrent carcinoma. Cell block shows CD31, ERG and CD34 positivity, and MYC amplification supports postradiation angiosarcoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant) or Category 3/4 when cells are scanty, with biopsy.
entities.ihc: Post-radiation angiosarcoma arises in the skin or breast after radiotherapy. IHC shows endothelial markers (CD31, ERG, FLI1, CD34 variable, D2-40 variable). Diffuse nuclear MYC staining reflects MYC amplification on 8q24, confirmed by FISH, and this separates it from an atypical vascular lesion (MYC negative) and from primary angiosarcoma (usually MYC-negative). FLT4 co-amplification occurs in some cases. Keratin can be focally positive in epithelioid angiosarcoma, a pitfall leading to a misdiagnosis of carcinoma, so ERG and CD31 should be included in any poorly differentiated tumour in a radiated breast. Ki-67 is high. Evaluate margins with ERG or CD31.

entities.variants: Low-grade (well-differentiated); intermediate; high-grade (poorly differentiated, solid/epithelioid, blood lakes, necrosis); Epithelioid angiosarcoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; young women (3rd–4th decade), parenchymal; anastomosing vascular channels dissecting lobules/fat, endothelial atypia; CD31/ERG/CD34+; MYC usually not amplified; grade correlates poorly with outcome in recent series.
entities.histo: Primary angiosarcoma of the breast parenchyma arises without prior radiotherapy, typically in young women in the third and fourth decades, and presents as a rapidly enlarging, painless deep mass, sometimes with blue skin discolouration. Grossly it is a spongy, haemorrhagic, ill-defined mass. Microscopically, anastomosing vascular channels lined by endothelial cells dissect around and into lobules, ducts and fat. Low-grade (well-differentiated) tumours have open, anastomosing channels with mild endothelial atypia and hyperchromasia that can mimic haemangioma. Intermediate tumours show more endothelial tufting and focal solid areas. High-grade (poorly differentiated) tumours show solid sheets of epithelioid or spindle cells, blood lakes, necrosis and many mitoses. The endothelial cells are positive for CD31, ERG and CD34, while MYC amplification is usually absent, unlike in post-radiation tumours. Recent series suggest that the histological grade correlates poorly with outcome, and the overall prognosis is guarded. Differentials include haemangioma, angiomatosis, PASH (CD31-negative, no red cells), angiolipoma and metaplastic carcinoma with pseudoangiomatous pattern.
entities.cyto: Primary angiosarcoma of the breast parenchyma, often in young women, yields bloody aspirates that may be deceptively hypocellular. High-grade tumours show atypical spindle or epithelioid cells singly and in clusters with pleomorphic nuclei and vasoformative fragments, while low-grade tumours may show only blood and a few bland endothelial cells, leading to false-negative results. Differentials include haemangioma, angiomatosis, PASH, metaplastic carcinoma and poorly differentiated carcinoma. Cell block immunochemistry (CD31, ERG, CD34) confirms endothelial origin. A bloody aspirate from a vascular-appearing mass should prompt core biopsy. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), or Category 3 or 4 if limited.
entities.ihc: Primary angiosarcoma of the breast parenchyma affects young women and dissects through lobules and fat. IHC shows CD31, ERG, FLI1 and CD34 positivity (variable in high grade), with D2-40 variable. Ki-67 is low in well-differentiated tumours but rises with grade, and the morphology determines grade. MYC is usually negative or not amplified, unlike post-radiation angiosarcoma. Keratin can be positive in epithelioid areas, so ERG is important. The key differentials are haemangioma and angiomatosis, separated by morphology (anastomosing channels, endothelial atypia, multilayering, infiltration of lobules), and PASH (CD34+, CD31 negative, ERG negative).

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; very rare; nipple-areolar or parenchymal; fascicles of atypical smooth muscle cells, mitoses, necrosis; exclude metaplastic carcinoma and malignant phyllodes with leiomyosarcomatous element.
entities.histo: Leiomyosarcoma of the breast is very rare, arising in the nipple-areolar region from dartos smooth muscle or in the parenchyma from vascular smooth muscle, usually in middle-aged to older women. It presents as a firm, slowly or rapidly growing mass. Grossly it is a well-circumscribed or infiltrative, grey-white, whorled tumour with necrosis or haemorrhage in larger lesions. Microscopically, intersecting fascicles of atypical spindle cells have eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm and blunt-ended, cigar-shaped, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei, with frequent mitoses including atypical forms and coagulative tumour necrosis. The cells are positive for SMA, desmin and h-caldesmon, and negative for keratins, p63 and S100. Before diagnosing primary leiomyosarcoma, spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma must be excluded with a broad keratin and p63 panel, because metaplastic carcinoma may express smooth muscle markers. Malignant phyllodes tumour with a leiomyosarcomatous element must also be excluded by thorough sampling for leaf-like epithelial structures. Other differentials are leiomyoma (no atypia or mitoses), myofibroblastoma, metastatic leiomyosarcoma and myoepithelial carcinoma. Haematogenous spread occurs.
entities.cyto: Leiomyosarcoma of the breast is rare and yields cellular aspirates with fascicles and single spindle cells with blunt-ended, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm, mitoses and sometimes necrosis or multinucleated tumour giant cells. Epithelial elements are absent. Differentials include malignant phyllodes tumour, spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, myoepithelial carcinoma and leiomyoma. Cell block shows SMA, desmin and h-caldesmon positivity with cytokeratin negativity. Diagnosis of primary breast leiomyosarcoma requires exclusion of malignant phyllodes and metastasis. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), malignant spindle cell neoplasm, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Leiomyosarcoma of the breast is very rare. It shows fascicles of atypical spindle cells that are SMA positive, desmin positive, h-caldesmon positive and SMMHC positive, often with aberrant p53 and a high Ki-67, and negative for keratins and p63. Primary sarcoma is a diagnosis of exclusion in the breast: spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma (broad keratins, p63, positive) and malignant phyllodes tumour with smooth muscle differentiation (adequate sampling for an epithelial component) must be excluded first. Myoepithelial carcinoma is also SMA positive and calponin positive but shows keratin (CK5/6, CK14) and p63 positivity. Metastatic uterine leiomyosarcoma (ER/PR often positive) should be excluded clinically.

entities.variants: Atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma (see Neoplastic-Others); myxoid liposarcoma; pleomorphic liposarcoma; dedifferentiated liposarcoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; primary breast liposarcoma rare — most liposarcomatous components arise in phyllodes tumour; myxoid liposarcoma in breast often actually phyllodes-associated (lacks DDIT3 rearrangement).
entities.histo: Primary liposarcoma of the breast is rare, and most liposarcomatous tissue in the breast arises as a heterologous component of a phyllodes tumour, so wide sampling for epithelial elements is essential. Atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma shows mature adipocytes of varying size with atypical, hyperchromatic stromal cells in fibrous septa and occasional lipoblasts, with MDM2 and CDK4 amplification. In a phyllodes tumour, this component alone no longer defines malignancy. Myxoid liposarcoma shows uniform round cells, a delicate plexiform capillary network and a myxoid stroma with lipoblasts. In the breast, apparent myxoid liposarcoma within phyllodes tumours often lacks the DDIT3 rearrangement and is better regarded as a phyllodes-associated liposarcomatous change. Pleomorphic liposarcoma shows highly pleomorphic multivacuolated lipoblasts in a high-grade sarcoma. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma shows non-lipogenic high-grade sarcoma adjacent to well-differentiated liposarcoma, and is MDM2-amplified. Differentials include lipoma, fat necrosis and silicone granuloma with pseudolipoblasts, and metaplastic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Primary liposarcoma of the breast is rare and must be distinguished from malignant phyllodes tumour with liposarcomatous differentiation, which is more common. Aspirates of well-differentiated liposarcoma may resemble mature fat with scattered atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells and occasional lipoblasts with indented nuclei by cytoplasmic vacuoles; myxoid liposarcoma shows myxoid matrix with arborising capillaries; pleomorphic liposarcoma shows bizarre pleomorphic cells and lipoblasts. MDM2 amplification supports well-differentiated or dedifferentiated liposarcoma. Differentials include lipoma, fat necrosis and silicone granuloma. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), or Category 3 or 4 for well-differentiated tumours.
entities.ihc: Primary breast liposarcoma is rare, and most liposarcomatous elements in the breast arise as heterologous components of malignant phyllodes tumour, which is MDM2-negative. Sampling for an epithelial or phyllodes component is therefore essential. Atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma, and dedifferentiated liposarcoma, show MDM2 and CDK4 amplification (FISH is the gold standard, and nuclear IHC is supportive). Myxoid liposarcoma has FUS-DDIT3 or EWSR1-DDIT3 fusion, and pleomorphic liposarcoma lacks MDM2 amplification. Lipoblasts may be S100 positive. Fat necrosis (CD68+) and lipoma (MDM2 negative) are the main benign mimics. Keratins exclude metaplastic carcinoma.

entities.variants: Primary extraskeletal osteosarcoma; chondrosarcoma; rhabdomyosarcoma (primary, adolescents); undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma; malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; fibrosarcoma; synovial sarcoma; malignant granular cell tumour; Kaposi sarcoma (breast skin); Mammary stromal sarcoma (historical term; most are now classified as malignant phyllodes or metaplastic carcinoma)
entities.remarks: Diagnosis of primary sarcoma requires exclusion of metaplastic carcinoma (extensive keratin/p63 panel) and malignant phyllodes (thorough sampling for epithelial component); classify per WHO Soft Tissue & Bone 5th ed.
entities.histo: Other primary sarcomas of the breast are rare and must be diagnosed only after excluding metaplastic carcinoma and malignant phyllodes tumour. This requires an extensive keratin panel, including AE1/AE3, HMW keratins, CK5/6 and 34betaE12, plus p63, and thorough sampling for epithelial elements. Primary extraskeletal osteosarcoma shows malignant cells producing lace-like osteoid, and chondrosarcoma shows atypical chondrocytes in a cartilaginous matrix. Rhabdomyosarcoma, which is mainly alveolar in adolescents and is often metastatic, shows desmin, myogenin and MyoD1 positivity. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma shows pleomorphic spindle and giant cells without a specific line of differentiation. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour shows fascicles of spindle cells with loss of H3K27me3 and patchy S100 positivity, often in NF1 patients. Fibrosarcoma shows a herringbone pattern, synovial sarcoma shows SS18::SSX fusion with SS18-SSX IHC positivity, and malignant granular cell tumour shows atypia and necrosis. Kaposi sarcoma occurs in the breast skin and is HHV8-positive. These tumours are classified according to WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours.
entities.cyto: Other primary sarcomas of the breast, such as undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, fibrosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma, are rare and yield cellular aspirates of malignant spindle, pleomorphic or round cells, sometimes with osteoid, chondroid matrix or necrosis. These features are non-specific, and a breast sarcoma is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out malignant phyllodes tumour (by sampling for epithelial elements) and metaplastic carcinoma (cytokeratin and p63 on cell block), as well as metastasis. Specific typing requires histology, immunochemistry and molecular studies. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), malignant spindle or pleomorphic neoplasm.
entities.ihc: Other primary sarcomas of the breast (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and others) are diagnoses of exclusion. First rule out metaplastic carcinoma with a broad panel of keratins (AE1/AE3, MNF116, 34βE12, CK5/6) and p63, then malignant phyllodes tumour by extensive sampling for an epithelial component. SATB2 supports osteoblastic differentiation, and S100 supports chondroid differentiation. Rhabdomyosarcoma is desmin positive, myogenin positive and MyoD1 positive, and in young women metastatic alveolar RMS (PAX3/7-FOXO1) should be considered. Molecular testing is used for specific sarcomas, for example SS18-SSX in synovial sarcoma. Metastatic sarcoma should be excluded clinically.

entities.entity: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
entities.variants: With plasmacytic differentiation; with amyloid
entities.remarks: WHO 5th breast; one of the commonest primary breast lymphomas; lymphoepithelial lesions; CD20+, CD5−, CD10−; indolent.
entities.histo: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) is one of the commonest primary breast lymphomas, often in older women and sometimes associated with autoimmune disease or lymphocytic mastopathy. It presents as a mass that may be bilateral. Microscopically, there is a diffuse or nodular infiltrate of small to medium-sized B cells, including centrocyte-like cells, monocytoid cells with pale cytoplasm and plasma cells, around and replacing reactive lymphoid follicles with follicular colonisation. Lymphoepithelial lesions are formed by neoplastic cells infiltrating and destroying ducts and lobular epithelium, which is highlighted by keratin. Variants include marked plasmacytic differentiation, with light-chain restriction on kappa and lambda ISH, and associated amyloid deposition, a cause of localised breast amyloid. The cells are positive for CD20 and BCL2, and negative for CD5, CD10, BCL6 (in the neoplastic cells) and cyclin D1. Clonality studies help in difficult cases. Differentials include reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (pseudolymphoma), lymphocytic mastopathy, follicular lymphoma, IgG4-related mastitis and ILC.
entities.cyto: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the breast yields cellular aspirates with a predominance of small to intermediate lymphoid cells, including centrocyte-like and monocytoid cells with moderate pale cytoplasm, plasmacytoid cells and plasma cells, with lymphoglandular bodies; lymphoepithelial lesions cannot be appreciated cytologically. The polymorphous appearance can mimic reactive lymphadenitis or lymphocytic mastitis. Flow cytometry demonstrating a monoclonal B-cell population (CD5 and CD10 negative) and cell block immunochemistry are crucial. Differentials include intramammary lymph node, lobular carcinoma and other small B-cell lymphomas. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or 5 (Malignant), lymphoma, with flow cytometry and core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of MALT type in the breast is a B-cell lymphoma: CD20 positive, PAX5 positive, CD79a positive, BCL2 positive, and CD5, CD10, BCL6, cyclin D1 and SOX11 negative, with CD43 positive in some. Kappa and lambda light-chain restriction (ISH, especially with plasmacytic differentiation) supports clonality. CD21 or CD23 shows colonised follicular dendritic cell meshworks. Keratin highlights lymphoepithelial lesions. Ki-67 is low. Separating it from lymphocytic mastopathy and IgG4-related mastitis requires clonality by light chains or IGH PCR. Amyloid deposition may be present. The differentials include SLL (CD5+, CD23+, LEF1+) and mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1+).

entities.variants: Grade 1–2; grade 3A (classic FL)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th breast; CD10+, BCL6+, BCL2+ (t(14;18) in most).
entities.histo: Follicular lymphoma of the breast is usually primary or part of systemic disease, presenting as a painless mass, often in older women. Microscopically, the breast parenchyma and fat are infiltrated by back-to-back, closely packed neoplastic follicles that lack polarisation and tingible-body macrophages, with attenuated or absent mantle zones and interfollicular spread. The follicles consist of centrocytes, which are small cleaved cells, and centroblasts, which are larger cells with vesicular chromatin and nucleoli. The grade is based on centroblast counts: grades 1 to 2 have up to 15 centroblasts per HPF, and grade 3A has more than 15 centroblasts per HPF with residual centrocytes. In WHO 5th edition haematolymphoid terminology, grades 1 to 3A are grouped as classic follicular lymphoma. Neoplastic follicles are positive for CD20, CD10, BCL6 and BCL2, the BCL2 positivity distinguishing them from reactive follicles, and most carry t(14;18) IGH::BCL2. CD21 or CD23 highlights expanded follicular dendritic cell meshworks. Differentials include reactive follicular hyperplasia (BCL2-negative germinal centres), MALT lymphoma with follicular colonisation, DLBCL (sheets of large cells) and mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1-positive).
entities.cyto: Follicular lymphoma involving breast yields cellular aspirates with a fairly monotonous population of small cleaved centrocytes with irregular, notched nuclei, admixed with variable numbers of large centroblasts, lymphoglandular bodies and occasional follicular dendritic cell clusters, but few tingible body macrophages. Low-grade cases closely mimic reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. Flow cytometry showing a monoclonal CD10-positive B-cell population and immunochemistry for BCL2 and BCL6 (and t(14;18) by FISH) support the diagnosis, while grading requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or 5 (Malignant), lymphoma, recommending core biopsy; secondary involvement should be excluded.
entities.ihc: Follicular lymphoma of the breast is positive for CD20, CD10 and BCL6, with neoplastic follicles that are BCL2 positive (from t(14;18)/IGH-BCL2), unlike reactive follicles (BCL2 negative). The follicles lack polarisation and tingible-body macrophages, and Ki-67 is low in grade 1–2. CD21 and CD23 outline the follicular dendritic cell meshworks. Some primary breast FLs are BCL2 negative or t(14;18) negative, so FISH may be needed alongside LMO2 and HGAL. The differentials include reactive intramammary lymph node and MALT lymphoma with follicular colonisation (CD10 and BCL6 negative). Grade 3B and DLBCL transformation (sheets of large cells) should be excluded.

entities.variants: Germinal centre B-cell (GCB) type; activated B-cell (non-GCB/ABC) type; high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC/BCL2 rearrangement (exclude)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th breast; commonest primary breast lymphoma; mostly ABC type (MYD88/CD79B); risk of CNS relapse; mimic of lobular/medullary-pattern carcinoma — keratin vs CD45/CD20.
entities.histo: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the commonest primary breast lymphoma. It typically presents as a rapidly growing, painless, often large mass in older women, sometimes bilateral. Microscopically, diffuse sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells, more than twice the size of normal lymphocytes, with vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli and frequent mitoses, efface the parenchyma. The infiltrate surrounds ducts and lobules and may infiltrate in single files that mimic lobular carcinoma, with necrosis and apoptotic bodies. The cells are positive for CD45 and CD20 (and PAX8 in rare cases), and negative for keratins. The Hans algorithm uses CD10, BCL6 and MUM1 to divide cases into germinal centre B-cell type and activated B-cell (non-GCB) type. Primary breast DLBCL is mostly ABC type, frequently with MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations, and carries a risk of CNS relapse. High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements should be excluded by FISH when indicated. Differentials include ILC and IBC-NST with a medullary pattern (keratin-positive), Burkitt lymphoma, myeloid sarcoma and melanoma.
entities.cyto: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common primary breast lymphoma and yields highly cellular aspirates of dyscohesive large lymphoid cells, two to three times the size of small lymphocytes, with vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli and scant basophilic cytoplasm, in a background of abundant lymphoglandular bodies and apoptotic debris. Pitfalls include poorly differentiated carcinoma, lobular carcinoma and melanoma; lymphoglandular bodies and true dyscohesion favour lymphoma. Cell block immunochemistry (CD45, CD20, PAX5; cytokeratin negative) and flow cytometry confirm the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), consistent with high-grade lymphoma, with core biopsy for subtyping.
entities.ihc: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the commonest primary breast lymphoma, is positive for CD20, PAX5 and CD79a, with a high Ki-67 (often above 60–80%). Cell of origin is assessed by the Hans algorithm: CD10, BCL6 and MUM1. Primary breast DLBCL is often non-germinal-centre (ABC) type with MYD88 and CD79B mutations, and carries a risk of CNS relapse. c-MYC (40% or more) and BCL2 (50% or more) identify double expressors, and MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 FISH exclude high-grade B-cell lymphoma. EBER excludes EBV-positive DLBCL. Keratin, ER and GATA3 negativity excludes poorly differentiated carcinoma, which is the key mimic in a core biopsy.

entities.variants: Endemic; sporadic; immunodeficiency-associated; pregnancy/lactation-associated bilateral massive involvement
entities.remarks: WHO 5th breast; starry-sky pattern, Ki-67 ~100%, MYC rearrangement; often bilateral in young women during pregnancy/lactation.
entities.histo: Burkitt lymphoma involving the breast typically occurs in young women, classically as a rapidly growing, bilateral, massive involvement during pregnancy or lactation, and endemic, sporadic and immunodeficiency-associated forms can all present here. Grossly the mass is soft, fleshy and fish-like, often with haemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, diffuse sheets of uniform, medium-sized lymphoid cells have round nuclei, multiple small nucleoli and a rim of basophilic cytoplasm containing lipid vacuoles visible on touch imprints. Tingible-body macrophages produce a classic starry-sky pattern, with numerous mitoses and apoptotic bodies. The cells are positive for CD20, CD10, BCL6 and MYC, and negative or only weakly positive for BCL2 and TdT. Ki-67 is close to 100%. MYC rearrangement, usually t(8;14), without BCL2 rearrangement is characteristic, and EBV may be positive in endemic and immunodeficiency cases. Differentials include DLBCL and high-grade B-cell lymphoma (more pleomorphic, BCL2-positive), lymphoblastic lymphoma (TdT-positive), myeloid sarcoma and small round cell tumours. The disease is treated urgently with intensive chemotherapy.
entities.cyto: Burkitt lymphoma of the breast, which may present bilaterally in pregnancy or lactation, yields highly cellular aspirates of monotonous, medium-sized lymphoid cells with round nuclei, finely granular chromatin, multiple small nucleoli and deeply basophilic cytoplasm with distinct lipid vacuoles (best on MGG), in a background of numerous tingible body macrophages, apoptotic bodies, mitoses and lymphoglandular bodies (starry-sky). Differentials include DLBCL, lymphoblastic lymphoma and other round cell tumours. Flow cytometry, cell block (CD10, BCL6, Ki-67 near 100%, BCL2 negative) and MYC rearrangement confirm the diagnosis. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), high-grade lymphoma.
entities.ihc: Burkitt lymphoma in the breast, often bilateral and associated with pregnancy, lactation or HIV, shows a starry-sky pattern with Ki-67 close to 100%. It is positive for CD20, CD10, BCL6 and MYC, and BCL2 negative or weak, with TdT negative, which separates it from lymphoblastic lymphoma. The defining event is MYC rearrangement (t(8;14), and less often t(2;8) or t(8;22)) without BCL2 rearrangement, confirmed by FISH. EBER is positive in endemic and some immunodeficiency-associated cases. The differentials are DLBCL and high-grade B-cell lymphoma (MYC and BCL2 double-hit), and poorly differentiated carcinoma (keratin).

entities.entity: Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)
entities.variants: In-situ (effusion/seroma-confined, capsule-lining) type; infiltrative (mass-forming) type
entities.remarks: WHO 5th breast; T-cell lymphoma associated with textured implants; delayed seroma (~8–10 years post-implant); large pleomorphic CD30+ (strong uniform), ALK− cells in effusion/capsule; JAK/STAT3 activation; complete en bloc capsulectomy curative for confined disease. Send effusion fluid for cytology & CD30 IHC/flow.
entities.histo: Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) is a T-cell lymphoma associated with textured breast implants. It typically presents as a delayed, unilateral, peri-implant seroma about 8 to 10 years after implantation, and less often as a capsular mass. The in situ type, confined to the effusion or capsule lining, shows large, pleomorphic, anaplastic cells with horseshoe or kidney-shaped hallmark nuclei and abundant cytoplasm. These cells are found in the seroma fluid and lie along the luminal surface of the capsule within fibrin, without invasion. The infiltrative (mass-forming) type shows sheets of these cells invading the capsule and adjacent tissue, often with eosinophils, and carries a worse prognosis. The cells show strong, uniform CD30 positivity and are ALK-negative. Variable CD4, CD43, CD2, cytotoxic markers and EMA positivity, loss of CD3 and other T-cell markers, and JAK/STAT3 activation are seen. Effusion fluid should be sent for cytology, cell block CD30 IHC and flow cytometry. Complete en bloc capsulectomy with implant removal is usually curative for confined disease. Differentials include reactive seroma with scattered CD30-positive activated lymphocytes, systemic ALCL and DLBCL.
entities.cyto: Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma usually presents as a late seroma around a textured implant, and cytology of the effusion is key to diagnosis. Smears and cell block show large pleomorphic cells with abundant cytoplasm, horseshoe or kidney-shaped hallmark nuclei, prominent nucleoli and occasional multinucleated or wreath-like forms, in a background of reactive lymphocytes and histiocytes. Immunochemistry shows strong uniform CD30 positivity with ALK negativity, and flow cytometry or T-cell receptor clonality studies support it. Reactive CD30-positive cells in benign seromas are scattered and heterogeneous. Reported as malignant (analogous to Yokohama Category 5), with capsulectomy staging.
entities.ihc: Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) is a T-cell lymphoma associated with textured implants. IHC shows strong, uniform membrane and Golgi CD30 staining in large pleomorphic cells, ALK negativity, and variable loss of T-cell antigens, with CD3, CD5 and CD7 often lost, CD4 often positive and CD43 positive. Cytotoxic markers (TIA-1, granzyme B, perforin) are positive, and so are EMA, MUM1 and pSTAT3. Clonal TCR rearrangement and JAK/STAT3 mutations support the diagnosis. The workup should include effusion cytology with a cell block for CD30, the capsule and any mass. Scattered reactive CD30+ cells are common, so morphology and uniformity matter.

entities.variants: Extramedullary plasmacytoma; myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma); lymphoblastic lymphoma; classic Hodgkin lymphoma (rare, usually secondary); peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS; secondary involvement by systemic lymphoma/CLL/leukaemia
entities.remarks: Rare; classify per WHO Haematolymphoid Tumours 5th ed; myeloid sarcoma: MPO/CD117/CD34/lysozyme.
entities.histo: Other haematolymphoid neoplasms of the breast are rare and should be classified according to WHO Haematolymphoid Tumours, 5th edition. Extramedullary plasmacytoma shows sheets of monoclonal plasma cells, CD138-positive with light-chain restriction, and must be distinguished from myeloma involvement and MALT lymphoma. Myeloid sarcoma presents as a mass of immature myeloid blasts, sometimes before or at relapse of leukaemia. It can mimic lymphoma or ILC in single files, and is positive for MPO, CD117, CD34, CD33 and lysozyme. Lymphoblastic lymphoma shows sheets of medium-sized blasts with fine chromatin, positive for TdT and CD34 with B or T lineage markers, usually in young patients. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is rare and usually secondary, with Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells (CD30-positive, CD15-positive, PAX5 weak) in a mixed inflammatory background. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS shows atypical T cells with loss of pan-T antigens. Secondary involvement by systemic lymphoma, CLL or leukaemia is more common than primary disease. A keratin and CD45 screen avoids misdiagnosis as carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Other haematolymphoid neoplasms of breast, including myeloid sarcoma, plasmacytoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and T-cell lymphomas, are rare. Aspirates show discohesive neoplastic cells according to type, such as immature myeloid blasts with granules (myeloid sarcoma), sheets of plasma cells (plasmacytoma) or Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background (Hodgkin lymphoma). Myeloid sarcoma is easily mistaken for lobular carcinoma or DLBCL. Flow cytometry and cell block immunochemistry (MPO, CD117, CD138, CD30, CD15) are crucial. Reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or 5 (Malignant), haematolymphoid neoplasm, with biopsy for classification.
entities.ihc: Other rare haematolymphoid neoplasms of the breast are classified per the WHO haematolymphoid volume, using entity-specific panels. Extramedullary plasmacytoma is CD138 positive, CD38 positive and MUM1 positive, with light-chain restriction, and is CD20 negative and cyclin D1 positive in some. Systemic myeloma should be excluded. Myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma) is MPO positive, CD117 positive, CD34 positive, lysozyme positive and CD68 positive (KP1/PG-M1), and is often mistaken for lobular carcinoma or lymphoma, so MPO and CD43 should be included in any keratin-negative round-cell infiltrate. Lymphoblastic lymphoma is TdT positive. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma and CLL/SLL are worked up as at other sites.

entities.entity: Carcinoma of the male breast (in situ and invasive)
entities.variants: DCIS (usually papillary/cribriform, low–intermediate grade); invasive carcinoma (mostly IBC-NST, also papillary/encapsulated papillary, lobular rare)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th tumours of the male breast; <1% of breast cancers; mostly ER+/PR+/AR+, luminal; BRCA2 germline association (also CHEK2, PALB2), Klinefelter syndrome, estrogen excess; nipple involvement and Paget disease common due to small breast volume.
entities.histo: Carcinoma of the male breast accounts for less than 1% of all breast cancers. It presents as a firm, eccentric subareolar mass, often with nipple involvement, ulceration or Paget disease, because the male breast is small. Risk factors include BRCA2 (and less often CHEK2 and PALB2) germline mutations, Klinefelter syndrome and conditions with oestrogen excess. DCIS is usually papillary or cribriform and of low to intermediate grade. Invasive carcinoma is mostly IBC-NST, with papillary and encapsulated papillary carcinoma relatively more frequent than in women, and lobular carcinoma rare because lobules are sparse. Tumours are graded with the Nottingham system and staged as in women, and are usually ER-positive, PR-positive and AR-positive, luminal-type and HER2-negative. Early skin and pectoral involvement is common. Differentials include gynaecomastia with florid gynaecomastoid hyperplasia (no atypia, heterogeneous CK5/6), metastatic carcinoma (especially prostate, which is NKX3.1-positive and PSA-positive, while breast carcinoma is GATA3-positive and TRPS1-positive), adnexal skin tumours and lymphoma. Germline genetic testing is recommended for all affected men.
entities.cyto: Male breast carcinoma is most often invasive carcinoma NST with ER positivity. Aspirates are cellular with dyscohesive groups and single intact atypical epithelial cells, nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli and absence of myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei; papillary carcinoma and DCIS also occur. Gynaecomastia is the main differential, and florid gynaecomastia with nuclear atypia can be misleading, whereas the presence of bare nuclei and cohesive sheets favours gynaecomastia. Metastatic carcinoma, especially from prostate, and lymphoma should be considered. In situ and invasive carcinoma cannot be separated on FNA. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, or Category 4 when limited.
entities.ihc: Carcinoma of the male breast is almost always ER-positive (over 90%) and PR-positive, usually HER2 negative, and AR positive. Most are luminal, NST or papillary types, with lobular carcinoma rare. ER, PR and HER2 testing per ASCO/CAP, and Ki-67, are reported as for female breast cancer. GATA3 positivity helps separate it from metastases and from cutaneous adnexal tumours. DCIS in men is usually papillary or cribriform and is assessed with myoepithelial markers. Gynaecomastoid hyperplasia (heterogeneous CK5/6) and gynaecomastia are the main benign mimics. Germline BRCA2 testing should be offered to all men with breast cancer. PALB2 and CHEK2 are also relevant.

entities.entity: Malignant cutaneous tumours of breast skin
entities.variants: Basal cell carcinoma (nipple-areola); squamous cell carcinoma of skin; melanoma of breast skin; extramammary-type adnexal carcinomas; Merkel cell carcinoma
entities.remarks: Primary skin malignancies; classify per WHO Skin Tumours; BCC of nipple may mimic Paget disease.
entities.histo: Malignant cutaneous tumours of the breast skin are primary skin cancers rather than mammary carcinomas, and should be classified according to WHO Skin Tumours. Basal cell carcinoma, rare on the nipple and areola, shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, stromal retraction clefts and a mucinous stroma. It is positive for BerEP4 and negative for EMA, and may clinically mimic Paget disease. Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, including Bowen disease, shows atypical keratinocytes and must be distinguished from metaplastic squamous carcinoma of the breast by its epidermal origin and the absence of a deep parenchymal tumour. Melanoma of the breast skin shows atypical melanocytes that are SOX10-positive, Melan-A-positive and HMB45-positive. Melanoma in situ must be separated from pigmented Paget disease, which is CK7-positive. Extramammary-type adnexal carcinomas, such as porocarcinoma and microcystic adnexal carcinoma, and Merkel cell carcinoma (CK20 perinuclear dot, neuroendocrine markers, MCPyV) are rare. The main differentials are cutaneous metastasis or direct skin involvement by breast carcinoma (GATA3-positive and TRPS1-positive) and mammary Paget disease.
entities.cyto: Malignant cutaneous tumours of breast skin, such as basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, may be aspirated or scraped. Basal cell carcinoma shows cohesive basaloid clusters with peripheral palisading; squamous cell carcinoma shows atypical keratinising cells; melanoma shows dyscohesive cells with prominent nucleoli, intranuclear inclusions and pigment; DFSP shows storiform bland spindle cells (CD34 positive). The main challenge is to distinguish skin tumours from breast carcinoma infiltrating the skin and Paget disease; clinical appearance and immunochemistry help. Reported descriptively, as malignant (Yokohama Category 5) where appropriate.
entities.ihc: Malignant cutaneous tumours of the breast skin are classified per the WHO skin volume, and IHC helps separate them from mammary carcinoma and Paget disease. Basal cell carcinoma of the nipple-areola is BerEP4 positive, BCL2 positive and EMA negative. Squamous cell carcinoma is p63, p40 and CK5/6 positive, and CK7 and GATA3 negative. Melanoma is S100, SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 positive, and keratin negative. Merkel cell carcinoma shows paranuclear dot CK20, is synaptophysin positive and INSM1 positive, and is MCPyV (CM2B4) positive. Extramammary-type Paget disease and dermal invasion of breast carcinoma are GATA3, CK7 and often HER2 positive. Post-radiation angiosarcoma (ERG, CD31, MYC) should also be considered.

entities.remarks: Not separately classified by WHO 5th; infiltrative malignant tumour of purely myoepithelial phenotype, often spindle cell; overlaps with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma; triple-negative.
entities.histo: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) is a rare malignant tumour of purely myoepithelial phenotype. WHO 5th edition does not classify it separately, considering it within the spectrum of metaplastic carcinoma and adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma. It presents as an enlarging mass, usually in older women. Microscopically, the tumour is infiltrative and consists predominantly of atypical spindle cells in fascicles, sometimes with epithelioid or clear cells, and often with myxoid or collagenous stroma. Nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and necrosis are present. The cells are positive for p63, SMA, calponin, SMMHC, CK5/6, S100 and often keratin, and are triple-negative for ER, PR and HER2. The tumour overlaps with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, which is also p63-positive and keratin-positive, and many pathologists group the two together. A residual adenomyoepithelioma component supports carcinoma arising in AME. Differentials include myoepithelioma, malignant phyllodes tumour, leiomyosarcoma, fibromatosis and other sarcomas. Haematogenous metastases occur, and treatment follows that of metaplastic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) yields cellular aspirates of atypical spindle, epithelioid or clear cells, singly and in fascicles or loose clusters, with nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, mitoses and sometimes necrosis or myxoid matrix, without a luminal epithelial component. The cytology overlaps substantially with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, malignant phyllodes tumour, sarcomas and malignant adenomyoepithelioma. Cell block immunochemistry shows myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin, S100) with high-molecular-weight cytokeratin, and the tumour is usually triple negative. Exact classification requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), malignant spindle cell neoplasm, or Category 4 when limited.
entities.ihc: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) is an infiltrative, triple-negative malignant tumour with a purely myoepithelial phenotype. IHC shows p63 positivity, CK5/6 and CK14 positivity, positivity for broad keratins (AE1/AE3, 34βE12), variable SMA, calponin and SMMHC, and often S100 positivity. EGFR is often positive and Ki-67 is high. ER, PR and HER2 are negative. Its phenotype overlaps almost completely with spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma, and many authors classify it as such. The distinction from benign myoepithelioma rests on atypia, necrosis, mitoses and infiltration. Malignant phyllodes tumour (adequate sampling for leaf-like architecture, CD34+ stroma) and sarcomas (keratin-negative, p63-negative) are excluded with the keratin and p63 panel. PD-L1 testing applies as for TNBC.

entities.remarks: Not separately classified by WHO 5th; very rare invasive carcinoma (often poorly differentiated, solid) arising from cystic hypersecretory DCIS; thyroid colloid-like secretions in the cysts.
entities.histo: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is a very rare invasive carcinoma arising from cystic hypersecretory DCIS. WHO 5th edition does not classify it separately.
