The in situ component shows cysts filled with dense, eosinophilic, colloid-like secretion resembling thyroid follicles, lined by micropapillary or stratified atypical epithelium. The invasive component is often poorly differentiated, with solid sheets or nests of high-grade tumour cells. It may lack the cystic hypersecretory features of the in situ component, so its origin is recognised from the associated DCIS. Receptor status is variable, with many tumours ER-negative or HER2-variable. The secretions are PAS-positive and thyroglobulin-negative, and the tumour cells are GATA3-positive and TTF-1-negative, which helps exclude metastatic thyroid carcinoma. Differentials include cystic hypersecretory DCIS without invasion, cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia, metastatic thyroid carcinoma, secretory carcinoma (ETV6::NTRK3) and IBC-NST. Thorough sampling of cystic hypersecretory lesions is advised to detect invasion, and the invasive component is graded, measured and staged as for IBC-NST.
entities.cyto: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is very rare and arises from cystic hypersecretory DCIS. Aspirates show abundant dense, homogeneous colloid-like secretion with cracking artefact, foamy macrophages, and malignant epithelial cells, often poorly differentiated in solid groups and singly, with nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli, sometimes alongside micropapillary groups from the in situ component. The colloid-like material may suggest metastatic thyroid carcinoma or mucinous lesions; thyroglobulin and TTF-1 negativity on cell block helps. Invasion cannot be assessed cytologically. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, or Category 4 when cells are scanty or less atypical.
entities.ihc: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is a very rare, often poorly differentiated, solid invasive carcinoma that arises from cystic hypersecretory DCIS with thyroid colloid-like secretions. IHC confirms invasion by the absence of myoepithelial cells (p63, SMMHC, calponin) around the solid nests, while the background in-situ cysts keep their myoepithelium. Breast origin is supported by CK7 positivity and GATA3 positivity, and negativity for TTF-1, PAX8 and thyroglobulin excludes metastatic thyroid carcinoma, which is the key differential given the colloid-like material. The invasive component is frequently ER-negative or ER-low and high grade with a high Ki-67, so ER, PR and HER2 per ASCO/CAP should be reported. Because the data are limited, the profile is described from case reports.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; intermediate features: well-defined to focally permeative border, moderate stromal cellularity/atypia, 2.5 to <5 mitoses/mm² (5–9/10 HPF), focal or absent stromal overgrowth; may recur, rarely metastasise. Not all criteria need to be present.
entities.histo: Borderline phyllodes tumour is a fibroepithelial neoplasm with features intermediate between benign and malignant phyllodes tumour, and not all criteria need to be present. It presents as an enlarging mass, often larger than a fibroadenoma. Microscopically, there is leaf-like architecture with periductal stromal condensation and moderate stromal hypercellularity with moderate nuclear atypia. Mitoses number 2.5 to fewer than 5 per mm², about 5 to 9 per 10 HPF. The border is well defined to focally permeative, and stromal overgrowth is focal or absent, with no malignant heterologous elements. Borderline tumours have a higher risk of local recurrence than benign phyllodes tumours, especially with positive margins, but metastasis is rare. Grading should be based on the most cellular and atypical areas, so generous sampling is required. Classification on core biopsy is often provisional. Differentials include benign phyllodes tumour, malignant phyllodes tumour (marked atypia, 5 or more mitoses per mm², overgrowth, permeative border), cellular fibroadenoma, and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, which is keratin-positive and p63-positive. Excision with clear margins is recommended.
entities.cyto: Borderline phyllodes tumour aspirates show a fibroepithelial pattern with epithelial sheets, myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, together with hypercellular stromal fragments and numerous single stromal spindle cells showing moderate nuclear atypia and occasional mitoses. Distinction from benign or malignant phyllodes tumour and from cellular fibroadenoma is not possible on cytology, as grading depends on histological criteria including stromal overgrowth, borders and mitotic count. Stromal-predominant smears with atypia should raise concern. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), fibroepithelial lesion with cellular stroma, recommending excision.
entities.ihc: Borderline phyllodes tumour is defined by intermediate morphological features: moderate stromal cellularity and atypia, 5–9 mitoses per 10 HPF, focally permeative borders and no stromal overgrowth. IHC doesn't determine grade. Stromal Ki-67 is intermediate, p53 is patchy, and CD34 may be partly lost, but these markers only support the grade. Broad-spectrum keratins and p63 are needed in any atypical spindle-cell tumour to exclude metaplastic carcinoma, and focal keratin can occur in phyllodes. MED12 and TERT promoter mutations are common. Additional TP53, RB1, NF1 or EGFR alterations suggest progression to malignant phyllodes. Margin status is key for management.

entities.remarks: Regarded as a variant/form of phyllodes tumour (WHO 5th): non-circumscribed stromal proliferation around open tubules lacking leaf-like pattern; grade as phyllodes.
entities.histo: Periductal stromal tumour is a rare biphasic lesion now regarded as a form of phyllodes tumour and graded in the same way. It usually presents as a mass in perimenopausal women. Microscopically, it is a non-circumscribed, infiltrative proliferation of spindle stromal cells that condenses around open, non-compressed ducts and tubules with a two-cell layer, forming cuffs of hypercellular stroma, and the stroma infiltrates the surrounding fat. Unlike a classic phyllodes tumour, the leaf-like intracanalicular pattern with elongated clefts and broad fronds is absent. The stromal cells show variable atypia and mitotic activity, and some lesions contain heterologous elements. Stromal cells are CD34-positive and may be CD117-positive, and are negative for keratins and p63. Because some cases progress to typical phyllodes tumour or recur, the lesion should be graded using phyllodes criteria and excised with clear margins. Differentials include benign phyllodes tumour, fibroadenoma, PASH, juvenile hypertrophy, and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin-positive).
entities.cyto: Periductal stromal tumour is a rare biphasic tumour with stromal proliferation around open ducts, regarded as part of the phyllodes spectrum. There are no specific cytological criteria. Aspirates would show bland ductal epithelial groups with myoepithelial cells and a population of spindle stromal cells with mild to moderate atypia and mitoses, overlapping with phyllodes tumour, fibroadenoma and spindle cell lesions. Definitive diagnosis requires histology showing periductal cuffing without leaf-like architecture. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), spindle cell or fibroepithelial lesion, with excision.
entities.ihc: Periductal stromal tumour is regarded as a form of phyllodes tumour in WHO 5th edition. It's a stromal proliferation around ducts without leaf-like architecture. The stromal cells are CD34 positive and often CD117 positive and BCL2 positive, with a variable Ki-67, and negative for keratins and p63, which excludes metaplastic carcinoma. Myoepithelial markers show the benign epithelial component. Grading follows phyllodes criteria for atypia and mitoses. Morphology, not IHC, separates it from PASH (CD34+, PR+, slit-like spaces) and myofibroblastoma (desmin+, RB1 loss). Molecular studies show MED12 and TERT alterations similar to phyllodes.

entities.variants: Lymphatic type; vascular (blood-vessel) type
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; post-radiation cutaneous vascular proliferation (circumscribed, superficial dermis, no multilayering/significant atypia); MYC not amplified; small risk of progression to angiosarcoma — complete excision & follow-up.
entities.histo: Atypical vascular lesion (AVL) arises in the skin of the breast after radiotherapy, usually several years after breast-conserving treatment. It presents as small, often multiple, flesh-coloured to erythematous papules or vesicles under 1 cm within the radiation field. Microscopically, it is a circumscribed, superficial, dermal proliferation of thin-walled, dilated, sometimes anastomosing vessels. The vessels are lined by a single layer of bland or slightly hyperchromatic endothelial cells, sometimes hobnail, without multilayering, significant atypia or mitoses, and they do not involve subcutaneous fat. The lymphatic type, the commonest, shows irregular dilated lymphatic channels that are D2-40-positive, often with stromal lymphocytes. The vascular (blood vessel) type shows capillary-sized vessels with red cells and pericytes. MYC is not amplified, and MYC IHC is negative, which is the key distinction from post-radiation angiosarcoma. Angiosarcoma shows infiltration of the deep dermis and fat, endothelial multilayering and atypia, and MYC amplification. AVL carries a small risk of progression to angiosarcoma, so complete excision and clinical follow-up are recommended. Differentials also include haemangioma, lymphangioma and recurrent carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Atypical vascular lesion arises in irradiated breast skin and is diagnosed by punch biopsy rather than FNA. Scrapes or aspirates, if obtained, show blood and a few bland or mildly atypical endothelial cells, without the cellularity or pleomorphism of angiosarcoma. Cytology cannot reliably distinguish AVL from well-differentiated postradiation angiosarcoma, for which MYC amplification on histology helps. The lesion is important as a possible precursor or mimic of angiosarcoma. A cytological specimen would be reported as non-diagnostic or Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: Atypical vascular lesion (AVL) is a post-radiation cutaneous vascular proliferation, of lymphatic or blood-vessel type. IHC shows endothelial markers: CD31 and ERG positive, D2-40 and PROX1 positive in the lymphatic type, and CD34 variable. The key test is MYC: AVL is MYC negative by IHC and lacks MYC amplification by FISH, whereas post-radiation angiosarcoma shows diffuse nuclear MYC staining and amplification. Ki-67 is low in AVL. Because sampling may be limited and AVL can coexist with or precede angiosarcoma, complete excision and MYC testing are recommended. FLT4 co-amplification is seen only in angiosarcoma.

entities.variants: Sporadic; post-surgical/post-implant; FAP (Gardner) associated
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; locally aggressive, non-metastasising; infiltrative long sweeping fascicles of bland myofibroblasts entrapping ducts/lobules; nuclear β-catenin (CTNNB1 or APC mutation); keratin negative (vs fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma).
entities.histo: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast is a locally aggressive, non-metastasising myofibroblastic neoplasm that arises from the pectoral fascia or within the breast parenchyma. It may be sporadic, follow surgery or implant placement, or occur in familial adenomatous polyposis (Gardner syndrome), and it presents as a firm, irregular mass that mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging. Grossly it is a firm, grey-white, trabeculated lesion with poorly defined, infiltrative margins. Microscopically, long, sweeping fascicles of bland, uniform spindle myofibroblasts with pale nuclei and small nucleoli lie in collagenous stroma with thin-walled vessels. The fascicles infiltrate fat and entrap ducts and lobules at the periphery, and lymphoid aggregates are present at the advancing edge. Mitoses are few, and necrosis is absent. Nuclear beta-catenin is positive, reflecting CTNNB1 or APC mutations, and the cells are SMA-positive and negative for keratins, p63, CD34 and S100. Differentials include fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma (keratin-positive and p63-positive clusters), scar, nodular fasciitis, myofibroblastoma and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma. Management increasingly favours active surveillance or systemic therapy rather than radical surgery.
entities.cyto: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast, often arising from the pectoral fascia, yields hypocellular aspirates with scattered bland spindle cells with oval to elongated nuclei, fine chromatin and small nucleoli, singly and in small fascicles, together with fragments of collagenous stroma and sometimes trapped skeletal muscle or breast tissue. Epithelial cells are absent. Low-grade fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma is the most important differential, requiring cytokeratin and p63 on cell block; nuclear beta-catenin positivity supports fibromatosis. Scar, nodular fasciitis and phyllodes stroma are other mimics. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), bland spindle cell lesion, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast consists of long fascicles of bland spindle cells that infiltrate fat and parenchyma. IHC shows nuclear β-catenin in most cases, reflecting CTNNB1 mutation (sporadic) or APC mutation (FAP/Gardner), together with SMA positivity, variable desmin and negative keratins, p63, CD34 and S100. The key differential is fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma, which is keratin positive (often focal, so use a broad panel including 34βE12 and CK5/6) and p63 positive. Nodular fasciitis (USP6) and myofibroblastoma (CD34+, desmin+) should also be considered. Post-implant and post-surgical cases occur, and CTNNB1 sequencing can help.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; intermediate (rarely metastasising); myofibroblasts with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; ALK rearrangement (ALK IHC+) in ~50%, also ROS1/NTRK fusions.
entities.histo: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT) of the breast is a rare intermediate (rarely metastasising) neoplasm of myofibroblastic spindle cells with a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. It presents as a painless, well-defined or irregular mass. Microscopically there are three patterns, which often coexist. The myxoid or vascular pattern resembles nodular fasciitis, with loose spindle cells and inflammation. The compact spindle cell pattern shows fascicles with a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. The hypocellular fibrous pattern shows scar-like collagen. The spindle cells have vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli, and the inflammation consists of plasma cells, lymphocytes and eosinophils. About half the cases harbour ALK rearrangements and show ALK IHC positivity, and other cases have ROS1, NTRK or other kinase fusions that may be targetable. The cells are SMA-positive and variably positive for desmin and keratin, which is a pitfall. Differentials include IgG4-related mastitis, nodular fasciitis (USP6-positive), desmoid fibromatosis (nuclear beta-catenin), spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (strong keratin and p63 positivity), and lymphoma. Complete excision is the treatment.
entities.cyto: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour of the breast is rare and yields aspirates of moderate cellularity with plump spindle or stellate myofibroblasts with oval nuclei, small nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm, in a myxoid or collagenous background, admixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils. Mild atypia may be seen. Differentials include nodular fasciitis, IgG4-related mastitis, granulomatous mastitis, fibromatosis and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma. ALK immunopositivity on cell block or ALK rearrangement supports the diagnosis, along with SMA. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion with inflammation, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour of the breast consists of myofibroblastic spindle cells in a lymphoplasmacytic background. IHC shows SMA positivity, variable desmin and keratin, and ALK positivity in about half of cases, reflecting ALK rearrangement (various partners), confirmed by FISH or NGS. ROS1, NTRK, PDGFRB or RET fusions occur in ALK-negative cases and can be targeted. The epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma variant shows nuclear membrane or perinuclear ALK staining (RANBP2-ALK). Separate it from IgG4-related mastitis (IgG4 ratio), nodular fasciitis (USP6), fibromatosis (nuclear β-catenin) and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma (strong keratins, p63+).

entities.entity: Other intermediate soft-tissue tumours in breast
entities.variants: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (breast skin; COL1A1::PDGFB, CD34+); solitary fibrous tumour (NAB2::STAT6, STAT6 nuclear); atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma (MDM2 amplification); giant cell tumour of soft tissue
entities.remarks: Rare in breast; classify per WHO Soft Tissue & Bone Tumours 5th ed; ALT component in phyllodes does not by itself upgrade to malignant phyllodes.
entities.histo: Other intermediate soft-tissue tumours of the breast are rare and are classified according to WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans of the breast skin shows uniform spindle cells in a tight storiform pattern infiltrating subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern, with CD34 positivity and a COL1A1::PDGFB fusion. Its fibrosarcomatous transformation shows herringbone fascicles. Solitary fibrous tumour is a circumscribed tumour of bland spindle cells in a patternless arrangement with staghorn haemangiopericytoma-like vessels, positive for CD34 and nuclear STAT6, reflecting NAB2::STAT6. Atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma shows atypical stromal cells within mature fat, with MDM2 amplification. When it occurs as a component of a phyllodes tumour, it does not by itself make the tumour malignant. Giant cell tumour of soft tissue shows nodules of mononuclear cells with osteoclast-like giant cells. Differentials include myofibroblastoma (desmin-positive, RB1 loss), metaplastic carcinoma, phyllodes tumour, lipoma and benign fibrous histiocytoma, so thorough sampling and IHC are needed.
entities.cyto: Other intermediate soft tissue tumours in breast, such as solitary fibrous tumour, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma and Kaposi sarcoma, are rare. Aspirates show variable bland to mildly atypical spindle cells in collagenous, myxoid or haemorrhagic backgrounds, features that are non-specific and overlap with phyllodes tumour stroma, metaplastic carcinoma and benign spindle cell lesions. Cell block immunochemistry (STAT6 for SFT, CD34 for DFSP, MUC4 for LGFMS, HHV-8 for Kaposi) and molecular tests are used for classification, which usually requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), spindle cell lesion, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Other intermediate soft tissue tumours of the breast are classified per the WHO soft tissue volume. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the breast skin is CD34 positive (diffuse), factor XIIIa negative, and carries COL1A1-PDGFB fusion (FISH or RT-PCR), which predicts response to imatinib. Solitary fibrous tumour is STAT6 nuclear positive and CD34 positive (NAB2-STAT6). Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is MUC4 positive (FUS-CREB3L2). Kaposiform and other vascular tumours are ERG and CD31 positive. In each case, metaplastic carcinoma should first be excluded with broad keratins and p63, and phyllodes tumour by adequate sampling for an epithelial component.

entities.entity: Metastases to the breast (and secondary tumours)
entities.variants: Contralateral breast carcinoma; melanoma (commonest extramammary source in many series); lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, small cell); ovarian (high-grade serous) carcinoma; gastric/colorectal adenocarcinoma; renal cell carcinoma; neuroendocrine tumours (GI, lung); thyroid carcinoma; sarcomas; alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (adolescents); haematolymphoid (leukaemia/lymphoma) secondary involvement; mesothelioma (direct/metastatic)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; ~0.5–2% of breast malignancies; clues: lack of in situ component, unusual morphology, multiple well-circumscribed nodules; IHC: GATA3, TRPS1, SOX10, mammaglobin, GCDFP-15 (breast) vs TTF-1/napsin A (lung), PAX8/WT1 (ovary), CDX2/SATB2 (GI), SOX10/S100/HMB45/Melan-A (melanoma). TRPS1 highly sensitive for breast including TNBC/metaplastic.
entities.histo: Metastases to the breast account for about 0.5 to 2% of breast malignancies. The commonest sources are the contralateral breast, melanoma, lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma and small cell), ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma, gastrointestinal and renal cell carcinomas, neuroendocrine tumours, thyroid carcinoma and sarcomas, and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma in adolescents. Haematolymphoid malignancies also occur, as does mesothelioma. Clinical clues include a known primary, multiple well-circumscribed nodules and rapid growth. Histological clues include the absence of an in situ component, unusual morphology for breast carcinoma (clear cell, serous papillary or mucinous intestinal types) and prominent lymphovascular involvement. IHC is essential. GATA3, TRPS1, mammaglobin, GCDFP-15 and ER support a breast primary, with TRPS1 being highly sensitive, including in triple-negative and metaplastic tumours. TTF-1 and napsin A suggest lung, PAX8 and WT1 suggest ovary, and CDX2, SATB2 and CK20 suggest the gastrointestinal tract. PAX8 and CA-IX suggest kidney, and SOX10, S100, HMB45 and Melan-A suggest melanoma. Accurate distinction is important because treatment differs fundamentally.
entities.cyto: Metastases to the breast are uncommon, most often from contralateral breast carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, lung carcinoma, ovarian serous carcinoma, gastrointestinal, renal and neuroendocrine tumours, and rhabdomyosarcoma in children. Aspirates show malignant cells whose morphology may suggest the primary, such as pigment and intranuclear inclusions in melanoma, psammoma bodies and papillae in ovarian carcinoma, clear cells in renal carcinoma or small round cells in rhabdomyosarcoma. Absence of DCIS and clinical history are clues. Cell block immunochemistry (GATA3, ER, TTF-1, PAX8, WT1, CDX2, SOX10) is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate surgery. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), with a comment on the likely primary.
entities.ihc: In metastases to the breast, IHC is central to identifying the primary site. Primary breast carcinoma is typically GATA3+, ER+ (in most cases), mammaglobin+ and SOX10+ (in TNBC), and TRPS1+, which is the most sensitive and specific marker, including in TNBC and metaplastic carcinoma. Melanoma is S100, SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 positive. Lung is TTF-1 and napsin A positive. Ovarian serous carcinoma is PAX8 and WT1 positive. GI is CDX2, CK20 and SATB2 positive. Renal is PAX8 and CAIX positive. Neuroendocrine tumours are synaptophysin positive, and lymphoma is CD45 positive. A lack of in-situ carcinoma and an unusual morphology are clues. Pitfalls: GATA3 is also positive in urothelial and other carcinomas, and SOX10 is shared with melanoma.

entities.variants: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (BRCA1 — TNBC/basal-like, medullary pattern; BRCA2 — luminal, male breast cancer); PALB2; Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53; HER2+ early-onset); Cowden / PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (hamartomas, multiple papillomas); hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1 — lobular carcinoma); Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11); ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM); CHEK2; NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1); Lynch syndrome (mismatch-repair genes, minor); Carney complex (myxoid fibroadenomas, ductal adenoma)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th chapter on genetic tumour syndromes of the breast; listed for completeness (not single histological entities); germline testing per guidelines; BRCA-associated tumours eligible for PARP inhibitors.
entities.histo: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes are covered in a WHO 5th edition chapter. They are not single histological entities, but recognising their associated morphology can prompt germline testing. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are typically high-grade, triple-negative and basal-like, often with a medullary pattern, pushing borders and abundant TILs. BRCA2-associated carcinomas are usually luminal, ER-positive tumours and account for a significant proportion of male breast cancers. PALB2 resembles BRCA2. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53) causes early-onset, frequently HER2-positive carcinomas. Cowden or PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome is associated with multiple hamartomas, papillomas and fibroadenomas. Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1) predisposes to invasive lobular carcinoma. Peutz-Jeghers (STK11), ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM), CHEK2, NF1 and Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair genes) confer moderate risk. Carney complex is associated with myxoid fibroadenomas and ductal adenomas. Germline testing follows established clinical criteria, and BRCA-associated tumours may be eligible for PARP inhibitor therapy. Pathologists can flag suggestive morphology, especially triple-negative carcinoma with a medullary pattern in young women and carcinoma in men.
entities.cyto: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PALB2, PTEN and CDH1, are a genetic diagnosis made by germline testing, not by cytology. Cytology of lesions in these patients is reported in the same way as in sporadic cases. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are often high-grade, triple-negative NST carcinomas with marked pleomorphism, necrosis and lymphocytic infiltrate on FNA, while CDH1-associated tumours are lobular. In high-risk patients a benign or atypical cytology should be correlated carefully with MRI and imaging, and there should be a low threshold for core biopsy. Yokohama categories apply to the lesion sampled, not to the syndrome.
entities.ihc: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes are diagnosed by germline testing, not IHC, but tumour phenotype can suggest them. BRCA1-associated tumours are usually high grade, triple-negative and basal-like (CK5/6+, EGFR+), with medullary-like features and dense TILs. BRCA2 and PALB2 tumours are usually ER-positive. CDH1 germline variants give lobular carcinoma (E-cadherin loss) and diffuse gastric cancer. TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) tumours are often HER2-positive at young age. PTEN (Cowden) tumours may show PTEN loss on IHC. MMR deficiency (Lynch) can be screened with MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 IHC. Germline BRCA testing guides PARP inhibitor therapy (olaparib).

entities.entity: Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis (occult breast primary)
entities.remarks: Axillary nodal adenocarcinoma with occult breast primary (GATA3/TRPS1/ER/mammaglobin+); MRI breast; managed as stage II breast cancer.
entities.histo: Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis is diagnosed when an adenocarcinoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma is found in axillary lymph nodes without a clinically or mammographically detectable breast primary. In women this usually represents an occult breast carcinoma. Microscopically the node shows metastatic carcinoma, often IBC-NST-like, sometimes lobular, apocrine or poorly differentiated, with possible extranodal extension. IHC supports a breast origin when GATA3, TRPS1, ER, PR, mammaglobin or GCDFP-15 are positive, and HER2 status is assessed for treatment. Exclusion of other primaries requires markers such as TTF-1 (lung), PAX8 (ovary or kidney), CDX2 (gastrointestinal tract) and SOX10 (melanoma), as well as consideration of lymphoma and skin adnexal carcinoma. Breast MRI detects the primary in a substantial proportion of cases. Mastectomy or whole-breast radiotherapy specimens may reveal small or multifocal carcinomas, and careful sampling is required. Management follows that of node-positive (stage II) breast cancer, with axillary dissection, systemic therapy and breast treatment.
entities.cyto: In carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis (occult breast primary), FNA of the axillary node shows malignant epithelial cells, often in dyscohesive groups and single cells, with morphology resembling breast carcinoma NST or lobular carcinoma, sometimes with intracytoplasmic lumina, in a lymphoid background. Cell block immunochemistry is essential: GATA3, ER, PR, mammaglobin, SOX10 and TRPS1 support a breast origin, while TTF-1, PAX8, CDX2 and others help exclude alternatives; HER2 testing is also possible. Breast MRI is used to search for the primary. Reported as malignant, metastatic carcinoma consistent with breast origin, using the Sydney System for lymph node cytology.
entities.ihc: For carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis, IHC is used to confirm an occult breast primary. Breast origin is supported by TRPS1 positivity, GATA3 positivity, ER and PR positivity, mammaglobin and GCDFP-15 positivity, CK7 positivity and CK20 negativity, with SOX10 often positive in triple-negative tumours. Lung (TTF-1, napsin A), melanoma (S100, SOX10, Melan-A), skin adnexal carcinoma and ovarian (PAX8, WT1) primaries must be excluded. Apocrine tumours are AR+ and GCDFP-15+. ER, PR and HER2 testing per ASCO/CAP and Ki-67 on the nodal metastasis guide treatment as for breast cancer, and breast MRI usually localises the primary. CK5/6 or p40 positivity raises the possibility of squamous carcinoma.

entities.variants: Rosai-Dorfman disease (S100+ histiocytes showing emperipolesis); Langerhans cell histiocytosis; Erdheim-Chester disease
entities.remarks: Rare; Rosai-Dorfman disease of breast mimics carcinoma or mastitis clinically; classified as histiocytic neoplasms in WHO Haematolymphoid 5th ed.
entities.histo: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are rare and are classified according to WHO Haematolymphoid Tumours, 5th edition. Rosai-Dorfman disease is the commonest. It presents as a firm, painless breast mass, with or without lymphadenopathy, and mimics carcinoma or mastitis clinically. Microscopically, it shows alternating pale and dark areas. The pale areas are sheets of large histiocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei with nucleoli, which show emperipolesis of lymphocytes and plasma cells. The dark areas are lymphoid aggregates and plasma cells, accompanied by fibrosis. The histiocytes are positive for S100, CD68, CD163 and OCT2, and negative for CD1a and langerin, and plasma cells may be IgG4-rich. Langerhans cell histiocytosis shows Langerhans cells with grooved, folded nuclei and eosinophils, positive for CD1a, langerin and S100, often with BRAF V600E mutations. Erdheim-Chester disease shows foamy CD68-positive, CD1a-negative and S100-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells and fibrosis, and is BRAF-mutated. Differentials include fat necrosis, granulomatous mastitis, IgG4-related mastitis, granular cell tumour, lymphoma and histiocytoid carcinoma, which is keratin-positive.
entities.cyto: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are rare. In Rosai-Dorfman disease, aspirates show numerous large histiocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei, showing emperipolesis of lymphocytes and plasma cells, in a lymphoplasmacytic background; the histiocytes are S100 and CD68/CD163 positive and CD1a negative. Langerhans cell histiocytosis shows grooved, folded Langerhans cells with eosinophils (CD1a, langerin, S100 positive). Erdheim-Chester disease shows foamy histiocytes with Touton giant cells and fibrosis. Differentials include granulomatous mastitis, fat necrosis, lymphoma and lipid-rich carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 3 with a comment suggesting the entity, and immunochemistry on cell block.
entities.ihc: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are diagnosed with IHC. Rosai–Dorfman disease shows large histiocytes with emperipolesis that are S100 positive, CD68 positive, CD163 positive and OCT2 positive, with nuclear cyclin D1, CD1a negativity and langerin (CD207) negativity, in a plasma-cell-rich background in which IgG4-positive cells may be increased. Langerhans cell histiocytosis is CD1a positive, langerin positive and S100 positive, and often BRAF V600E mutated (VE1 IHC). Erdheim–Chester disease shows foamy histiocytes that are CD68+, CD163+ and factor XIIIa+, with CD1a and S100 negative or weak, and BRAF V600E or MAP2K1 mutations. All are keratin negative, which separates them from histiocytoid or lobular carcinoma, the key clinical and morphological mimic.
